("What is the matter with you? Why do you not help one another?")(37:25) means, "This Day, you shall not have a refuge from Us. There will be no helpers for them nor ransom accepted from them even if they had the fill of the heavens and earths.

**Good deeds alone.**

In relation to this office, they were granted many other blessings and facilities: victory over their enemies, forgiveness of their sins, special help in times of peril, divine provision for their physical needs, and so on. But such matters as salvation are not a hereditary right of any group. On the Day of Judgement people will be judged individually, according to their actions. Protect yourselves against the Day of Judgement by following Allah’s instructions and staying away from what He has prohibited. On that day no soul will be able to help another in any way, and no pleading on their behalf will be accepted to benefit them or protect them from harm, except with Allah’s permission, and no ransom will be taken, even if it were to be the earth filled with gold. Act for God will surely see your actions and [so will] His Messenger [9:105] and He said And you are not occupied with any busi ness... but We are witnesses over you when you are engaged therein [10:61]. On the Day of the Resurrection no intercession will be heard except for the one whom the Real has commanded to intercede for Him.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Verse 47 asks the Israelites to call to their minds the blessing of Allah, so that the recognition of the benefits they have received may induce them to be thankful to Allah and thus to obey Him. The verse is addressed to the Jews contemporaneous with the Holy Prophet while the blessing had been received by their forefathers. The point is that when a man receives a special favour, his children and grand children too usually partake of the benefits flowing from it; in this sense, the Jews who are being addressed may be said to have received the blessing themselves. The day referred to in verse 48 is the Day of Judgment. As for no one being able to suffice another on that day, the phrase should be understood in the sense of one man paying the dues on behalf of another man. Let us, for example, suppose that a man is found wanting in the performance of obligatory acts of worship like Salah and Sawm (fasting), and another man should suggest that his own prayers and fasts may be transferred to the account of the former in order to make up the deficiency. Such a transaction shall not be possible on that day. Ransom, of course, means the money paid for securing the release of a criminal - this too shall be out of the question. In short, none of the ways of receiving help possible in this world will be effective in the other world unless one possesses 'Iman . On the basis of verse 48, the Mu'tazilah and some other groups of a more recent origin have denied the possibility of all intercession in favour of Muslims.

49.text:
"Remember how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh" is the second call to memory in these verses, and it is more concrete than the first. The favour is now a particular act of rescue, and the verse names the people from whom the rescue came. "who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women" describes the suffering in plain terms, and the verse does not soften it, because the scale of the favour depends on the scale of the harm. The phrase about the women is the other half of that cruelty, and it is stated without comment. "That was a severe test from your Lord" then gives the meaning of the whole episode, and the word test is the key. The rescue was not only a deliverance, it was a trial, something that tested the people by what they had suffered. The verse before opened the account of the favours, and this verse gives the first favour in full. The name of the people is given with the act, so the rescue is tied to a particular community and not to a general hope of deliverance, and the reader is taught that the favours of the past have a shape that can be traced in the story itself. The reader sees the rescue and the suffering together, and is asked to hold them both in the same frame when the verse after names the sea.

**The sons and the females.**

But he would spare the females, as there was nothing to fear from them, and, moreover, they could, on growing up, serve as maid-servants. (slaying your sons) in their tender years (and sparing), using (your women) who were of age: It was also said that it means, "They used to exaggerate in tormenting you" according to Al-Qurtubi.

**The prediction made to Pharaoh.**

Someone had made a prediction to the Pharaoh that a child was going to be born among the Israelites who would destroy his kingship. Now, with Verse 49 begins the account of these favours. And remember when We delivered you your forefathers the address here and henceforth directed to those living at the time of the our Prophet is about how God blessed their forefathers and is intended to remind them of God’s grace so that they might believe; from the folk of Pharaoh who were visiting you with that is making you taste evil chastisement of the worst kind the sentence here is a circumstantial qualifier referring to the person of the pronoun suffixed in najjaynākum ‘We delivered you’; slaughtering your newly-born sons this is explaining what has just been said; and sparing retaining your women doing so because of the saying of some of their priests that a child born among the Israelites shall bring about the end of your rule Pharaoh; and for you therein chastisement or deliverance was a tremendous trial a test or a grace from your Lord.

**What the great trial was.**

What the verse refers to as "a great trial" is either the slaughter of the sons - which was a calamity, and it is the quality of patience that is tested in a calamity - or the deliverance from the people of the Pharaoh - which was a blessing, and it is the quality of thankfulness which is tested when one receives a blessing. (That was a tremendous trial from your Lord), a tremendous calamity from your Lord; and it is also said this means: a tremendous blessing. And for you therein was a tremendous trial from your Lord:

**Blessing and trial together.**

It is said that [it was] a great blessing niʿmatun ʿaẓīma and a severe trial miḥnatun shadīda. This misled later generations of Jews into thinking that they were God’s chosen people, and were assured of salvation in the next world. But such matters as salvation are not a hereditary right of any group.

**The children of Israel were patient.**

The children of Israel were patient in enduring injury from Pharaoh and his people so He appointed prophets from among them and made them kings. When you were saved from the oppression of Pharaoh and his people, it was a great test for you from your Lord, to see if you would be thankful. Ibn Jarir commented that this part of the Ayah means, "Our saving your fathers from the torment that they suffered by the hand of Pharaoh, is a great blessing from your Lord.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Verse 47 had spoken of the special favours shown to the Israelites by Allah. And (remember) when We delivered you from Fir'awn's (Pharaoh) people, who were afflicting you with a horrible torment, killing your sons and sparing your women, and therein was a mighty trial from your Lord And (remember) when We separated the sea for you and saved you and drowned Fir'awn's (Pharaoh) people while you were watching The Children of Israel were saved from Pharaoh and His Army Who drowned So, he began slaughtering all the male infants as soon as they were born. So, even this leniency was motivated by self-interest. The next verse gives us the details about this deliverance. Allah said to the Children of Israel, "Remember My favor on you (And (remember) when We delivered you from Fir'awn's (Pharaoh) people, who were afflicting you with a horrible torment,) meaning, 'I - Allah - saved you from them and delivered you from their hands in the company of Musa, after they subjected you to horrible torture.' This favor came after the cursed Pharaoh had a dream in which he saw a fire emerge from Bayt Al-Maqdis (Bayt al-Maqdis), and then the fire entered the houses of the Coptics in Egypt, with the exception of the Children of Israel. Its purport was that his kingship would be toppled by a man among the Children of Israel. It was also said that some of Pharaoh's entourage said that the Children of Israel were expecting a man among them to arise who would establish a state for them. We will mention the Hadith on this subject when we explain Surat Ta Ha , Allah willing. After the dream, Pharaoh ordered that every newborn male among the Children of Israel be killed and that the girls be left alone. He also commanded that the Children of Israel be given tasks of hard labor and assigned the most humiliating jobs. The torment here refers to killing the male infants. In Surat Ibrahim this meaning is clearly mentioned, (Who were afflicting you with horrible torment, and were slaughtering your sons and letting your women live.)(14:6). We will explain this Ayah in the beginning of Surat Al-Qasas , Allah willing, and our reliance and trust are with Him. (who were afflicting you) is, "They humiliated you," as Abu 'Ubaydah stated.

50.text:
"And remember when We parted the sea, rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh's people before your very eyes" is the third and most vivid of the favours, and the sentence is built as a sequence of three acts. The first is the parting of the sea, which opens a way where none existed. The second is the rescue, which is the favour done to the people who are walking through. The third is the drowning, which is the same event seen from the other side, and the verse puts it in the same sentence so that the reader does not forget who was saved and who was lost. "before your very eyes" is the closing phrase, and it is the one that makes the witness personal. The verse does not claim that the event was carried to them by others. It names that they saw it, so the favour is theirs by sight and not by hearsay. The verse before named the rescue from the people of Pharaoh, and this verse names the place where that rescue happened, which is the sea. The verse after moves from the favours to the story of the calf, so this verse is the last of the three acts of deliverance before the account turns to the failure that followed them.

**The sea that parted.**

And remember when We divided split in two for you on account of you the sea such that you were able to cross it and escape from your enemy; and We delivered you from drowning and drowned Pharaoh’s folk his people with him while you were beholding the sea crashing down on top of them. Allah commanded the sea to split, and make way for Sayyidna Musa and his people. And (remember) when We delivered you from Fir'awn's (Pharaoh) people, who were afflicting you with a horrible torment, killing your sons and sparing your women, and therein was a mighty trial from your Lord And (remember) when We separated the sea for you and saved you and drowned Fir'awn's (Pharaoh) people while you were watching.

**Pursued to the water.**

On their way, they came across a sea while the Pharaoh was behind him with his army in hot pursuit. But when the Pharaoh and his army followed them into the sea, it gathered the water back so that the Pharaoh and his men were drowned then and there. (And (remember) when We separated the sea for you and saved you and drowned Fir'awn's (Pharaoh) people while you were watching) means, 'After We saved you from Fir'awn and you escaped with Musa; Fir'awn went out in your pursuit and We parted the sea for you.' Allah mentioned this story in detail, as we will come to know, Allah willing.

**Saving and drowning.**

(And (remember) when We delivered you from Fir'awn's (Pharaoh) people, who were afflicting you with a horrible torment,) meaning, 'I - Allah - saved you from them and delivered you from their hands in the company of Musa, after they subjected you to horrible torture.' This favor came after the cursed Pharaoh had a dream in which he saw a fire emerge from Bayt Al-Maqdis (Bayt al-Maqdis), and then the fire entered the houses of the Coptics in Egypt, with the exception of the Children of Israel. Ibn Jarir commented that this part of the Ayah means, "Our saving your fathers from the torment that they suffered by the hand of Pharaoh, is a great blessing from your Lord. Then Allah mentioned the favour of saving them from drowning and the drowning of Pharaoh and his folk, saying (And when We brought you through) split (the sea and rescued you) from drowning,(and drowned the folk of Pharaoh) and his folk (in your sight) while you were looking at them, three days later. Remember Allah’s favour in saving you when He parted the sea and made it a dry path for you to go through, while drowning your enemies, Pharaoh and his followers, before your very eyes, as you looked on.

**Signs before their eyes.**

When [the children of Israel] saw these manifest signs in the splitting of the sea and the drowning of the people of Pharaoh they were seized with doubt and said They did not drown even though they were cast into the sea but the children of Israel did see them drowning. For those who are sharper in the perceptive faculty the matter will be more subtle for them and the allusions within it more abundant. [The Prophet] said I was given the all-comprehensive words jawāmiʿ al-kalim and then the speech kalām was shortened for me. This misled later generations of Jews into thinking that they were God’s chosen people, and were assured of salvation in the next world.

**The community that followed later.**

On the other hand in this community because of their being foremost in their belief in the Messenger of God and because of the power of their perceptive faculties one youth said It is as if I was with the people of the garden exchanging visits and as if I was with the people of the fire clamoring to one another and as if I saw the throne of my Lord in plain sight. When We divided for you the sea and We delivered you and drowned Pharaoh's folk while you were beholding. On the Day of Judgement people will be judged individually, according to their actions. He, in his capacity as a messenger of Allah, continued efforts for a long time to make the Pharaoh and his people see Truth, but when they persisted in their denial, Allah commanded him to take the Israelites along with him and leave Egypt surreptitiously.

51.text:
"And remember when We appointed forty nights for Moses" opens with the memory again, and this time the memory is of an appointment, a fixed period set apart by the Lord for a particular purpose. The verse does not say that Moses went up to receive the Scripture on a whim. It names that the nights were appointed, which means they had a limit and an end, and a people who waited for them were waiting for a term that had been set. "then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully" is the turn, and it is joined to the appointment by the word "then", so the failure follows the time of waiting directly. The phrase "in his absence" is the key to the whole sentence. The people did not turn away while Moses was in their midst. They turned while he was out of sight, and the verse makes the absence the occasion of the fault. The closing words describe the judgement on what they did, and the verse does not soften it or explain it away. It names the act and the wrong in the same breath, so the wrong is not a slip of the mind but a deed done with the Scripture still on its way. The verse before ended with the favour of the sea, and this verse sets a second favour beside it, the appointment and the Scripture, so the reader sees the gift and the failure side by side.

**The forty nights.**

And (remember) when We appointed for Musa (Moses) forty nights, and (in his absence) you took the calf (for worship), and you were Zalimun (polytheists and wrongdoers)Then after that We forgave you so that you might be grateful And (remember) when We gave Musa the Scripture (the Tawrah) and the criterion (of right and wrong) so that you may be guided aright. And when We appointed for wā‘adnā or wa‘adnā Moses forty nights at the end of which We shall give him the Torah for you to implement then you took to yourselves the calf the one which the Samaritan fashioned for you as a god after him that is after he departed for Our appointment and you were evildoers for taking it in worship because you directed your worship to the wrong place. (And when We appointed for Moses forty nights) by giving him the scripture, (and then you chose the calf), you worshipped the calf, (when he had gone from you) to the mountain, (and you were wrong-doers) harmful both to yourselves and others.

**The calf of gold.**

He fashioned the figure of a calf out of gold or silver, and put into it some of the dust which he had picked up from under the hooves of the horse of Jibra'il (the Archangel Gabriel), at the time when the Pharaoh and his army had been drowned by the Archangel. When the Pharaoh had been drowned, the Israelites, according to one report, went back to Egypt, or, according to another, began to live somewhere else. They said This is your God and the God of Moses but he has forgotten [20:88]. [On the other hand] the community of Muḥammad the Chosen spent many years with their prophet.

**Taking the Scripture.**

(And (remember) when We gave Musa the Scripture) means, the Tawrah,. He gladly obeyed the Commandment, and was granted the Torah . Also, remember that the forty nights appointed to Moses were from the blessings of Allah, in which the revelation of the Torah, with its light and guidance, was completed.

**The office Moses was given.**

He selected them for a special task: they were to receive God’s scriptures and pass His commandments on to the rest of mankind. In relation to this office, they were granted many other blessings and facilities: victory over their enemies, forgiveness of their sins, special help in times of peril, divine provision for their physical needs, and so on. But such matters as salvation are not a hereditary right of any group.

**The brother entrusted with the people.**

It is said that Moses entrusted his community to his brother saying Take my place with my people [7:142]. But he was ordered to continue to worship for ten days more, because he had broken his fast after a month and thus lost the special odour which rises from the mouth of a fasting person and which is very pleasant to Allah; so Allah commanded him to fast for ten additional days and regain that odour. Allah then said, "Remember My favor on you when I forgave you for worshipping the calf. When Moses withdrew from the community for forty days they took the calf as their object of worship and were pleased with that. Yet you went and worshipped the calf during that period, which made you into wrongdoers.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Verse 51 refers to other incidents in the same story. Having at last found a peaceful existence, they now wished they could receive a Shari ah, or a religious code of laws, from Allah which they should follow. Allah answered the prayer of Sayyidna Musa and promised that if he came to the Mount Tur (Sinai) and devoted himself to worship for a month, he would receive a Divine Book. Thus, Sayyidna Musa completed forty days of total fasting and devotion. Sinai, something very odious happened to the Israelites. The ignorant among the Israelites were so impressed that they started worshipping it. Verse 51 calls them "unjust" for having committed this sin, for 'injustice' lies in putting things in the improper places, and idolatory is essentially just that. " This happened after Musa went to the meeting place with his Lord at the end of that period which was forty days. These forty days were mentioned in Surat Al-A'raf, when Allah said, (And We appointed for Musa thirty nights and added (to the period) ten (more)(7:142). It was said that these days were during the month of Dhul-Qa'dah plus the first ten days in Dhul-Hijjah, after the Children of Israel were delivered from Fir'awn and they safely crossed the sea. (And the criterion) that is that which differentiates between truth and falsehood, guidance and deviation.

52.text:
"Even then We still forgave you so perhaps you would be grateful" is the reversal of the sentence before, and the reversal is what the verse is built around. "Even then" puts the pardon after the act, so the Lord's mercy is not held back until the wrong is undone but comes in the middle of it. The word "still" carries the same weight: the forgiveness is not withdrawn because the people sinned, it is given in spite of what they did. "so perhaps you would be grateful" then gives the purpose of the pardon, and the purpose is gratitude rather than relief. The verse does not say the people earned the pardon. It names the pardon was given so that they would be thankful, which turns the forgiveness into an opening for a new relationship. The verse before named the calf and the wrong, and this verse names what came after it, which is pardon before the account of any punishment. The sentence is short, and it carries the whole mercy of the passage in its last phrase.

**The pardon after the calf.**

Then We pardoned you erasing your sins after that act of worship so that you might be thankful for Our favour upon you. Then Allah forgave you when you asked for forgiveness, and did not take you to account for it, so that you might be thankful to Him, worshipping Him in the best way and doing as He instructed. (Then, even after that), after you worshipped the calf, (We pardoned you), left you alone and did not exterminate you (in order that ye might give thanks), so that you might give thanks to Us for pardoning you.

**Taubah and the forgiveness.**

The Israelites were forgiven only when they had offered Taubah (repentance), as recounted in Verse 54. In saying that they were pardoned so that they might learn gratefulness, the present verse employs the Arabic word La lla which indicates expectation. Allah then said, "Remember My favor on you when I forgave you for worshipping the calf.

**Being thankful.**

Then We pardoned you after that so that you might be thankful. The children of Israel worshiped the calf so God most high said Then We pardoned you after that. In the present context it does not mean that Allah had or could have any doubt or misgiving about this or any other matter; what the word implies here is just that when a man receives a pardon, the onlookers may expect him to feel grateful.

**The forty days in the month.**

It was said that these days were during the month of Dhul-Qa'dah plus the first ten days in Dhul-Hijjah, after the Children of Israel were delivered from Fir'awn and they safely crossed the sea. And (remember) when We appointed for Musa (Moses) forty nights, and (in his absence) you took the calf (for worship), and you were Zalimun (polytheists and wrongdoers)Then after that We forgave you so that you might be grateful And (remember) when We gave Musa the Scripture (the Tawrah) and the criterion (of right and wrong) so that you may be guided aright. (And (remember) when We gave Musa the Scripture) means, the Tawrah,.

**The office of the Scripture.**

He selected them for a special task: they were to receive God’s scriptures and pass His commandments on to the rest of mankind. But such matters as salvation are not a hereditary right of any group. On the Day of Judgement people will be judged individually, according to their actions. The quickness [with which God] pardoned such a grave sin indicates the lesser weight of those who were pardoned.

53.text:
And remember when We gave Moses the Scripture carries the memory forward from the calf to the book. The verse does not say the Scripture came as a reward for anything. It says that it came, and the word "remember" asks the reader to hold the gift beside the wrong just named, so that the two sit in the same frame. The Scripture here is the Torah given to Moses, and the sources take it to be the book of the law that the Children of Israel were to live by. The clause that follows, "the standard to distinguish between right and wrong that perhaps you would be rightly guided", carries the word the verse uses for the criterion and tells you what the book is for. The standard is a measure by which one thing can be told from another. The people who had just worshipped the calf had lost the ability to tell the true from the false, and the book is given as the means of getting it back. The clause closes the sentence with the purpose, and the word "perhaps" in it is not a doubt about the Lord's intention. It is the form of an aim, a wish on the Lord's side that the people choose the guidance the book offers, and the choice is left to them. So the sentence moves from memory, to gift, to the nature of the gift, to its purpose, and each phrase is a step on the same road. The verse before, 2:52, ended with a pardon given so that the people would be thankful. This verse carries that thanks forward into the means of guidance, so the reader sees the Scripture as the form the gratitude is to take. The sentence is also a point of return in the account. The people have been shown the calf and the pardon, and now they are shown what they were given in place of the image they had made, a book to judge by rather than a figure to bow to.

**What the Scripture was.**

The sources agree on the identity of the book. One short commentary reads the Scripture as the Torah, and the Torah is named again in the commentary on the same verse, which places the gift of the book after the forty nights and the forgiveness, so that the order of events is the order of the verses. The commentary on the Torah given to Sayyidna Mūsā makes the same identification and adds that the Torah is a book of Allah and not a human writing. That is the first thing the verse establishes. The book is not the product of the people's reflection, and it is not a set of customs that grew up among them. It is given from outside, to a prophet, and it is given to a people who had just shown how badly they judge when left to themselves. The gift of the book is therefore a correction to the calf and to the forty nights, and the sources read the sequence as deliberate.

**Furqān, the criterion.**

The word the translation renders as the standard is furqān, and the commentary on it is the longest in the block. The commentary on the Torah gives three readings that the sources allow. It may mean the rulings of the law found in the Torah, since the law settles the differences that arise over belief and over right action. It may mean the signs and miracles that decide between a true claim and a false one in a way that can be seen. Or it may mean the Torah itself, which is at once the book of Allah and the instrument by which truth is separated from falsehood. The commentary on the Torah, in the sense it gives the word, takes it as what differentiates between truth and falsehood, guidance and deviation. The lawful-and-unlawful commentary narrows the sense to the lawful and the unlawful, the commands and the prohibitions, and adds other things that the book carries. These are not three separate books. They are three ways of naming one function, which is to make a difference that can be acted on. The verse uses the word once, and the commentaries keep returning to it because a criterion is useful only if it can be applied in practice.

**The guidance it was for.**

The verse ends with the hope of guidance, and the sources take that hope as the true purpose of the book. The short commentary treats the giving as one of the blessings of Allah, and places the purpose in the guidance a person draws from the book to the truth. the commentary on the forty days, in the same vein, reads the phrase so that you may be guided aright as set after escaping the sea, which links the book to the deliverance that came before it and to the land that follows. The Qurʾān in the other chapter of al-Aʿrāf says the Scripture was an enlightenment, a guidance and a mercy, and the sources bring that into this verse as a reminder that guidance is the purpose and mercy is its form. The commentary on piety gives the content of the guidance in plain terms: to worship God alone, to believe in Him without having seen Him, to fear the Day of Judgement, to take only the pure things of the earth, and to keep oneself from sin. It is those who take up this way of life, the source says, who will prosper in the next world. The commentary does not separate the guidance of the book from the way of life that the book requires.

**Remember the order of favours.**

The verse is the third of a short run that begins with the forty nights, and the run is one account read in sequence. the commentary on the forty days quotes Allah's own speech, remember My favour upon you when I forgave you for worshipping the calf, and places the appointment of Moses at the end of the forty days that were added to the thirty nights mentioned in another chapter. He also gives the month as Dhū al-Qaʿdah with the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah. The sources do not claim more about the calendar than the verses themselves give, and the point the commentary keeps is the order: the people were delivered, they worshipped the calf in the absence, they were pardoned, and then the book was given. Read in that order, the book is the answer to the calf rather than a separate matter, and the reader is asked to see the sequence before taking the lesson from it.

**Discernment in the heart.**

The allusive reading of the verse, moves the criterion from the book to the inward faculty that the book is meant to form. The commentator says that the discernment was given to Moses's people outwardly, and that the same discernment was placed in the inwardness of the community of the Prophet. He describes the discernment as something that appears in a person's inner life, and that purifies the aspiration of the one who has it. These sayings are not a ruling and they settle nothing about the law. They are a reading of what the criterion does to the reader who receives it, and the commentary is careful to present them as allusion rather than as a claim about what the book says. Read beside the legal sense, the allusion adds one thing: a book that separates truth from falsehood outside a person has to be matched by a faculty inside him that can use it, and the verse asks for both.

54.text:
The verse opens on the speaker and the people he is speaking to: "And remember when Moses said to his people". The calf is what gives him the need to address them at all, and this is not a voice from outside the community but the prophet speaking to his own folk, the ones who made the image and bowed before it. "O my people!" comes first, and the phrase carries affection inside the rebuke that follows. "Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf" is the charge, and the verb is turned back on the people, so the wrong is not done to Moses or to the Lord but to themselves. The charge names the act, worship of the calf, and places the injury in the soul of the one who worshipped. "so turn in repentance to your Creator and execute the calf-worshippers among yourselves" is the remedy, and it is a hard one. The turn to repentance is the way back, and the words about execution are the cost the people are asked to carry as part of returning. The verse does not pretend the way back is easy. "That is best for you in the sight of your Creator" gives the reason the hard remedy is the better course: it is best in the sight of the One who made them, which is the measure that counts. "Then He accepted your repentance" turns the sentence from command to result. The people did what was asked, and the Lord accepted it. "Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful" closes the verse on the Lord's nature, the one who receives the return and is merciful in receiving it. The verse before gave the book as the standard, and this verse shows the people using that standard in the hard hour: they are asked to judge their own offence by it and to return.

**Who was to be killed.**

(and kill (the guilty) among yourselves) let those who did not worship the calf kill those who worshipped it. This was the repentance required from the Children of Israel for worshipping the calf. (to your Bari' (Creator) alerts the Children of Israel to the enormity of their error and means, "Repent to He Who created you after you associated others with Him in worship."

**Turning in repentance to the Creator.**

Moses told you to ask for forgiveness and repent to your Creator by some of you killing others, because turning to Him in this way was better for you than persisting in disbelief, which would lead to an eternity in the fire of Hell. This verse describes the special mode of offering their Taubah (repentance) which was prescribed for the Israelites in this situation, -- that is to say, those who had not indulged in the worship of the golden calf should execute those who had.

**Taubah, and the sins of the Shari'ah.**

Similarly, in the Islamic Shari'ah too, certain major sins necessarily entail capital punishment even when the sinner has offered this Taubah -- for example, life in return for a life in the case of intentional homicide, or death by stoning in the case of adultery established through proper evidence. Then the Israelites acted upon this divine commandments, they became worthy of receiving the mercy and favour of Allah in the other world. True piety is to worship God alone, to believe in Him though one has not seen Him, to live in fear of Judgement Day, to subsist on the pure things of the earth, to prevent whomsoever one can from falling into sin.

**What the calf-worshippers did.**

(And when Moses said unto his people: O my people! Ye have wronged yourselves) harmed yourselves (by your choosing of the calf) by worshipping the calf; and when Moses was then asked what to do, he said to them: (so turn in penitence to your Creator), again they asked him how to turn in penitence to Allah, and he said: And when Moses said to his people those who worshipped the calf ‘My people you have done wrong against yourselves by your taking the golden calf for a god; now turn to your Creator away from that worship of the calf and slay one another that is let the innocent of you slay the guilty; That slaughter will be better for you in your Creator’s sight’ who made it easier for you to accomplish this and sent down a dark cloud over you so that none of you was able to see the other and show him mercy such that almost seventy thousand of you were killed; and He will turn to you relenting before your turning in repentance; truly He is the Relenting the Merciful.

**The Lord's acceptance of the return.**

So, you did this with Allah’s approval, and He forgave you, for He is Forgiving and Merciful with His servants. "Take care not to suppose that your worship of the calf has harmed the majesty of the Self-Sufficient or that it is a defect for His kingship and lordhood. Sahl ʿAbdallāh Tustarī said, "God spoke to Moses at Mount Sinai, and the exaltedness of the Lord God's speech made that mountain like carnelian.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Allah then mentioned the story of Moses with his people, saying: Also, remember that Allah’s allowing you to ask His forgiveness for worshipping the calf, when Moses ﷺ told you that you had wronged yourselves by taking the calf as a god and worshipping it, were from the blessings of Allah. When Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged your souls by taking up the calf, so kill your own souls! It is those who adopt this way of life who will be successful in the next world. Verily, you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf. So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves (the innocent kill the wrongdoers among you), that will be better for you with your Creator. (That) penitence and killing (will be best for you with your Creator and He will relent towards you) He will forgive you. Rather, the harm and bad fortune belong to you. Truly, He is the One Who accepts repentance, the Most Merciful (Lo! He is the Relenting) towards the penitent, (the Merciful) towards any that die repentant. If something bad has happened, it has happened to you by your being held back from a Lord like Him. Otherwise, He has plenty of servants like you. Moses' turned his gaze to himself: 'Who is like me? For the God of the world and the world's folk is talking to me without intermediary, and my standing place has turned into carnelian!' "God did not let that pass. What do you see?' "Moses looked around and saw a thousand mountains of carnelian like Mount Sinai, on each mountain a man in the form of Moses, wearing a blanket like him, a hat on his head, a staff in hand, and talking to the Lord of the universe. The Children of Israel kill each other in Repentance (And when they regretted and saw that they had gone astray, they (repented and) said: "If our Lord does not have mercy upon us and forgive us")(7:149). " Abu 'Al-'Aliyah, Sa'id bin Jubayr and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas commented on, (So turn in repentance to your Bari') that it means, "To your Creator. An-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded Ibn 'Abbas saying, "Allah told the Children of Israel that their repentance would be to slay by the sword every person they meet, be he father or son. Those were guilty whom Musa and Harun were not aware of their guilt, they admitted their sin and did as they were ordered. So Allah forgave both the killer and the one killed. " This is part of the Hadith about the trials that we will mention in Surat Ta Ha, Allah willing. Ibn Jarir narrated that Ibn 'Abbas said, "Musa said to his people, Allah ordered Musa to command his people to kill each other. He ordered those who worshipped the calf to sit down and those who did not worship the calf to stand holding knives in their hands. When they started killing them, a great darkness suddenly overcame them. After the darkness lifted, they had killed seventy thousand of them. Those who were killed among them were forgiven, and those who remained alive were also forgiven."

55.text:
"And remember when you said, O Moses!" turns the address to the people again, this time in their own voice, and what they put into words is a demand. The speech is addressed to Moses by name, so the demand is made to the one who has just brought them the Scripture, in his own presence. "We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes" is the whole claim, set down in the first person, so the reader hears them making it. The demand is not for a sign that might confirm the message. It asks to see the Lord directly and openly, and the sentence joins belief to that sight, so that belief is made conditional on something they have set. "so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on" is the answer, and the verse makes the answer a thing that happened in plain view. The phrase "while you were looking on" is the key, because it is the watching that is punished, not the speaking alone. They were looking when it struck, and the verse does not let the reader forget that the people were present at their own judgement. The verse before ended with the return accepted, and this verse goes back to an earlier stage of the same people, when they were still refusing the one who brought them the message. Read in order, the two verses show the same community at two moments, a refusal and then a return, and the sources keep both in view.

**Seeing Allah with their eyes.**

(And (remember) when you said: "O Musa ! We shall never believe in you until we see Allah plainly.") means, "Publicly", "So that we gaze at Allah. Demanding to see the Essence without divine blessing is an open act of sacrilege which is one of the signs of distance and misery whereas attest ing to the attribute of [divine] governance in the unveilings of might as linked to the kindnesses of nearness is one of the marks of communion and the tokens of felicity.

**The thunderbolt and the watching.**

(While you were looking) means, "Some of them were struck with lightning while others were watching. Al-Qurtubi said that this is what is correct, because, he said, although the Children of Israel witnessed these tremendous calamities and incidents, that did not mean that they were not responsible for fulfilling the commandments any more. Also, remember when you shamelessly addressed Moses ﷺ, saying that you would not believe him until you saw Allah with your own eyes, in the open before you, and the lightning struck you and killed you, whilst some of you looked at the others.

**The Torah brought down from the mountain.**

Then Sayyidna Musa (Moses) brought the Torah from Mount Tur (Sinai) and presented it to the Israelites as the book of Allah, some of them were insolent enough to say that they could not believe it until and unless Allah Himself told them in so many words. With the permission of Allah, Sayyidna Musa replied that even this condition would be fulfilled, if they went with him to Mount Tur . But they promised that they would be finally convinced if they could see Allah with their own eyes.

**Hearing the words of Allah.**

Arriving there, they heard the words of Allah with their own ears. (Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might be grateful), and said, "Musa said to them, 'Take the Book of Allah.' They said, 'No.' He said, 'What is the matter with you' They said, 'The problem is that we died and came back to life.' He said, 'Take the Book of Allah.' They said, 'No.' So Allah sent some angels who made the mountain topple over them."

**The demand made in ignorance.**

Surely when they spoke from ignorance without any sense whatsoever of shame the convulsion and the thunderbolt blast overtook them. True piety is to worship God alone, to believe in Him though one has not seen Him, to live in fear of Judgement Day, to subsist on the pure things of the earth, to prevent whomsoever one can from falling into sin. It is those who adopt this way of life who will be successful in the next world.

**What else the same passage holds.**

And when you said having gone out with Moses to apologise before God for your worship of the calf and having heard what he had said to you; ‘O Moses we will not believe you till we see God openly’ with our own eyes; and the thunderbolt the shout took you and you died while you were beholding what was happening to you. The Israelites chose seventy men for this purpose. We shall never believe in you until we see Allah plainly. " But you were seized with a bolt of lightning while you were looking Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might be grateful Now, in their perversity, they invented a new ruse. It was not enough, they said, to hear the speech, for they could not be sure whether it was Allah Himself who had spoken to them or someone else. Since it is beyond the power of a living being to be able to see Allah in the physical world, they had to pay for their impertinence, and were killed by a thunderbolt -- the next verse reports their death. The Best among the Children of Israel ask to see Allah; their subsequent Death and Resurrection Allah said, 'Remember My favor on you for resurrecting you after you were seized with lightning when you asked to see Me directly, which neither you nor anyone else can bear or attain.' This was said by Ibn Jurayj. " Also, 'Urwah bin Ruwaym said that Allah's statement, " Allah resurrected those, and struck the others with lightning. (But you were seized with a bolt of lightning) saying; "They died, and Musa stood up crying and supplicating to Allah, 'O Lord! What should I say to the Children of Israel when I go back to them after You destroyed the best of them, (If it had been Your will, You could have destroyed them and me before; would You destroy us for the deeds of the foolish ones among us)' Allah revealed to Musa that these seventy men were among those who worshipped the calf.

56.text:
"Then We brought you back to life after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful" is the reversal of the thunderbolt, and it is stated in one sentence with its purpose attached. "Then" joins the restoring to the striking before it, so the life given back follows the death directly. The word "after your death" names the state from which they were brought, and the verse does not hide that it was a real death and not a faint. "so that perhaps you would be grateful" gives the aim, and the aim is gratitude again, the same word that closed the pardon in the verse before. The verse does not say that they deserved the life. It states that the life was given so that they might be thankful, which keeps the favour in the register of thanks and not of reward. The sentence is short and it carries the whole of the return, from the death of the watching to the life of the gratitude, so the reader is asked to measure the one against the other.

**Death and its meaning.**

This verse refers to death, which suggests that the thunderbolt had killed them. Since the Israelites had always been mistrusting Sayyidna Musa he feared that they would suspect him of having taken the men to a solitary place and got them slaughtered.

**The prayer for life.**

So, he prayed to Allah to save him from such a vile accusation. Allah granted his prayer, and gave those a new life. He returned them to consciousness after the blows of punishment over whelmed them in order to fulfill the decree for them and to implement [God's] way of pardoning sin.

**The new life given.**

(Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might be grateful), and said, "Musa said to them, 'Take the Book of Allah.' They said, 'No.' He said, 'What is the matter with you' They said, 'The problem is that we died and came back to life.' He said, 'Take the Book of Allah.' They said, 'No.' So Allah sent some angels who made the mountain topple over them." Then We raised you up after you were dead so that you might be thankful. (Then We revived you) We brought you back to life (after your death) after burning you, (that ye might give thanks) that you might give thanks that I brought you back to life.

**What was required of them.**

This shows that the Children of Israel were required to fulfill the commandments after they were brought back to life. Al-Qurtubi said that this is what is correct, because, he said, although the Children of Israel witnessed these tremendous calamities and incidents, that did not mean that they were not responsible for fulfilling the commandments any more. True piety is to worship God alone, to believe in Him though one has not seen Him, to live in fear of Judgement Day, to subsist on the pure things of the earth, to prevent whomsoever one can from falling into sin.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Then We raised you up brought you back to life after you were dead so that you might be thankful for this favour of Ours. We shall never believe in you until we see Allah plainly. " But you were seized with a bolt of lightning while you were looking Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might be grateful The Best among the Children of Israel ask to see Allah; their subsequent Death and Resurrection Allah said, 'Remember My favor on you for resurrecting you after you were seized with lightning when you asked to see Me directly, which neither you nor anyone else can bear or attain.' This was said by Ibn Jurayj. " Also, 'Urwah bin Ruwaym said that Allah's statement,

57.text:
"And remember when We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails, saying" begins with the call to memory again, and then the favour is laid out in three acts. The first is the shade, cloud over people in an open land, which is a protection given before anything is asked of them. The second is the food, manna and quails sent down, which is the provision that keeps the people alive in the wilderness. The third is the instruction that comes with it: "Eat from the good things We have provided for you". The command is to eat, and the goodness of the food is named as the thing the Lord has provided. "The evildoers certainly did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves" then turns to the response, and the sentence makes the same move as the verse about the calf. The people did not harm the Lord by their ingratitude, since nothing given to them could be taken from Him by their refusal. They harmed themselves, and the verse states so in the same breath as the favour. The contrast is built into the sentence, so the reader sees the gift and the failure to take it as one movement. The verse before gave life after death, and this verse gives the food and the shade that keep that life going. The shade comes first in the sentence and the food second, and the order is the order of need: a people in the open needs shelter from the sun before it needs bread, and the Lord supplies both. The two together show the favour continuing after the return.

**The clouds for shade.**

Another of Allah’s blessings was that He sent clouds to shade you from the heat of the sun when you were wandering the earth; and He sent down manna, a sweet drink similar to honey, and quails for you, telling you to consume of the good things He had provided you with. And We made the cloud overshadow you that is We sheltered you with fine clouds from the heat of the sun while you were in the wilderness; and We sent down in them the clouds upon you manna and quails — which are respectively a type of citrus known as turunjabīn and the quail — and We said ‘Eat of the good things We have provided for you’ and do not store any of it away but they were not grateful for this favour and stored the food and so they were deprived of it; And they did not wrong Us in this but themselves they wronged since the evil consequences of this befell them. (And We caused the white cloud to overshadow you) in the wilderness (and sent down on you honey and quails) also in the wilderness, (Eat of the good things) of the lawful things (wherewith We have provided you) that We have given you and do not keep any provision for future days.

**Manna and quails in the wilderness.**

That is why the wilderness is called Tih which signifies 'having lost one's way'. When they began to starve, Allah blessed them with Mann (manna) and Salwa . Then, quails would not flee but come around them, so that they could catch the birds with little effort.

**Eat of the good things.**

(Eat of the good lawful things We have provided for you,)(7:160) this form of command is a simple order of allowance, guiding to what is good. True piety is to worship God alone, to believe in Him though one has not seen Him, to live in fear of Judgement Day, to subsist on the pure things of the earth, to prevent whomsoever one can from falling into sin.

**Wronged themselves, not Us.**

(And they did not wrong Us but they wronged themselves) means, 'We commanded them to eat from what We gave them, and to perform the acts of worship (but they rebelled).' This Ayah is similar to Allah's statement,. Their ingratitude and disbelief for these blessings did not affect Allah in any way, but they wronged themselves, losing their share from the good they had done and exposing themselves to suffering.

**Food saved against the days.**

Yet they did save food for future days-(They wronged us not) by saving food, (but they did wrong themselves) they harmed themselves. The Israelites started on the expedition, but, on approaching Syria, when they came to learn about the military strength of the foe, their courage failed them, and they refused to engage themselves in the Jihad. "Look at what I did with the Children of Israel, how many blessings I poured down upon them, how much I caressed them in that empty desert!

**What else the same passage holds.**

These two incidents took place in the wilderness of Tih. And We shaded you with clouds and sent down on you Al-Manna and the quail, (saying): The Israelites belonged to Syria, but had gone to Egypt in the time of Sayyidna Yusuf (Joseph), and settled there, while Syria itself had come under the domination of a people called the Amaliqah (Amaleks). "Eat of the good lawful things We have provided for you," (but they rebelled). When the Pharaoh had been drowned and the Israelites could live in peace, Allah commanded them to go to war against the Amaliqah, and to free their homeland. And they did not wrong Us but they wronged themselves Allah punished them for their disobedience, so that for full forty years they kept wandering about in a wilderness, and could not even go back to Egypt. The wilderness was not very vast, but only a stretch of some ten miles, lying between Egypt and Syria. They would make a day-long march in the direction of Egypt, and stop somewhere for the night. But, on getting up the next morning, they would always find themselves just where they had started from. Thus, they spent forty years wandering about in the wilderness in futile rage and exasperation. The wilderness was just a barren space without a tree or a building which could offer protection against heat or cold. There was no food to eat, and no clothes to wear. But in answer to the prayer of Sayyidna Musa Allah made a miraculous provision for all their needs. When they could not bear the scorching sun, Allah sent them the shade of a thin, white cloud. That is to say, Allah produced honeydew in abundance which they could easily gather. Hence it has been designated as mann which signifies "a gift or favour". The two things being unusual, the Holy Qur'an says that Allah made them "descend" for the benefit of the Israelites. Similarly, when they were thirsty, Allah commanded Sayyidna Musa to strike a rock with his staff, which made twelve streams gush forth, as the Holy Qur'an narrates in another place. When they complained of the thick darkness of the night, Allah produced for them a constant pillar of light. When their clothes began to wear out, Allah showed another miracle - their clothes would neither go dirty nor wear out, while the clothes of the children grew with their growth. Allah had commanded the Israelites to take as much of the miraculous food as they really needed, and not to store it for future use. After Allah mentioned the calamities that He saved the Children of Israel from, He mentioned the favors that He granted them, saying, But when they disobeyed this commandment, the meat began to rot. This is how they harmed, not Allah, but themselves. This Ayah mentions the white clouds that provided shade for the Children of Israel, protecting them from the sun's heat during their years of wandering. In the Hadith about the trials, An-Nasai recorded Ibn Abbas saying, Allah shaded the Children of Israel with clouds during the years of wandering.

58.text:
"And remember when We said" opens with the memory again, and the speech is the Lord's, set against the wandering that has just ended, since the people have come out of the wilderness. "Enter this city and eat freely from wherever you please" is the gift: a settled town and plenty in place of the long hunger. "enter the gate with humility, saying, Absolve us" is the condition, and it is the first thing asked of them, before any of the gift is theirs. The gate is to be entered bowed, and the word they are to speak is a request for pardon. The verse does not make the gift a price paid for by the entering, and the gift is not presented as a wage. It states the entering is done in humility, so the reader is taught the posture before the reward. "We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers" closes the verse with the promise on the Lord's side: pardon for the sins, and a larger reward for those who do well. The verse before, 2:57, gave the shade and the food in the wilderness, and the people have now walked out of that place into the settled land the Lord promised them, and this verse moves them to a town. The change of place is the change of trial, because a settled life can be as hard a test as the desert, and the verse asks for the same humility in both.

**The city and the gate.**

(And when We said: Go into this township) the village of Jericho (Ariha) (and eat freely of that which is therein) whenever you will, (and enter the gate prostrate, and say: " Repentance ".) i.e. say: He told you to prostrate in humility to Him when you entered, asking Him to remove your sins, so that He might answer you, and increase those who do good actions, rewarding them in this way. They were given possession of a great city and told to enter it—not in a vainglorious manner—but in humility and repentance; but instead they started rejoicing in their victory.

**Forgive our sins.**

" there is no god save Allah " ; (We will forgive your sins and increase for the right-doers) increase their good deeds.

**The humility asked at the gate.**

He told you to prostrate in humility to Him when you entered, asking Him to remove your sins, so that He might answer you, and increase those who do good actions, rewarding them in this way. The children of Israel persisted in neglecting that which they were com manded to do to the point that they were entrusted to preserve [their] speech but they altered it and they were commanded [to take] a position of prostration upon entering [the city] but they did not. They exposed themselves to the arrows of the unseen and then were not able to with stand the injury of their strikes lam yuṬīqū l-iṣābata bi-qarʿihā.

**Avoiding the entry.**

Allah admonished the Jews for avoiding Jihad and not entering the holy land as they had been ordered to do when they came from Egypt with Musa. But those who did wrong changed the word from that which had been told to them for another, so We sent upon the wrongdoers Rijz (a punishment) from the heaven because of their rebellion. So, the commandment in the present verse pertains to the mode of entering this city, and lays down the spiritual etiquette for action and speech on this occasion.

**The blessing and the thanks owed.**

God bestowed special blessings upon the Israelites. They should have shown their gratitude by remaining obedient to Him, but they did quite the opposite. Remember, from Allah’s blessings upon you, when He told you to enter Bayt al-Maqdis and abundantly consume, with ease, from the good things in it from any place you wanted.

**What else the same passage holds.**

And when We said to them after they came out of the wilderness ‘Enter this city either the Holy House of Bayt al-Maqdis Bayt al-Maqdis or Jericho Arīhā and eat freely therein wherever you will plentifully and without any restrictions and enter it at the gate its gate prostrating bowing and say ‘our request is for an exoneration’ that is ‘That we be exonerated from our transgressions’ and We shall forgive naghfir a variant reading has one of the two passive forms yughfar or tughfar ‘they will be forgiven’ you your transgressions and We shall give more to those who are virtuous’ — through obedience — in terms of reward. There are two views as to when this incident took place. According to Shah Abd al-Qadir when the Israelites grew weary of eating the same Mann and Salwa every day and prayed for being granted the kind of food they were used to (2:61), they were commanded to go to a certain city where they could get what they wished for. On the other hand is the view that the commandment pertains to the city against which the Israelites had been ordered to engage themselves in a Jihad . They obeyed it only after their long wanderings in the wilderness, and conquered the city. The commandment reported in Verse 58 was sent to them through Sayyidna Yusha' (Joshua) who was the prophet among them at the time. The discrepancy between the two views, which raises a question about the chronological sequence of the events, should not confuse us as to the nature of the stories narrated in the Holy Qur'an. The Holy Qur'an does not tell the stories for the sake of telling stories, the usual purpose of which is to provide entertainment. The real intention here is to draw certain conclusions from the stories, and to illustrate or point out certain spiritual principles. Now, the various episodes of a story help to bring out various principles. So, in view of a particular effect sought in a particular context, the chronological sequence of the episodes may be invented and the incidents re-arranged to serve the interest of the pattern of meaning that is intended. This is just what the Holy Qur'an does; in fact, this is a quite usual literary method, and the disturbance of the chronological order in the stories narrated by the Holy Qur'an should not raise irrelevant questions in the mind of the reader - after all, in any and every piece of writing, or even speech, it is the intention which governs the ordering of the material. The Verse holds out the promise that if the Israelites obeyed the commandment, their errors would be forgiven.

59.text:
"But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say" is the turn from the gate to the failure at it, and the verse makes the failure a matter of words. The people were told what to say, and they altered it. The sentence puts the fault in the change itself, not in the failure to speak at all, since they did speak, only not what they had been given. The people in the verse are not described as silent or as refusing outright, and that detail matters, because it means the fault is the falsifying of a command rather than a plain refusal to hear it. The word the verse uses for the people is wrongdoers, and the sentence keeps that word for the ones who made the change, so the blame lands on them and on no one else. The change was made by choice, in the very place where the command had been given, and the verse wants the reader to see the choice as the wrong. "So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their rebelliousness" gives the answer in the same plain order as the offence: the change is named, and then the consequence, a punishment from above. The word "rebelliousness" is the verse's own judgement on the cause. The act of altering the words was a refusal of the command, and the punishment is taken to fit it. The verse before asked for humility at the gate, and this verse shows what happened when humility was replaced with a changed word, so the reader sees the lesson in the contrast between the two.

**The words changed.**

But those who did wrong changed the word from that which had been told to them for another, so We sent upon the wrongdoers Rijz (a punishment) from the heaven because of their rebellion. (But those who did wrong changed the word from that which had been told to them for another). The wrongdoers among them changed what they were told to do and say, and entered dragging themselves on their rears, saying, ‘A grain in a hair’, mocking Allah’s sacred law.

**What the wrongdoers substituted.**

Then the evildoers substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them; so We sent down upon the evildoers wrath from the heaven for their wickedness. Then the evildoers among them substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them and said instead ‘A grain inside a hair’ and entered the town dragging themselves on their rears; so We sent down upon the evildoers the replacement of the second person of the previous verse with the overt identification in the third person alladhīna zalamū ‘the evildoers’ is intended to emphasise the depravity of their action wrath a punishment of plague from the heaven for their wickedness for deviating from obedience and within a very short period of time just under seventy thousand of them were dead. They could neither ward off the opening of heaven above them with their stratagems nor avert the cords of affliction below them by relying on their usual states.

**The punishment from the heavens.**

Due to their actions He sent down a torment from the sky upon the wrongdoers among them, because they trespassed over the limits of the law and disobeyed His command. (But those who did wrong) to themselves, and these are the people who said: �Repentance� (changed the word which had been told them for another word) they disobeyed the command and said �Wheat!�, (and We sent down upon the evil-doers) who changed the word they were ordered to say (wrath) the plague (from Heaven for their evildoing) for changing the commands they were ordered to fulfil. They gnashed the teeth of remorse when the fangs of pain bit them.

**Rebelliousness and what it cost.**

They should have shown their gratitude by remaining obedient to Him, but they did quite the opposite. How could this have benefited them when the situation was hopelessḍ. (The Children of Israel were commanded to enter the door while bowing and to say 'Hittah'. Yet, they entered the door on their behinds, distorting the words. They said; 'Habbah (seed), in Sha'rah (a hair).')

**The commandment and its meaning.**

It appears from the present verse that Allah had commanded the Israelites to say this particular word, Hittatun , while offering their Taubah (repentance), and hence changing the ordained word was in itself a sin. Now, as for other kinds of speech in which it is the meanings that are really intended and not the words, the masters of the science of Hadith and the jurists in general believe that in such places words can be changed provided that the meaning does not suffer but remains in-tact. Most of the jurists and the masters of the science of Hadith, however, believe that although it is better to report a hadith as far as possible in exactly the same words as one has heard without making any change intentionally, yet if one cannot recall the exact words, it is also permissible to report the meaning in one's own words, and that the words of the hadith quoted above - "... conveyed it exactly as he had heard" - might also mean that one should report the meaning of a hadith exactly and without any alteration.

**What else the same passage holds.**

This verse is a continuation of the preceding verse. Allah had commanded the Israelites to keep, while entering the city, repeating the word Hittatun (which indicates repentance for one's sin and the request for pardon). But they replaced this word with another phrase by way of mockery, and started saying, Habbatun fi sha irah (grain in the midst of barley), or Hintatun (wheat). The punishment which descended on them was plague that wiped out seventy thousand men (Qurtubi). In passing, we may recall a hadith which says that plague is a punishment for the disobedient, and a blessing for the obedient. The Israelites were punished for having changed a word ordained by Allah, and substituted a phrase of their own invention, thus distorting the meaning itself. According to the consensus of the Fuqaha ' (Muslim jurists), a change in the words of the Holy Qur'an, or of a Hadith, or of a divine commandment which invents or distorts the actual meaning is impermissible. But there is another question -- is it permissible to change the words in such a way that the meaning does not suffer but remains intact? In his commentary, Imam al-Qurtubi says that in certain texts and in certain kinds of speech the words are as much a part of the intention as the meanings and equally necessary for conveying an idea, and that in such a case it is not permissible to change the words. For example, in the Adhan (the call for prayers) it is not permissible to employ words other than those which have been laid down for the purpose by the hadith.

60.text:
"And remember when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, Strike the rock with your staff" begins with a call to memory, then the prayer of a leader for the people he leads, and then the answer to that prayer. The request is for water, which in the desert is the thing a community cannot do without, and the verse names the need before the answer, so that the reader sees the thirst before the spring. The reply is an instruction, not a miracle performed by a word alone. The staff is in Moses's hand and the rock is in front of him, so the act is his, carried out at the Lord's command. "Then twelve springs gushed out, and each tribe knew its drinking place" gives the result, and the detail is careful: twelve springs for twelve tribes, each with its own place, so that no tribe need quarrel over the water. "We then said, Eat and drink of Allah's provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land" closes the verse with the charge that comes with the provision. The water is a gift, and the people are told to use it without turning it to disorder, since a gift used for disorder is the same ingratitude in a different form. The staff is a plain thing, the sort a traveller carries, and the verse does not make it a wonder in itself. The wonder is the rock answering the stroke, and the sentence keeps the two apart so that the reader sees the ordinary tool and the Lord's act together. The verse before named the shade and the food, and this verse gives the water that matches them, so the wilderness trials are answered one by one.

**Water from the rock.**

Parched with thirst, they requested Sayyidna Musa 1t to pray to Allah for water. Allah commanded that he hit the rock with his stick, and when he hit it, twelve springs appeared from it, the same number as the number of your tribes. It had 12 nipples that resemble the nipples of women and upon striking each one of these a spring gushed therefrom. One who is capable of extracting water from solid rock is capable of quenching thirst without water.

**The twelve springs and the tribes.**

Water gushed from them, and Allah made clear to each tribe which was their spring to drink from, so that there would be no conflict between you.

**What Moses prayed.**

And mention when Moses sought water for his people for they suffered thirst in the wilderness We said ‘Strike with your staff the rock the one that ran off with his robe a light cube-like rock about the size of a man’s head made of marble and he struck it and there exploded there burst and gushed forth from it twelve fountains equal to the number of tribes each people each tribe among them came to know their drinking-place which they did not share with any of the others.

**Eat, drink, and do not spread corruption.**

And We said to them ‘Eat and drink of that which God has provided and do not be degenerate in the earth seeking corruption’ mufsidīn is a circumstantial qualifier emphasising its operator the subject of the verb lā ta‘thaw ‘do not be degenerate’ derived from ‘athiya meaning afsada ‘to corrupt’. the honey and quails (and drink of) all the springs (that which Allah hath provided. And do not act corruptly, making mischief in the earth) and do not cause mischief on the earth, or act contrary to what Moses commanded. And He told you to eat and drink from what He provided for you, without any effort or work from you, and told you not to put your efforts into ruining things on earth. When He had met their needs He bid them to be grateful to preserve the command and to stop choosing sin and so He said and do not be degenerate in the earth seeking corruption.

**The favour and the thanks.**

Allah said, "Remember My favor on you when I answered the supplication of your Prophet, Musa, when he asked Me to provide you with water. And when Moses sought water for his people We said Strike the rock with your staff and there exploded from it twelve fountains and each people came to know their drinking place Eat and drink of that which God has provided and do not be degenerate in the earth seeking corruption. One who is capable of extracting water from solid rock is capable of quenching thirst without water. This in order for Moses to work with his self nafs in mov ing the stone and give him responsibility in striking it with his staff. They should have shown their gratitude by remaining obedient to Him, but they did quite the opposite.

**What else the same passage holds.**

This incident too belongs to the story of the wanderings of the Israelites in the wilderness. And (remember) when Musa asked for water for his people, We said: Allah commanded him to strike a certain rock with his staff. " Then gushed forth therefrom twelve springs. As he did so, twelve streams gushed forth out of the rock, one for each of the twelve tribes. Sayyidna Ya qub (Jacob) had twelve sons, and each had a large family of his own. So, the families were considered as tribes, each with its own administrative organisation and its own head. What they have been asked to eat is the Mann and the Salwa (manna and quails), and the water is, of course, the one which had come out of the rock. The Israelites have, in this verse, been asked not to spread disorder which in this context signifies disobedience to Allah and transgression of His Commandments. The great Commentator al-Qadi al-Baydawi points out that it is a great error22 to deny miracles. When Allah has given a certain stone the unusual property of drawing iron to itself, it cannot be, logically and rationally speaking, impossible that He should also give another stone the property of absorbing water from the earth and of releasing it again. Even this explanation is meant for those who take a superficial view of things. Otherwise, it is in no way impossible that Allah should produce water within a stone itself. Those who call it impossible do not actually understand the technical meaning of the term "impossible." It has been asked whether it is necessary, in times of drought, to offer formal prayers in order to beseech Allah for rains. The present verse tells us that Sayyidna Musa just prayed for water, and Allah made a miraculous provision. It shows that the essential thing in beseeching Allah for rains is just a prayer. In the Shari'ah of Sayyidna Musa a mere prayer was considered to be sufficient for the purpose. According to Imam Abu Hanifah this principle holds good for the Islamic Shari ah too. The Holy Prophet has, in this respect, acted differently on different occasions. An authentic hadith reports that once he went outside the city to the open space where the congregational prayers were held on the day of the Id offered formal prayers, delivered a Khutbah (address), and then prayed to Allah for rains. According to another hadith reported by Al-Bukhari and Muslim from the blessed Companion Anas once the Holy Prophet prayed for rains while delivering the Khutbah on Friday, and Allah sent down rains. No matter what form the prayer takes, all the scholars agree that it cannot be effective unless it is accompanied by a repentance for one's sins, a confession of one's powerlessness, a sincere expression of humility and an affirmation of servitude to Allah. So long as one persists in sin and transgression, one has no right to hope that the prayer would be answered. But if Allah may, in His mercy and benevolence, grant the prayer without this condition being fulfilled, it is His will, and He is All-Powerful.

61.text:
"And remember when you said, O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal every day" moves the address to the people in their own voice, and it is a complaint. The word "every day" is the grievance: the manna and the quails were not enough for them, and they wanted a different table. "So just call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions" is the request that follows, and the list is concrete. Each item is a food the people knew, and the naming of them shows how closely the complaint is tied to appetite. They name the vegetables they want, so the complaint is about what they desire and not about the want of food. "Moses scolded them, Do you exchange what is better for what is worse?" is his answer, and the word "exchange" carries the whole fault: they are trading the better gift for the lesser thing. "You can go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for" is the rebuke's last turn, a dismissal of the demand, and the phrase "what you have asked for" shows the people had got what they wanted and wanted more. "They were stricken with disgrace and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah's signs and unjustly killing the prophets" is the verse's account of the result, and it turns from one complaint to a whole history of refusal. "This is a fair reward for their disobedience and violations" closes the verse by naming the judgement as fair. "Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians, whoever truly believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord" is a sentence of wide reach, and the wideness is the first thing a reader meets in it, before any of the conditions. 67.text:
"And remember when Moses said to his people, Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow. They replied, Are you mocking us?" opens with the memory and the command, and the command is simple and strange. The people are told to sacrifice a cow, an act with no obvious link to the problem they face in the story, and the simplicity of the order is part of what the verse tests. The reply to the command is a question, and it assumes the command is a joke. The people hear a command from the prophet and take it as mockery, which shows a reflex of suspicion before any attempt to obey. "Are you mocking us? Moses responded, I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!" is the exchange, and his answer, and the answer is given as a reply to the mocking, not as a debate about the cow, and it turns the accusation back.
