"This is when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed" opens the new episode, and the verse names the event before the Lord's part in it. A man has been killed among the Israelites and the people argued over the killer, so the dispute is a crime added to a crime. The sentence then turns to the answer, and the word revealed is the reversal: what was kept hidden was brought into the open. The verse does not say how the revealing happened. It states that the concealment was undone by the Lord, and the reader is left to see that the wrong could not stay buried. The episode belongs to the same account as the cow, since the cow was the means by which the hidden act was brought to light. The verse before showed the people slow to act on the command, and this verse shows them failing to speak the truth about a killing, so the reader sees a community in which a command and a truth have both gone unfulfilled.

**The killing and the dispute.**

And when you killed a living soul and disputed thereon iddāra’tum the tā’ of the root-form itdāra’tum has been assimilated with the dāl — and God disclosed what you were hiding this is a parenthetical statement; the story begins here with wa-idh qataltum nafsan ‘and when you killed a soul’… and continues in the following. (And (remember) when you killed a man and disagreed among yourselves as to the crime) means, some of them said, "You killed him," while the others said, "No you killed him. Allah reminds the Israelites about when they killed one of their own. They accused each other of it, each rejecting the accusation of having killed him, and accusing someone else, until they fought.

**What Allah revealed.**

(But Allah brought forth that which you were Taktumun) means, "what you were hiding." Instead, Allah made this matter vague, so this is why we should leave it vague. But Allah revealed what they were hiding about the murder of the innocent person.

**The method of identifying.**

The method that God revealed to His prophet to identify the killer was that an animal should be sacrificed, and the dead man’s corpse be struck with a piece of it. A murder was committed among the Israelites in Moses’ time. (And (remember) when ye slew a man) 'Amil (and disagreed concerning it) concerning his murder (and Allah brought forth that which ye were hiding) thus demonstrating what you hid with regard to his murder.

**Life after death in the lesson.**

The third lesson in this instance was that life after death is no less a reality than life before death. Just as the dead corpse was revived, so every soul will be raised up in the Hereafter and given new life. Then Allah mentioned the murdered person, saying:

**The sources on the chronology.**

With regard to this event one may ask as to why Allah made the resurrection of the dead man depend upon his being touched with a part of flesh when he had the power to bring the man back to life without the intervention of any such device; or, one may ask as to why the dead man should have been brought back to life when the name of the murderer could have been revealed even otherwise. In answer to this, we shall say that Allah is omnipotent, and does not act under any kind of compulsion, but that all His actions proceed from His all-embracing wisdom. This chronological order has not been preserved in the narration, but inverted, and this re-arrangement has a subtle significance. This long section of the Surah (Chapter) has been dealing with the transgressions of the Israelites, and this is just what the Holy Qur'an intends to bring out in narrating different stories, the narrating of stories not being an object in itself here. This is also the Tafsir of Mujahid. 'Ata' Al-Khurasani and Ad-Dahhak said, "Disputed about this matter. And when you killed a living soul and disputed thereon-and God disclosed what you were hiding One who is disloyal is afraid and out of fear that his secret will become manifest relies on concealment deception denial and evasion. His fault ʿawāruhu is inevitably discovered his secrets asrāruhu exposed and the coverings astāruhu fall because of the shame of his action.

73.text:
"So We instructed, Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow. This is how easily Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs so that you may understand" carries the command that the cow was for, and the strike is done with a part of the animal. The instruction is precise: a piece of the slaughtered cow is to touch the dead man. The sentence then names the act for what it is, a demonstration of ease. The Lord does not need a labour to raise the dead, and the verse makes the thing done look small beside what is shown. The phrase about the signs gives the purpose, and the purpose is understanding, not a spectacle for its own sake. The strike is made with the flesh of the slaughtered animal, and the verse does not say how the blow was given or how long the dead man took to rise. It states what was done and what followed, and the attention stays on the Lord's act rather than on the instrument. The sentence is short and it moves quickly from command to effect, so the reader is shown the sign before being asked to reflect on it. The verse before gave the murder and the dispute, and this verse answers it with the sign: the hidden killer is found through the revived man, and the lesson is the Lord's power over death. The reader is led from the dispute to the sign by the two verses together.

**Strike with a piece of the cow.**

so We said ‘Smite him the slain man with part of it’ and so when he was struck with its tongue or its tail he came back to life and said ‘So-and-so killed me’ and after pointing out two of his cousins he died; the two killers were denied the inheritance and were later killed. When this was done, the dead man came back to life, announced the name of his murderer, and died again. Allah told them to hit the murdered man with a piece of the cow which they had been told to sacrifice. (Thus Allah brings the dead to life) means, "They struck him with it, and he came back to life.

**How easily the dead come to life.**

God says even so is the revival for God brings to life the dead and He shows you His signs the proofs of His power so that you might understand that you might reflect and realise that the One capable of reviving a single soul is also capable of reviving a multitude of souls and then believe. As this man was brought back to life by Allah, so will He bring the dead back to life on the Day of Judgement. God wanted to give life to the dead man so that he could expose his killer through the testimony [of the slain] so He commanded them to kill one of their animals and made it the cause of bringing the slain man to life. Allah gives humanity clear signs of His power, to make them reflect and understand, and have true faith in Him.

**Signs so that you may understand.**

He would then bring him to life to tell them who the murderer was. The allusion here is to anyone who desires the life of his heart; he will only attain it by sacrificing his lower self since the heart of anyone who sacrifices his lower self through struggle mujāhadāt comes to life by the lights of witnessing mushāhadāt. (Thus) just as He brought 'Amil back to life (Allah bringeth the dead to life) for the Resurrection (and showeth you His portents) bringing the dead to life (so that ye may understand) in order that you may believe in resurrection after death.

**The revived man and the killer.**

But Allah willed that the criminal should be brought to book, and appointed a miraculous way of identifying him -- that is, the dead body of the murdered man should be touched with a part of the flesh of the sacrificial cow. (But Allah brought forth that which you were Taktumun) means, "what you were hiding." Instead, Allah made this matter vague, so this is why we should leave it vague. The method that God revealed to His prophet to identify the killer was that an animal should be sacrificed, and the dead man’s corpse be struck with a piece of it.

**Life after death in the lesson.**

The third lesson in this instance was that life after death is no less a reality than life before death. Just as the dead corpse was revived, so every soul will be raised up in the Hereafter and given new life. (And We said: Smite him) the murdered person (with some of it) with an organ of the cow; and it is also said: with its tail or tongue. Likewise when God wants someone's reputation to live forever He causes his reputation in this world to pass into obscurity.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The murderer had his supporters who wanted to hide his crime, and hence began accusing different people. This miraculous event is a manifestation of the omnipotence of Allah, and Holy Qur'an presents it as an argument against those who deny the Resurrection of the dead for the Last Judgment. Verse 73 says that this precedent should induce people to make use of their reason, and see that what has happened in a past instance can as easily happen in a future instance. With regard to this event one may ask as to why Allah made the resurrection of the dead man depend upon his being touched with a part of flesh when he had the power to bring the man back to life without the intervention of any such device; or, one may ask as to why the dead man should have been brought back to life when the name of the murderer could have been revealed even otherwise. In answer to this, we shall say that Allah is omnipotent, and does not act under any kind of compulsion, but that all His actions proceed from His all-embracing wisdom. Moreover, it is He alone who knows, and can know, the raison d'etre of what He does.

74.text:
"Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah. And Allah is never unaware of what you do" marks the sharpest turn yet in the account, and the word "even" makes the hardening the reaction to every sign just given. The heart is set against the rock, and the comparison is one of hardness. "for some rocks gush rivers" begins the contrast, and the stones of the earth are shown to do what the people's hearts did not. "others split, spilling water" carries a second kind of rock that yields, and "while others are humbled in awe of Allah" completes the set with rocks that bow before the Lord. The sentence lists three kinds of stone in a row, and each one is a different response to the same world: one gives forth a river, another splits to release water, and the last bows low. The people are set against the whole range of these responses and placed at its hardest end. The comparison is the verse's method throughout, and it keeps the people to a standard that stone already meets. The verse does not say that rocks have hearts. It uses the rocks as a measure, and the people fall short of the measure. "And Allah is never unaware of what you do" closes the verse with the knowledge that will judge the hardening. The verse before showed the sign given, and this verse shows the hearts that did not respond, so the reader is asked to measure the people against the stones and find them lacking.

**Hearts hardened like a rock.**

(And indeed, there are stones out of which rivers gush forth, and indeed, there are of them (stones) which split asunder so that water flows from them, and indeed, there are of them (stones) which fall down for fear of Allah), means, "Some stones are softer than your hearts, they acknowledge the truth that you are being called to,. On the contrary, their hearts became all the more hardened against divine guidance. Their hearts became hard after these great lessons and incredible miracles, until they became like rocks, and even harder than rocks, because they never changed, whereas rocks change and transform.

**Rocks that gush rivers.**

Rivers spring from some rocks, and some split, and water comes out of them, gushing and flowing on the earth, benefitting people and animals. Further, Ibn Jarir commented that this Tafsir means that some of their hearts are as hard as stone and some hearts are harder than stone. And there are stones from which rivers come gushing, and among them are those that split and water comes forth from them, and among them are those that fall down in fear of God. " There are stones from which rivers come gushing, and among them are those that split and water comes forth from them, and among them are those that fall down in fear of God.

**Others that fall in awe.**

Still others do not give forth water, but fall down from their place for fear of Allah. And some rocks fall from the heights of the mountains in awe of Allah. In contrast to them, it has been suggested, the hearts of the Jews are so hard that they are incapable of feeling any sympathy for their fellow-men even in suffering and pain, and hence incapable of wishing to do them good. This then means that some of them are like the first example, and some others are like the second example.

**Hearts that manipulate.**

But when the heart is hardened, people begin to manipulate the divine scriptures, for they are used to doing the same with human writings. Three aspects of the symbolic meaning of rocks have been mentioned in this verse: 1. Some rocks seem to be nothing more than dry boulders; but when cracked, reveal huge pools of water beneath them—wells from which people quench their thirst. But then he is struck by some calamity, which shakes his soul.

**Allah is not unaware.**

Allah is not unaware of anything we do, but knows everything, and will hold us to account for it. (Allah is not unaware of) will not leave unpunished (what ye do) of transgressions; and it is said the meaning is: what you hide of transgression. Some other scholars said that this Ayah means their hearts are only of two types, as hard as stone or harder than stone. But the hearts of Jews are harder than even these. Whenever he saw that someone was weeping and twisting in himself because of listening to the Qur'an, he would say, "I was like that until the hearts became hardened.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Then your hearts became hardened O you Jews they your hearts became stiffened against acceptance of the truth thereafter that is after what is mentioned of the bringing back to life of the slain man and the other signs before this; and they are like stones in their hardness or even yet harder than these; for there are stones from which rivers come gushing and others split yashshaqqaq the initial tā’ of the root-form yatashaqqaq has been assimilated with the shīn so that water issues from them; and others come down from on high in fear of God while your hearts are unmoved unstirred and not humbled; And God is not heedless of what you do but instead He gives you respite until your time comes ta‘malūna ‘you do’ a variant reading has ya‘malūna ‘they do’ indicating a shift to the third person address. The Surah has been relating a number of incidents which show that the Israelites were always prone to disobedience and rebellion and had to undergo punishment again and again. Then after that your hearts were hardened and became as stones or even worse in hardness. Such an experience should have taught them humility and obedience. This insensibility led them into further misdeeds and transgressions. The present verse describes their degeneracy, and warns them that Allah knows everything they have been doing, and will punish them for their evil deeds. In contrasting the hearts of the Israelites with stones, the verse refers to three states of the latter: Some stones give forth a great amount of water. The first two of these states are a matter of everyday observation, but the third may be subject to doubt, for the ability to feel fear requires reason and sensibility, and the stones, as one supposes, do not possess these faculties. But reason is not always a necessary requisite for the ability to feel fear - after all, animals do feel fear, even though they do not possess reason. But there is no rational argument which should deny sensibility to minerals. For sensibility depends on life, and the minerals may possibly possess a kind of subtle life which man may not be aware of. In fact, scientists have recently discovered the signs of life and sensibility in minerals too. Anyhow, an explicit statement in the Holy Qur'an carries a validity and an authority which no physical science or rational argument can dispute. Then, we do not claim that fear of Allah is always the only cause which makes a stone fall down. For, the Holy Qur'an itself says that this cause operates only in the case of some stones. So, there may be different causes which make stones fall down; some of these causes may be purely physical, while one of them may be the fear of Allah. The order in which the three kinds of stones have been mentioned is very subtle, and, in view of the meaning and purpose intended, extremely expressive and significant. The verse places in the highest degree those stones whose affectivity is so strong that rivers gush forth from them, and provide sustenance to beasts and men. In the second degree come the stones which do serve the creatures of Allah, but to a lesser extent. To the lowest degree of affectivity belong those stones which do not benefit anyone, but can at least 'feel' the fear of Allah. But the Jews are devoid of even this minimum degree of sensitivity.

75.text:
"Do you believers still expect them to be true to you, though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it" is a question put to the faithful, and it asks them to examine their own hope. The believers are tempted to hope that the Jews of that generation will accept their message, and the verse asks whether that hope is well founded. "though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it" gives the answer in the form of an accusation: some of them heard the Lord's word, understood it, and then corrupted it with full knowledge. The corruption is not an error of the mind. It is the choice to alter a message after grasping it, and the verb in the sentence keeps that knowledge in view. The verse does not condemn the whole community. It names a group within it, and that restraint is part of the verse's weight. The question is asked of the faithful and not of the Jews, which means the believers are the ones being corrected. Their eagerness is named as a hope that outruns the evidence, and the sentence asks them to look at what the evidence already shows. Of the two parties named, the believers are the ones addressed, and the sentence does not claim to speak for the whole of the other community. The verse before gave the hardened hearts, and this verse explains one of the forms the hardening took, so the reader sees the hope of the faithful measured against a known fact about a part of the community.

**Are you still hoping.**

Are you then so eager O believers that they the Jews should believe you seeing there is a party of them a group of their rabbis that heard God’s word in the Torah and then tampered with it changing it and that after they had comprehended it after they had understood it knowingly? knowing full well that they were indulging in mendacity the hamza at the beginning of the verb a-fa-tatma‘ūn is an interrogative for rejection in other words ‘Do not be so eager for they have disbelieved before’. Do you (faithful believers) covet that they will believe in your religion inspite of the fact that a party of them (Jewish rabbis) used to hear the Word of Allah (the Tawrah), then they used to change it knowingly after they understood it And when they (Jews) meet those who believe (Muslims), they say, "We believe," but when they meet one another in private, they say, "Shall you (Jews) tell them (Muslims) what Allah has revealed to you that they (Muslims) may argue with you (Jews) about it before your Lord? Are you then so eager that they should believe you seeing there is a party of them that heard God's word and then tampered with it and that after they had comprehended it knowinglyḍ He informed them of [the status] of their belief and related that after hearing the address of God they engaged in tampering [with it] and altering [it]: (Have ye any hope that they will be true to you) do you hope, O Muhammad, that the Jews will believe in you (when a party of them) the 70 men who were with Moses (used to listen to the Word of Allah) used to listen to Moses reciting the Word of Allah, (then used to change it) alter it, (after they had understood it) after knowing it and fully understanding it (knowingly?) while knowing that they were altering it?

**A group that heard the word.**

(Inspite of the fact that a party of them (Jewish rabbis) used to hear the Word of Allah (the Tawrah), then they used to change it) meaning, distort its meaning,. (used to hear the Word of Allah (the Tawrah), then they used to change it) "They altered the Tawrah that Allah revealed to them, making it say that the lawful is unlawful and the prohibited is allowed, and that what is right is false and that what is false is right. A group of their scholars heard the word of Allah, revealed to them in the Torah, and then changed its words and meanings after they had understood what it really meant; and they did this fully aware of the seriousness of the crime. This was revealed about the seventy men who were chosen by Moses to go with him to Allah, exalted is He.

**Knowingly corrupting it.**

The "Word of Allah" mentioned in the verse refers to the Torah which the Jews had "heard" from the prophets, and the distortion pertains to the changes made in the words themselves or in the sense or in both; or it refers to the words of Allah which the seventy men had heard directly on the Mount Tur (Sinai) where they had gone to seek divine confirmation of what Sayyidna Musa (Moses) had been telling and the distortion pertains to their declaration before their people that Allah had promised to forgive them if they could not act upon certain commandments. As for the Jews, they had already altered their own scriptures, though they knew them to be the word of God. Seeking out loopholes in any part of the Holy scriptures that did not conform to their wishes, they altered the word of God at will; religion was subordinated to their worldly interests. But a group of them said: we heard Allah at the end of His speech say: if you can do these things, then do them; but if you wish, don't do them and there is no harm upon you .

**The Jews of the time.**

The Jews who were the contemporaries of the Holy Prophet may not have themselves been involved in some of these transgressions, but since they did not abhor the misdeeds of their forefathers, they are to be considered as their counterparts. For, some of the Jews have been committing an even more heinous sin - they used to change and distort the Word of Allah in spite of knowing the ignominy of such a deed. If he were truly a prophet, the Jews would have been the first to believe in him, for their knowledge of what is written in the scriptures is greater than yours. Why would they believe you when they already heard by means of the messageḍ How can those who do not remain in a state of faith imān after eyewitnessing ʿiyān believe by means of demonstrative proof burhānḍ That which does not hold true for the Real does not hold true for you.

**Not ashamed before the Real.**

How can those who are not ashamed before the Real be ashamed before youḍ. O believers, do not expect, after knowing their true nature and how stubborn they are, that they will be truthful and respond to you. One who has such irreverent attitude towards the divine scriptures can never appreciate the gravity of matters concerning God: he hears the word of God, but he can always find words to show that the commandment does not apply to him; he believes in God, but his insensitivity makes him commit acts of flagrant rebellion against Him which no one who really believes that God is watching over him, and hearing what he says, would ever dare to perpetrate. As for the true amongst them, they delivered exactly what they had heard.

"When they meet the believers they say, We believe. But in private they say to each other, Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?" shows the hypocrisy in its first form, which is a profession of faith made in front of the believers. The words are the words of belief, and the speaker chooses them for the company he is in. "But in private they say to each other" turns to the other company, the one the believers do not see, and the same people say something different there. "Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord" is the private speech, and it is a plan to keep the Lord's knowledge away from the faithful. "Do you not understand?" closes the verse with a question that reproaches the speakers for not seeing the folly of what they propose. The verse shows the same people speaking two ways in two rooms. The sentence does not give their words a single meaning. It shows the division between the public face and the private plan, and leaves the reader to see how the two fit together. The reader is put in the position of someone who has heard both rooms and can judge the difference. The verse before showed a group that corrupted the word, and this verse shows the same people concealing it from the believers, so the reader sees the two halves of the same deception.

**When they meet the believers.**

And when they the hypocrites from among the Jews meet those who believe they say ‘We believe’ that Muhammad is a prophet and that he is the one of whom we have been given good tidings in our Book; but when they go in private one to another they their leaders the ones not involved in the hypocrisy say to those hypocrites ‘Do you speak to them the believers of what God has disclosed to you that is what He has made known to you of Muhammad’s s description in the Torah so that they may thereby dispute the lām of li-yuhājjūkum ‘that they may dispute with you’ is the lām of ‘becoming’ with you before your Lord? in the Hereafter and hold the proof against you for not following him Muhammad despite your knowledge of his sincerity? **In private to each other.**

But when they met other Jews who openly declared their adherence to Judaism, they would admit that they were only trying to deceive the Muslims, and were otherwise quite loyal to their own faith. On such occasions, those of the other group used to reprimand them for revealing to the Muslims what they themselves were trying to keep concealed, for a knowledge of the relevant verses of the Torah could be very useful for the Muslims in order to defeat the Jews in their argument. But when they were alone with one another they blamed each other because of these acknowledgments, saying that the Muslims might use them as proof that they recognised the truth of Muhammad’s prophethood. (But when they go apart one with another) when these lowly people return to their leaders (they say) the leaders say to the lowly:

**Disclosing the knowledge.**

Do you speak to them of what God has disclosed to you so that they may thereby dispute with you before your Lordḍ Have you no understandingḍ Do they not know that God knows what they keep secret and what they proclaimḍ They encouraged one another among themselves to reject the Real and to hide the situation from the Muslims. But they did not know that God was informing His Messenger of their secrets and that a light the Real makes manifest cannot be extinguished by the efforts of anyone other than Him. (used to hear the Word of Allah (the Tawrah), then they used to change it) "They altered the Tawrah that Allah revealed to them, making it say that the lawful is unlawful and the prohibited is allowed, and that what is right is false and that what is false is right. Muhammad and his Companions (of that which Allah hath disclosed to you) about that which Allah has shown you regarding the description and traits of Muhammad in your Book (so that they may contend with you) argue against you (before your Lord concerning it? Have ye then no sense?) do you not have any common sense?

**Do you not understand.**

Have you no understanding?’ of the fact that they will contend with you if you speak to them in this way? In order to assure the Muslims of their sincerity and to win their favour, these hypocrites would now and then disclose to them that the Torah itself had given out the good tidings of the coming of the Holy Prophet and mentioned the Holy Qur'an. **The tongue and the mind.**

When the tongue agrees but the mind162 objects it only increases separation. Then Allah mentioned the hypocrites of the people of the Book, and it is also said that the reference here is to the lowly from among the people of the Book, saying: (And when they fall with those who believe) Abu Bakr and his companions, (they say: We believe) in your Prophet, and his description and traits are mentioned in our Book.

Do you (faithful believers) covet that they will believe in your religion inspite of the fact that a party of them (Jewish rabbis) used to hear the Word of Allah (the Tawrah), then they used to change it knowingly after they understood it And when they (Jews) meet those who believe (Muslims), they say, "We believe," but when they meet one another in private, they say, "Shall you (Jews) tell them (Muslims) what Allah has revealed to you that they (Muslims) may argue with you (Jews) about it before your Lord? 78.text:
"And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and so they wishfully speculate" is a sentence about the people themselves, and it sorts the community into those who read and those who do not. It begins with the people themselves, and the sentence sorts the community into those who read and those who do not. The word illiterate names a lack of reading, not a lack of intelligence. The sentence then gives that lack its content. These people know the Scripture only as a set of lies, so what they hold about the book is not knowledge at all. The phrase "wishfully speculate" carries the point: they guess, and they guess in the direction they would like. The verse before named the concealing of what is known. This verse turns from the learned who hid the truth to the ordinary people among them, who had no direct access to the book and filled the gap with what they hoped was true. The reader is shown a community in which some handled the Scripture and others knew it only through rumour and talk, and the two groups were led astray in different ways. The unlettered had no book in their hands to check a rumour against, so whatever they heard was the whole of what they had.

**The unlettered among them.**

And there are some of them the Jews that are illiterate unlettered not knowing the Scripture the Torah but only desires lies which were handed down to them by their leaders and which they relied upon; and in their rejection of the prophethood of the Prophet and fabrications of other matters they have mere conjectures and no firm knowledge. And there are among them (Jews) 'Ummyyun (unlettered) people, who know not the Book, but they trust upon Amani (false desires) and they but guess Then woe to those who write the book with their own hands and then say, "This is from Allah," to purchase with it a little price! (Among them are unlettered folk who know not the scripture) they do not know how to read or write it (except from hearsay) except the unfounded things they hear.

**What they guess.**

(But they trust upon Amani) means, "It is just a false statement that they utter with their tongues. (They but guess) their talk is all surmise based on what they heard from their leaders. "And remember when We took a covenant from the children of Israel, stating" opens with the memory and the covenant, and the verb is the Lord's, not the people's. The covenant is taken from the children of Israel, which is a bond placed on a whole line, not on one generation alone. "Worship none but Allah; be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy; speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax" is the content of the covenant, and it runs through five obligations in sequence. The first is the worship of the one God, and the rest are duties to people and to the Lord together: kindness to parents and to those who depend on others, gentle speech, prayer, and the alms. "But you Israelites turned away, except for a few of you, and were indifferent" is the failure, and the verse names it precisely. Most turned away and the rest were indifferent, which is two faults. The verse does not list the obligations as options to be chosen from. They come as one covenant, and each item in it is a part of the same bond that the Israelites accepted. The first item is the one all the others depend on, since a people that worships none but the Lord has a single measure for its kindness and its prayers alike. The verse before named the Lord's favour to the people, and this verse shows the favour paired with a bond, and the bond broken. The Israelites are reminded of their own promise, and the sentence gives them no room to say the terms were unclear, since the promise is named in full and then the turning away is named beside it. The reader sees the whole covenant set out first and then the breach, so the failure is measured against a clear standard.

This verse speaks of the pledge which Allah had made the Israelites take, and the few people it refers to as having been true to the pledge were those who acted upon the Shari'ah of Sayyidna Musa (Moses) as long as it was in force, and when it was abrogated, followed the Shari ah of Sayyidna Muhammad . 87.text:
"Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers" begins the account of the favours given to the people, and it begins with the Book and then the line of messengers that followed. "And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit" continues the list with the later prophet, and the two gifts are named in parallel: a book to Moses, proofs and support to Jesus. "Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you Israelites with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others" turns to the response, and the question asks for a reason. The people are described as arrogant whenever a messenger brings what they do not want. They reject some and kill others, so the refusal goes as far as murder. The list of messengers is not a list of accidents. Each one came after the Book, and each was received in a way that the people were asked to answer, so the sentence treats the whole line as a single record of their response. The verse gives Jesus the clear proofs before it gives him the support of the holy spirit, and the order keeps the proofs in view as the first thing the people were offered. The sentence is one of the most direct rebukes in the passage, and it names the sequence of the people's behaviour rather than a single fault. The whole list is read by the reader as a history of the same response repeated. The verse before named the trade of the Hereafter, and this verse shows the pattern of rejecting the messengers that lay behind it. The gifts are set out first and the rejection second, so the reader sees the favour and the response together.

**The Torah and the messengers after Moses.**

The Qur'an again reminds the Israelites how Allah in His mercy forgave them their transgressions again and again, and provided them with all the means of guidance. First of all, He gave them a Divine Book, the Torah, through Sayyidna Musa (Moses); then, sent them a number of prophets; and, at the end of this line, sent down Sayyidna Isa (Jesus) along with clear and irrefutable evidences of his prophethood, like the Evangel and miracles, and appointed the Archangel Jibra'il (Gabriel) to give him support. The Torah was the Book of God revealed to the Jews.

"They say, Our hearts are unreceptive, In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief. They have but little faith" opens with the people's excuse and then turns it round. The heart is the place where understanding sits, so the complaint is that this place is closed to the message. The word In fact is the rebuttal the verse sets against the excuse, and the condemnation that follows is placed on their disbelief rather than on the heart by nature. The verse keeps the cause and the effect in one line, so the closing of the heart is traced back to the choice that caused it. The little faith at the end names the result, and it describes people who chose the closed door first and then blamed the house. The excuse is given as a claim of sincerity, yet the verse exposes it as a cover for refusal. The sentence does not mock them in its tone. It states the cause of their state, which is their disbelief, and it leaves the reader to see that the excuse has been turned back on them. A reader who hears only the words Our hearts are unreceptive would take the people at their word, and the verse exists to correct that reading at once. The verse therefore teaches that the closing of the heart is not a fact to be accepted with resignation. It is a state with a cause, and the cause can be seen in the disbelief the verse names. 89.text:
"Although they used to pray for victory by means of the Prophet over the polytheists" opens with a fact about the past, and although sets that hope against what follows. The prayer asked for victory over the polytheists through the one who was yet to be sent, so the people were looking forward to a helper against the idolaters. "when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized" is the turning point, since the word when marks the moment the expectation was tested. The Book is described as from Allah and as something they recognized, and the recognition is the heart of the charge. The verse does not say the people failed to understand what came to them. They knew it, and that knowledge is what makes the rejection so serious. "confirming the Scripture they had in their hands" explains why the Book was recognized, because it agrees with the Scripture they already held. "they rejected it" closes the account with the act, and the sentence stops there. "So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers" is the verdict, and the word So links the curse to the rejection so that the curse is its result. The verse moves from a prayer, to the arrival of a Book, to the recognition, to the rejection, and to the condemnation, and each step makes the next one heavier. The people wanted the help and recognized its source, yet they turned away when the help came in a form they had not chosen. The reader sees a clear line from the hope they expressed to the curse they incurred.

**Praying for victory before the Book.**

The sources explain the prayer as a request for victory against the idolaters before the prophet came. When there came to them a Book from God confirming what was with them in the Torah that is the Qur’ān — and they formerly before it came prayed for victory for assistance over the disbelievers saying ‘God give us assistance against them through the Prophet that shall be sent at the end of time’; but when there came to them what they recognised as the truth that is the mission of the Prophet they disbelieved in it out of envy and for fear of losing leadership the response to the first lammā particle is indicated by the response to the second one; and the curse of God is on the disbelievers. In fact, the Jews themselves used to tell the Arabs that a new prophet and a new Divine Book was soon to come. We beseech You by the truth of the unlettered Prophet whom You promised to send forth to us at the end of time to give us victory over them'. Before it was revealed, they used to say that they would be helped against the idolaters, who worship others alongside Allah, and would have success over them when a prophet was sent, since they would have faith in him and follow him.

And when there came to them (the Jews), a Book (this Qur'an) from Allah confirming what is with them (the Tawrah) and the Injil (Gospel), although aforetime they had invoked Allah (for the coming of Muhammad) in order to gain victory over those who disbelieved, then when there came to them that which they had recognised, they disbelieved in it. (confirming what is with them) meaning, the Tawrah. The verse says that the Holy Qur'an confirms the Torah it means that the Holy Qur'an is a concrete evidence of the truth of the prophecies made in the Torah with regard to the coming of the Holy Prophet and of the Holy Qur'an.

But when the Holy Qur'an came down from Allah, and even when they had recognized its authenticity, the Jews denied it out of sheer spite. But when the Qur’ān and Muhammad ﷺ came to them, according to the description they recognised and the truth they knew, they disbelieved him. They had seen prophecies of the coming of a final prophet in their scriptures, and had eagerly anticipated his arrival. But these proved to be empty words on their part, a pretence aimed at consolidating their status as undisputed guardians of divine faith. \ When there came to them a Book from God confirming what was with them-and they formerly prayed for victory over the disbelievers; but when there came to them what they recognized they disbelieved in it; and the curse of God is on the disbelievers.

(And when there cometh unto them a Scripture from Allah, confirming that in their possession) which accords with that which is in their possession (though before that) before Muhammad ﷺ (they were asking for a signal triumph) through Muhammad and the Qur'an (over those who disbelieved) of their enemies: the tribes of Asad, Ghatafan, Muzaynah, and Juhaynah (and when there cometh unto them that which they knew) of his traits and description in their Book (they disbelieved therein) they denied it was him.
