The Jews were awaiting the Prophet's coming, but They disbelieved in Him when He was sent.

**The curse on the disbelievers.**

(The curse of Allah) His wrath and torment (is on disbelievers) the Jews. Allah curses those who disbelieve Him and His Prophet. It is due to this that Allah, exalted is He, revealed ( though before that they were asking for a signal triumph over those who disbelieved) i.e. by means of you, O Muhammad, up to His saying (The curse of Allah is on disbelievers) . One may want to know why the Holy Qur'an calls the Jews Kafirin (infidels), when they did recognize the truth as truth, which should qualify them to be called "believers.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The Torah had in several places foretold the coming of the Holy Prophet . So let the curse of Allah be on the disbelievers One who believes in the Torah cannot justifiably deny the Holy Qur'an and the Holy Prophet for such a denial would involve a denial of the Torah itself. " Let us explain that 'Iman (faith) does not merely mean "knowing the truth", but really signifies "accepting the truth and affirming it deed-wise. " Otherwise, Satan too will have to be called a believer, for he knows fully well what the truth is. In fact, this knowledge of the truth on the part of Satan intensifies the gravity of his Kufr (infidelity) all the more. However, the next verse attributes the infidelity of the Jews to their malice. (And when there came to them) meaning, the Jews, (a Book from Allah) meaning, the Qur'an that Allah sent down to Muhammad, (although aforetime they had invoked Allah (for coming of Muhammad) in order to gain victory over those who disbelieved) meaning, before this Messenger came to them, they used to ask Allah to aid them by his arrival, against their polytheistic enemies in war. They used to say to the polytheists, "A Prophet shall be sent just before the end of this world and we, along with him, shall exterminate you, just as the nations of 'Ad and Iram were exterminated.

90.text:
"Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for, denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants" opens the verse with a judgment on a trade, and the word miserable is the verdict on the bargain before the bargain is named. The verse uses the sale as its image, since the people are described as having exchanged something of their own for a return that is worth far less. The sources read the price as their share of faith, the portion of guidance and of belief in Allah and His messengers that they could have kept and instead gave up. The second part of that run then names what the trade consists of. The first act is denial, the rejection of what Allah has sent down, and the second is resentment, which is a feeling directed not at a message but at the giving itself. The grace is described as His bounty, and the verse says that Allah gives it to whoever He wills among His servants. So the resentment is against a choice that belongs to Allah, and the sentence shows the people placing their own envy in the place of the Lord's decision. The two halves are joined by the word for resenting, and the reader sees that the denial is driven by the feeling rather than by any argument about the message. "They have earned wrath upon wrath" is the consequence, and the phrase upon wrath is the verse's way of marking a doubled anger. The jalalayn-style reading in the sources takes the indefinite form of the word for anger as a sign of its greatness, so that the anger is not one ordinary anger but a weight of anger that is repeated. The sources tie the doubling to two offences, the first being the rejection of the prophet who had been sent and the second being the distortion of the Torah that had come before. Another line of reading has the anger come once for each of the two acts, and the commentary that speaks of curse upon curse gives the same two-part sense in other words. "And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment" closes the verse with the outcome, and it moves from the people who made the trade to a general category of disbelievers. The sources note that the humiliation is part of the punishment, and the verse uses it to set these people apart from anyone who is punished for sin but is still among the believers. A sinner of the faithful is punished for his purification, while the disbeliever is punished with disgrace, and the verse names the disgrace so that the reader knows what kind of loss is meant.

**The trade in the soul.**

The sources read the word for the price as the portion of reward that the people could have had in the afterlife, the share of faith that would have been theirs had they accepted the message. The picture of selling is therefore an account of exchange rather than of loss in the abstract. They gave away their own portion in return for a feeling, and the verse calls the bargain miserable because the thing they received is so small. The commentary that treats the trade as a choice notes that the people had the faith available to them in the Torah and in the earlier prophets, and that they rejected the faith when it came in the form of a new prophet. Miserable is therefore a word used of the outcome, and the people are shown to have made the bad bargain with their eyes open.

**Envy and the will of the Lord.**

The sources use a strong word for the resentment, which the commentary on the verse glosses as grudging out of envy that Allah should reveal His bounty. The verse does not describe the people as ignorant of what the message contains. It describes them as envious that the bounty fell on someone outside their own line. The Maʿārif commentary makes the point that prophethood cannot be earned by effort or merit and that it is a grace given by Allah to whomever He likes. The Jews, on this account, were so malicious that they denied the prophet and the Qurʾān out of sheer spite, and in doing so they were challenging the will of Allah Himself. The verse therefore has two faults in view, the denial of a true prophet and the envy that moved them to deny him. The sources connect the first to the anger that comes once and the second to the anger that comes again, so that the wrath is doubled by the two faults.

**The anger upon anger.**

The commentary on the phrase anger upon anger takes the repeated word as a measure of the weight of the punishment. The jalalayn-style reading gives the sense that the people earned the anger for their disbelief in what Allah had revealed, and that the earlier anger came when they neglected the Torah and disbelieved in Jesus. The commentary on the same phrase, in the short commentary, reads it as curse upon curse, and it explains that the people deserved the curse because of the rejection of the prophet and the corruption of the Book. The two readings agree that the wrath is not a single event but a sequence, and the verse presents the sequence in one short clause so that the reader feels its size. The word upon links one anger to the next, which is how the verse makes the repetition visible in Arabic and how the sources read it.

**The two causes of the wrath.**

The Maʿārif commentary gives the reason the wrath came twice in the form of two offences. The first was the denial of a true prophet, a fault against the one who was sent. The second was the envy and malice that moved them to deny him, a fault in the heart that was there before the denial. The commentary says that the people earned divine wrath in both ways, and that the one does not cancel the other. The sources read the doubled anger as the sum of these two faults, so that the reader is not asked to count the anger twice but to see that each fault brought its own weight. The jalalayn-style reading places an earlier anger in the history of the people, when they neglected the Torah and disbelieved in Jesus, and it presents the present anger as the second load laid on a people already burdened. The verse thus joins the history and the present, and it teaches that a people which has broken its covenant once is not made safe by its earlier claim to the Book.

**The grace that cannot be earned.**

The sources return to the point that prophethood is not a reward for effort or merit. The Maʿārif commentary states that it is a special grace which Allah bestows on whomsoever He likes, and that the Jews, by denying the prophet, were questioning the will of Allah Himself. The tanwir reading of the bounty describes it as the sending of Gabriel with the Book and prophethood, and identifies the one chosen as Muhammad. The phrase of His servants in the verse therefore includes the Prophet within the people Allah chooses, and the people who resented the choice were resenting a decision that was not theirs to make. The verse holds the reader to a plain fact, which is that no lineage or effort can secure the gift, and that the envy of those who do not receive it is the root of the trade the verse condemns.

**The shameful end of the disbelievers.**

The closing words of the verse name the outcome for disbelievers as a humiliating punishment, and the commentary observes that the humiliation is the particular mark of disbelief. The Maʿārif commentary argues that the disgrace has been added to suggest this kind of punishment belongs to the infidels and is not for a true Muslim, since a Muslim who has sinned is punished for purification and not for disgrace. The verse thus sets the end of the people who sold their souls against the end of the faithful, and it shows that the difference lies not only in the pain but in the shame that accompanies it. The reader is left with the trade, the envy, the doubled anger, and the disgrace, and each of these is a step in the same account. The verse before named the Jews' expectation of a prophet who would stand with them, and this verse shows what they did when the prophet came, which is to sell their share of faith for envy.

91.text:
"When it is said to them" opens the verse with a command given to a group, and the phrase sets the scene before the people speak. The sources identify the group as the Jews who were addressed by the Prophet, and the verse records the call they were given before it records their reply. "Believe in what Allah has revealed" is the content of the call, and the run "Believe in what Allah has revealed, they reply" joins that call to the reply that follows, with the comma marking the turn from one to the other, and the sources read the revelation as the Qurʾān, which the Prophet brought to them. The call is not to abandon their own Book but to believe in the new revelation as well, and the verse keeps the two in view. "they reply" marks the moment of answer, and the word reply shows that the people were not silent. Their answer is "We only believe in what was sent down to us", and the word only is the hinge of the reply, since it restricts their faith to one revelation and excludes the rest. The sources read what was sent down to us as the Torah, the book given to their own prophets, and the people are shown to be drawing a line around their own scripture. "and they deny what came afterwards" is the verse's reply to the reply. The phrase what came afterwards is the Qurʾān, which came after the Torah, and the word deny is the act that the verse sets against their claim to believe. The run "though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures, Ask them, O Prophet" carries the point forward, so that the description of the truth runs straight into the challenge, and the description makes the point decisive, because the new Book is described as the truth and as the one that confirms what they already held. The verse therefore presents the denial as a contradiction, since the thing denied is the thing that confirms the faith they claim. "Ask them, O Prophet, why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before, if you are truly believers?" closes the verse with a question that turns the argument on them. The question is put to the Prophet, who is instructed to ask it, and it asks why the people killed the prophets of Allah in the past if they are truly believers. The question is a challenge, not an invitation to answer, because the killing of the prophets is already known to the people who are being addressed.

**The call and the reply.**

The sources read the verse as the account of a dialogue in which the Jews were told to believe in what Allah had revealed and replied that they believed only in what had been sent to them. The word only is the key to the reply, and the commentary on the verse observes that the people made the Torah the measure of all faith and therefore excluded the Qurʾān from it. The short commentary states that when they were told to believe in the truth and guidance Allah revealed to His Prophet, they answered that they believed in what had been revealed to their prophets and denied anything beside it. The reply is thus an attempt to keep the faith within their own boundary, and it is presented in the verse as a refusal dressed as loyalty.

**Denying the book that confirms the Torah.**

The sources give the reason the denial is a contradiction. The Maʿārif commentary states that the Jews flatly refused to believe in any Book of Allah other than the Torah, and that they claimed to believe in the Torah because it had been sent down to them. The verse answers this with several arguments, and the first is that when the truth of the other Books has been established on irrefutable grounds, a flat refusal makes no sense. If they had doubts they could have voiced them and settled them. The second argument is that the other Books confirm the Torah, so that a denial of them is at the same time a denial of the Torah. The jalalayn-style reading supports this by noting that the Torah itself confirms the Qurʾān as what is with them, and the verse calls the Qurʾān the truth that confirms their own Scripture.

**Killing the prophets.**

The question at the end of the verse is answered by the sources through the history of the people. The commentary on the killing of the prophets states that to slay a prophet is a form of disbelief in every Divine Book. The prophets the Jews killed were themselves Israelites, and their teaching rested on the commands of the Torah, so the killing was a direct denial of the book the people claimed to follow. The Maʿārif commentary adds that the people not only killed the prophets but also accepted the killers as their leaders, and this acceptance falsified their claim to hold the Torah. The verse therefore asks the people to explain a history that contradicts their claim, and the sources treat the question as a demonstration that the claim does not stand.

**The circumstantial words.**

The jalalayn-style reading treats the small words in the verse as the key to its meaning. The particle wa introduces a circumstantial qualifier, so that the people disbelieve in what is beyond the Torah while the Qurʾān is the truth, and the verse marks the truth as a state in which the Qurʾān stands, not as a separate claim. The reading calls the confirming a second circumstantial qualifier added for emphasis, so that the Qurʾān confirms what is with them and does so in the way the people already know. The reading also explains that the question about the killing is addressed to those present in the time of the Prophet, because they approved of what their forefathers had done. The grammar therefore carries the argument, since the verse presents the denial as a present state, the truth as a present fact, and the approval of the killings as a present choice of the people addressed.

The verse says the people disbelieve in what came after the Torah, and the sources identify that later book as the Qurʾān. The phrase what came afterwards is therefore not a vague term but a precise reference to the revelation that followed theirs. The Maʿārif commentary observes that the people denied the other Books only because they had not been sent down to them, which is an argument from envy rather than from evidence. The verse meets the argument by pointing out that the later Book confirms the earlier one, so that to deny it is to deny the Torah in the same act.



**The claim of the forefathers.**

The short commentary and the commentary on the reply note that the people spoke of their forefathers, saying that their forefathers were believers, and that this claim is what the verse is answering. The address about the killing of the prophets concerns what the forefathers did, and it is directed to the people present in the time of the Prophet, because they approved of their forefathers' conduct. The commentary on the claim observes that the people were defending the deeds of their ancestors as a way of defending their own position. The verse meets the defence by asking the question about the prophets, so that the reader sees that a claim of ancestral faith cannot cover the killing of the messengers who came in that same line.

**The tribal sense of truth.**

The commentary in the sources on the phrase they believe only in what was sent to us describes a feeling of ethnic superiority which the people mistook for love of truth. They were sure that belonging to the largest group of the followers of truth, the Israelites, would be enough to earn them salvation. The communal values of the group came to occupy the place of pure truth, and so when the truth appeared in its original form they failed to accept it. The sources note that the predictions of the coming of the Qurʾān were in the Torah itself, so that a search for pure truth would have led them to accept the new Book. The question about the killing of the prophets is thus the test of whether the people were seeking truth or their own group's standing. The verse before, 2:90, named the trade of the soul, and this verse shows the reasoning that made the trade seem acceptable, namely that the group's faith was enough and that the new revelation was not for them.

92.text:
"Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs" opens the verse with a reminder of what the people already had, and the word indeed marks the passage as a further charge after the question about the prophets. The sources read the clear proofs as the signs Moses brought, which the verse names as proofs that left no room for doubt. "then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully" is the turn in the sentence, since the word then sets the act of worship immediately after the proofs. The calf is the object of the worship, and the phrase in his absence gives the reason the act is so shameful, which is that the people did it when the one who had brought the signs was away from them. The run closes the sentence with the judgment on the act, and the word wrongfully names the worship as an injustice done to the Lord and to the one who had carried the message. The sentence stays short so that the act and its judgment sit close together, and the reader is not given time to excuse the worship before the verdict arrives.

**The clear proofs.**

The Maʿārif commentary reads the clear signs as the miracles that manifested themselves before the Torah was given to Moses, and it lists the staff that became a serpent, the hand that shone, and the parting of the sea that made a path for the Israelites. The jalalayn-style reading gives the same examples, the staff, the hand, and the splitting of the sea. The short commentary speaks of commands, prohibitions and signs, which widens the proofs from miracles to the law as well. The verse opens with the word indeed as a further charge after the question of the prophets, so that the reader is brought from the killing of the prophets back to the first of the prophets who came with proofs. The verse uses the word proofs to say that the people were given enough evidence, so that their later worship of the calf cannot be explained as ignorance of what Moses could do.

**The calf in his absence.**

The sources explain that the people took the calf as a god after Moses had gone to the appointment at the mountain. The jalalayn-style reading says that the people took to themselves the calf in worship after he had gone, and that they were evildoers for taking it so. The absence is part of the point, because the people were kept in line by the presence of the prophet and did their worship when that presence was lacking. The verse is thus a reminder that the people's faith depended on the messenger in front of them, and that it failed once he was out of sight.

**The shirk of the forefathers.**

The Maʿārif commentary argues that although the Jews of the Prophet's time did not themselves take part in the worship of the golden calf, they respected those of their forefathers who had done so and took their side, so that for all practical purposes they shared the sin. The commentary notes that the claim to faith was joined to the practice of association, and that this association denies not only Moses but Allah Himself. The verse suggests in its context that people whose forefathers denied Moses are unlikely to accept the Prophet, and the reader is asked to see the continuity from one generation to the next.

**The wrongdoing.**

The shortest commentary in the sources explains the closing words as a statement that the people were wrongdoers for worshipping others alongside Allah, since only He is worthy of worship. The short commentary of the sources also reads the word for wrongdoers as unbelievers, which is the stronger sense. The verse therefore ends with a judgment that makes the worship of the calf a form of disbelief, and it places the act in the same category as the denial of the Book and the killing of the prophets in the preceding verse. The three verses together show a single pattern, in which the people are given proofs, take a false course in the absence of the messenger, and then refuse what is sent after.

**The turning of the people.**

The Maʿārif commentary makes the sharpest point of the passage, which is that the people did not take part in the worship of the calf themselves, yet they respected those who had and took their side. The commentary concludes that for all practical purposes they were guilty of the same sin. The tazkirul reading of the wider passage supports this by describing a people who looked to the saved status of their group rather than to the content of the faith. The verse therefore places the sin of the forefathers within the present generation that defends it, and it leaves the reader to see that loyalty to a group can carry the guilt of an act one did not do. The sentence about wrongdoing thus closes a long account in which the past and the present are bound together.

93.text:
"And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you saying" opens the verse with a memory of the covenant, and the act is first the taking of the covenant and then the raising of the mountain. The sources read the mountain as Mount Tur, which Allah lifted over the people so that they would be awed into accepting the command. The covenant is the bond the people made, and the raising of the mountain is the sign that gave the bond its weight. The run "Hold firmly to that Scripture which We have given you and obey, they answered" keeps the command and the reply together, and the words hold firmly are the most vivid part of it. The sources read the phrase as taking the Scripture with effort and seriousness, so that the people would not hold it loosely. "they answered, We hear and disobey" is the reply, and it sets two verbs side by side. The people said that they heard, and then that they disobeyed, so that the reply contains the hearing and the refusal in one breath. Read as one run, "The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief, Say, O Prophet" moves from the calf to the Prophet, and the comma marks the turn. The clause explains the reply, since the verse does not treat the disobedience as an accident but as the expression of a love that had taken root. "Say, O Prophet, How evil is what your so-called belief prompts you to do, if you actually believe in the Torah!" closes the verse by turning the charge back on the people, as a question about what their belief enjoins. The word evil is the same word used for the trade in the verse before, and the question asks whether their claim to believe in the Torah can be squared with the act of worshipping the calf.

**The covenant and the mountain.**

The Maʿārif commentary sets the verse against the claim the Jews made to be authentic and true, which was already referred to earlier in the surah. It tells the story of the Israelites who escaped from Egypt and came upon a people who worshipped idols, and who found that cult attractive enough to ask Moses to make a visible god for them too. When Moses reproved them they repented, but their repentance was of a low order, so that the darkness of the error did not leave their hearts and grew into the worship of the golden calf. The tanwir reading of the raising of the mountain says that the Lord took the consent of the people and fixed the mountain above their heads, so that they accepted the covenant under the threat. The covenant and the mountain are therefore the setting in which the people agreed and then broke the agreement. The Maʿārif commentary also lists the fuller details of the scene, in which the people had asked for a visible god before and had been reproved for it, so that the mountain stands as a second reproof laid over the first. The short commentary speaks of the raising of the mountain as a means of extracting the consent that the people had not given freely, and the reader is left to see that the covenant made under threat is weaker than one made in the heart. The verse therefore keeps the image of the mountain in view as the thing that made the words of the people possible, and that also showed how little those words were worth when the threat was not there.

**Hold firmly and listen.**

The jalalayn-style reading takes the command to hold firmly to mean taking the Scripture with effort and earnestness, and it adds that the people were to listen to what they had been commanded and be ready to accept it. The short commentary reads the same command as asking them to be diligent and earnest with what was given in the Book. The verse uses the word hear for the second part of the command, and the answer that the people gave turns the verb hear into a refusal. The sources read the answer as a statement that, had it not been for the mountain, they would have heard the command and disobeyed it, which shows how the threat of the mountain was the only thing that kept them to the words they gave.

**The calf sinking into the heart.**

The verse says that the love of the calf was made to sink into their hearts, and the commentary on the phrase takes it as the people's love of worshipping the calf sinking deep, as a punishment for their disbelief. The jalalayn-style reading uses the image of drink, which makes the calf a thing the people took in as they would take wine, so that their love of it was not a passing fancy but a state of the heart that was fed again and again. The image of drink also explains why the people could not simply put the worship aside once they had been reproved, saying that they were made to drink the calf in their hearts, and that the love of the golden calf intoxicated their hearts the way wine does, on account of their unbelief. The commentary also observes that the worship had taken root so deeply that the people's love of it was equal to their love of the Creator in their own practice, and the verse asks the Prophet to measure the two loves against each other in the closing question.

**The repentance that was not complete.**

The Maʿārif commentary traces the calf back to an earlier moment. When the Israelites escaped from Egypt and came upon a people who worshipped idols, they found that cult attractive and asked Moses to make a visible god for them too. When he reproved them they realized their error and offered repentance, but the commentary observes that repentance has many degrees, and theirs was not of a very high order. The darkness of the error did not leave their hearts altogether, and it continued to grow until it showed itself in the worship of the golden calf. Some of those who had worshipped were slain as a penance, and others, as some commentators report, were forgiven. Those who had not worshipped did not hate the act as much as they should have, so their hearts also carried a trace of association. The commentary concludes that through the feebleness of their repentance or the want of proper hatred for infidelity, their hearts became indolent in religious matters, and that this indolence is why the mountain was needed when the covenant was taken.

The commentary makes a distinction that the reader should not miss. The people who had not joined in the calf were not free of its taint, because they did not hate the act as they ought, and the verse includes them in the account by its wording. The sources therefore do not place the whole guilt on those who made the image. They place part of it on those who looked on and kept silent, and the mountain over the heads of the whole people is the sign that the covenant bound all of them and not only the makers of the calf.

**The so-called belief.**

The question at the end of the verse, about what their belief enjoins on them, is answered by the sources as a point about the claim itself. The Maʿārif commentary and the jalalayn-style reading agree that faith in the Torah does not command the worship of a calf, so that the people who worship the calf cannot be believers in the Torah. The commentary notes that the forefathers are meant here and that the people's claim to follow the Torah is not borne out by their conduct. The short commentary states the same point in plainer words, saying that the people are not truthful in their claim unless they are truthful in the claim that their forefathers were believers.

**The love of the present world.**

The tazkirul reading of the wider passage points out that the Israelites were not truly seeking God, since their attention was on this world and not on the life after death. It recounts how the people, when the mountain was raised, agreed to do all that the Lord had spoken, and how most of them then returned to their earlier ways. The sources treat this return as the sign that the covenant had never been fully taken into the heart. The verse before and this verse together show a people who agreed under pressure, broke their word once the pressure was gone, and then argued that their own belief justified their conduct.

94.text:
"Say, O Prophet, If the eternal Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you Israelites out of all humanity" opens the verse with a command to the Prophet to speak, and the conditional that follows is the form of a challenge. The eternal Home is the Hereafter, and the people are told that it is with Allah and is exclusively theirs, and not shared with other people. The sources read the claim as the belief of the Jews that Paradise was reserved for them. The run "then wish for death if what you say is true" is the consequence the people are asked to accept if their claim is true, and the verb wish carries the sense of longing or asking. The run closes the verse with the condition on which the challenge rests, and the word true is the test that the people must meet. The claim being tested is one about belonging, since the people treated their place in the Home as a matter of their descent and not of their conduct. The verse does not ask them to prove their lineage. It asks them to prove the claim by a sign that their own love of the Home would have to show.

**The claim to the Home.**

The Maʿārif commentary states that the Jews used to claim the blessings of the other world were reserved for them and for no other people. It cites other passages of the Qurʾān on the same claim, including the claim that the fire would not touch them except for a few days, and the claim that no one would enter Paradise except a Jew or a Christian. The commentary explains that the people meant that their own faith was the true one, so that they must attain salvation, with the repentant and forgiven admitted from the beginning, sinners released from the fire after a few days, and the obedient welcomed like sons and beloved friends. The claim is correct in itself, the commentary notes, provided it pertains to people who follow a valid faith, and the difficulty is that the Jews of the time followed a faith that had been altered.

**Wish for death.**

The jalalayn-style reading takes the phrase wish for death as a conditional linked to the verb long for. The sense is that if the people speak truly when they claim that the Home is theirs, they will naturally incline to what is theirs, and since the path to it is death, they should long for death. The tanwir reading gives the same sense with the words ask for death, and it adds that the people must long for death if they are truthful in their claim. The mukhtasar reading makes the point practical, saying that a true believer in the promise of Paradise would want to reach it quickly and be relieved of the burdens of this world.

**The exclusive home.**

The short commentary reads the word exclusively as meaning that Paradise is specifically for the people alone, and not for the believers in the Prophet and his Companions. The tanwir reading makes the same restriction, saying the Home is specifically theirs and not for others of mankind. The commentary on the claim explains that the Jews thought of Paradise as a reward for their lineage, so that membership of their group would be enough to enter. The verse therefore tests the claim of lineage against the claim of truth, and the challenge invites the people to show that the Home is theirs by wishing for the death that would take them to it.

**The history of the people.**

The tazkirul reading of the wider passage points to the history of the Israelites as the proof of their lack of concern for truth. It records how they killed their own prophets, such as Zachariah and John the Baptist, because these prophets criticised their way of life and called them back to the divine way. The same reading notes that after Moses had left them for forty days they worshipped the golden calf, and that when the mountain was raised over them they agreed to do all that the Lord had spoken, but then most of them went back to their disobedience. The sources conclude that a people really seeking God would have had their attention fixed on the life after death, and that the people of the Book were more obsessed with the love of the present world than any others.

**A challenge that exposes the claim.**

The verse does not argue against the claim in abstract terms. It asks the people to act on the claim, and the act it asks for is the wish for death, which the people would not make. The sources take the challenge to show that the people's love of this life was greater than their confidence in the Home they claimed, and that their claim to exclusive possession of Paradise was therefore not sincere. The verse before, 2:93, showed them a love of the calf that had sunk into their hearts, and this verse shows a love of the present life that keeps them from the death they claim would lead them to the Home. The reader is left with the test, and the test is the one the verse gives, which is whether the claim is true.

95.text:
"But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done" opens the verse with a refusal, and the word never closes the door on the wish that the previous verse put to them. The test was the wish for death, and the verse states plainly that they will not make it. The cause is named at once, because of what their hands have done. The hands stand for the deeds, and the sentence ties the refusal to the record of their conduct rather than to any doubt about the Home itself. "And Allah has perfect knowledge of the wrongdoers" then closes the verse with the knowledge that will judge the refusal. The word wrongdoers names the people who have done the wrong, and the reader is asked to see the refusal as one more act of that wrong. The verse before set the claim beside the test, and this verse shows the result of the test, which is that the claim is not backed by any willingness to die for it. The sentence keeps the speaker and the knowledge apart, so the reader sees the refusal first and then the Lord who knows it. The wish is not made, and the knowledge of the Lord is the answer that stands in its place. The commentary that follows gives the detail of why the people would not wish.

**The wish that is not made.**

The proposed trial consists in this -- if the Jews are so sure of the blessings of the other world being reserved for themselves, they should declare that they wish to die, and this declaration would establish them as being genuine in their faith; but if they refuse to accept the challenge, it would show that they were liars. But they knew very well in their heart of hearts that the Holy Prophet a and the Muslims stood for the truth, while they themselves were the champions of falsehood, and were, in actual fact, infidels. ((Say (O Muhammad): "O you Jews! If you pretend that you are friends of Allah, to the exclusion of other mankind, then long for death if you are truthful. "But they will never long for it (death), because of what (deeds) their hands have sent before them! And Allah knows well the Zalimin. Say (to them): "Verily, the death from which you flee will surely meet you, then you will be sent back to (Allah) the Knower of the unseen and the seen, and He will tell you what you used to do.")(62:6-8).

**The deeds of their hands.**

(But they will never long for it because of what their hands have sent before them (i.e.what they have done). And Allah is Aware of the Zalimin. And verily, you will find them (the Jews) the greediest of mankind for life.) meaning, greedy to live longer, because they know their evil end, and the only reward they will have with Allah is total loss. (But they will never long for it) they will never ask for death, (because of that which their own hands have sent before them) because of what they themselves have done in the religion of Judaism. But they did not long for the garden-and God said that they will never long for it-and this information was a miracle for the Messenger since it was as He had said.

**The knowledge of the wrongdoers.**

(And Allah is Aware of evil-doers) i.e. the Jews. Allah knows the wrongdoers among them and other people: each person will be given what they have earned. God knows the evildoers the disbelievers and He will requite them. He only bestows the ardent longing on them so that it may be actualized [when] they reach the garden.

**The Mount and the covenant.**

When the Mount was raised threateningly above their heads, they temporarily agreed to do ‘all that the Lord hath spoken’ (Exodus, 19:5 , 8, 16 , 18), but, after that, most of them returned to their disobedient ways. If they had really been seeking God, their attention would have been entirely focused on the life after death; but, in fact, they, more than all the others, were obsessed with the love of the present world. It was they who had slain their own prophets, such as Zachariah and John the Baptist, the only reason for these actions being that these prophets had criticized the Israelites’ mode of living, and sought to bring them back to the divine way (Nehemiah, 9:26). They had seen Moses perform undeniable miracles, but when he was not with them in person, having left them to spend forty days on Mount Sinai, they started worshipping the golden calf; it had only been his personal authority which had kept them under control.

**The trial and its proposal.**

Here we must note that the trial was proposed not for all the Jews of all the ages, but specially for those who were the contemporaries of the Holy Prophet and who used to deny him out of sheer envy and malice, in spite of having recognized that he was a genuine prophet. The use of certain improper expressions like "sons of Allah" not-withstanding, these claims are in themselves quite correct, provided that they pertain to people who follow a true and valid faith. God most high said But they will never long for it because of that which their own hands have sent before them. But they will never long for it because of that which their own hands have sent before them as a result of their rejection of the Prophet s the consequence of their mendacity.

96.text:
"You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists" opens the verse with a sight that the listener is asked to see, and the word surely makes the finding certain. The people are described as clinging to life, and the picture is of hands that hold on to something they cannot bear to lose. The verse states that they are more eager than any other people, and it brings in the polytheists to the comparison, so the attachment is measured against those who did not believe in the Book at all. The eagerness is the point of the sentence, since the verse is about the wish they would not make and this is the reason they would not make it. "Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years" moves from the people as a group to each one of them, and the number a thousand years marks the extreme length a life could be wished for. The word each makes the wish personal, so that no one among them is exempt from the desire. "But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment" turns the wish against the wisher. The length of the life is granted in the sentence only for the sake of the argument, and the verse states that it would not save them from the punishment. The sentence is built so that the wish is shown to be useless even when it is granted. "And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do" closes the verse with the knowledge that makes the wish irrelevant, since the one who sees their deeds is not moved by their longing for a long life. The verse before showed the refusal to wish for death, and this verse shows the reason for it, which is the attachment to life. The reader is left with a people who hold to the present life so tightly that they will not let go of it even for the Home they claim as their own.

**Clinging to life.**

This verse shows the basic weakness of the Jews which did not allow them to accept the challenge proposed in Verse 94, and thus exposes the hollowness of their claim to the blessings of the other world being reserved for them. The Holy Qur'an puts a special emphasis on the fact that the Jews loved physical life much more than did the Arab polytheists. Such an inclination should not have been surprising on the part of the latter, for, after all, they did not believe in the other world, and physical life was the be-all and end-all for them. You will find, O Prophet, that the Jews are the most desirous for life, even if it is miserable and lowly.

**The greediest of mankind.**

They are even greedier for it than the idolaters, who worship others alongside Allah, who do not believe in being brought back to life after death or in being held to account for what they have done. Despite being People of the Scripture, and believing in the resurrection and the reckoning, they would love to live a thousand years. (wilt find them) the Jews (greediest of mankind for any life) to remain in this world (and (greedier) than the idolaters) even greedier than the Arab idolaters. And you shall find them the people most covetous of life and the idola ters; any one of them would love that he might be given life for a thousand years; yet his being given life shall not budge him from the chastisement.

**A thousand years.**

((Each) one of them would like) would hope (to be allowed to live a thousand years. And to live (that long) would by no means remove him) save him (from the doom) if he were to live a thousand years. But the Jews acknowledged the existence of the other world, and even had the illusion that they alone deserved its joys, and yet it was they who, above all others, wished to live in this world as long as possible.

**No protection in long life.**

It was they who had slain their own prophets, such as Zachariah and John the Baptist, the only reason for these actions being that these prophets had criticized the Israelites’ mode of living, and sought to bring them back to the divine way (Nehemiah, 9:26). They had seen Moses perform undeniable miracles, but when he was not with them in person, having left them to spend forty days on Mount Sinai, they started worshipping the golden calf; it had only been his personal authority which had kept them under control. But they will never long for it because of what their hands have sent before them (i.e. what they have done). (But they will never long for it because of what their hands have sent before them (i.e. what they have done). And Allah is Aware of the Zalimin (polytheists and wrongdoers).) meaning, "Since they know that they recognize you, and yet disbelieve in you.

**The Seer of their deeds.**

(And Allah is Seer of what they do) of contraventions, rebellion and what they conceal about the description and traits of Muhammad ﷺ. Those who are heedless and insolent are eager for life only because they know of their failure to be obedient. But for believ ers the transition [of death] to One from whom only good is expected is better than remaining with those against whose evil they are not secure. The prolonging of life in spite of the certainty of death holds no value for them since [death] comes unexpectedly and life is cut off.

**What else the same passage holds.**

God sees what they do ya‘malūna may be alternatively read ta‘malūna ‘you do’ and will requite them. "If the abode of the Hereafter with Allah is indeed for you especially and not for others of mankind, then long for death if you are truthful. ‘Abd Allāh Ibn Sūryā asked the Prophet s or ‘Umar b. al-Khattāb about which angel brings down the revelation and he replied that it was Gabriel; he Ibn Sūryā then said ‘He is our enemy because he brings chastisement with him; had it been Michael we would have believed in him because he brings fertility and security. And Allah is Aware of the Zalimin And verily, you will find them (the Jews) the greediest of mankind for life and (even greedier) than those who ascribe partners to Allah. This very desire shows how baseless their pretention was, and how they themselves knew that they would have to face the fires of Hell in the other world, and that physical life was, as long as it lasted, a kind of protection against their final fate. One of them wishes that he could be given a life of a thousand years. But the grant of such life will not save him even a little from punishment. Calling the Jews to invoke Allah to destroy the Unjust Party Muhammad bin Ishaq narrated that Ibn 'Abbas said, "Allah said to His Prophet , (Say to (them): "If the home of the Hereafter with Allah is indeed for you especially and not for others, of mankind, then long for death if you are truthful.") meaning, 'Invoke Allah to bring death to the lying camp among the two (Muslims and Jews).' The Jews declined this offer by the Messenger of Allah ." " Had they wished death that day, no Jew would have remained alive on the face of the earth. Moreover, Ad-Dahhak said that Ibn 'Abbas said that, (Then long for death), means, "Invoke (Allah) for death. " Also, 'Abdur-Razzaq narrated that 'Ikrimah said that Ibn 'Abbas commented, (Then long for death if you are truthful), "Had the Jews invoked Allah for death, they would have perished.

97.text:
"Say, O Prophet, Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this Quran to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it, a guide and good news for the believers" opens with a command to the Prophet to speak, and the sentence that follows is addressed to those who took offence at Gabriel. The word enemy is the key, because the verse treats enmity toward the angel as enmity toward the one who sent him. The sentence then names the bringer of the revelation, which is Gabriel, and the revelation is described as coming to your heart by Allah’s Will. The heart receives the message, and the Will of Allah is the source of its arrival, so the verse ties the messenger and the message to the Lord. "confirming what came before it" tells the reader what the Quran does for the earlier Books, which is to confirm them and not to replace them. "a guide and good news for the believers" closes the verse with the purpose of the Quran, which is guidance and glad tidings for those who believe. The sentence therefore moves from the command, to the enemy, to the messenger, to the message, and then to its benefit. The verse before showed the people clinging to their lives, and this verse turns to their complaint about the one who brought the Book, so the reader sees the objection set against the good that the Book does. The objection is not new, and the verse answers it at the root, by pointing to the Lord who sent both the angel and the Book.

**Enmity toward the angel.**

Say to them ‘Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel let him die in exasperation — he it was that brought it the Qur’ān down upon your heart by the leave by the command of God confirming what was before it of scriptures a guidance from error and good tidings of Paradise for the believers. (Verily, those who disbelieve in Allah and His Messengers and wish to make distinction between Allah and His Messengers (by believing in Allah and disbelieving in His Messengers) saying, "We believe in some but reject others.")(4:150) Say, O Muhammad, to those of the Jews who say that Gabriel is their enemy among the angels, that whoever is against Gabriel – who revealed the Qur’ān to your heart, with Allah’s permission, affirming the sacred scripture that came before it, such as the Torah and the Gospel, showing the way to what is good, and bringing the good news to the believers of the bliss Allah has prepared for them – then he is misguided.

**The messenger and the heart.**

When they learnt that it was Archangel Jibra'il (Gabriel) who brought the Glorious Qur'an to the Holy Prophet they said that the Archangel was their enemy, as it was through him that rigorous commandments or catastrophic punishments had always descended on them,. and that for this reason they would not accept a Book which had been revealed through his agency. In refuting this argument, the Holy Qur'an points out that Jibra'il is only a messenger, and has, acting only as a messenger, brought down the Holy Qur'an under a divine command to the Holy Prophet . (For he it is who hath revealed to your heart) sent Gabriel to you with the Qur'an (by Allah's leave) by Allah's command, (confirming) affirming the Oneness of Allah (that which was before it) of the Book, (and a guidance) from error (and glad tiding) good news (to believers) that Paradise will be theirs.

**Confirming the Books before it.**

As for the Book, it confirms the earlier Books of Allah, provides guidance to men, and gives good tidings to the believers. The error would lie in drawing from this phrase the conclusion that Allah has not revealed the words of the Holy Qur'an but only the meanings. (Whoever is an enemy of Jibril (let him die in his fury). 'Ikrimah said, "Jibr, Mik and Israf all mean, worshipper, while il means, Allah". " Magnanimous and beautiful is the Qur'an that Gabriel brought down from the All-Merciful.

**Warnings and the Israelites.**

It was God’s way to warn them of these impending punishments beforehand, and such warnings came to them through the prophets, who were acting on the words of the Archangel Gabriel. But, instead of heeding these admonitions, the Israelites came to regard Gabriel as their enemy, because it had always been he who gave prior warning through the prophets about impending doom. Consequently, when the Prophet Muhammad proclaimed that he was receiving his revelation through Gabriel, they said, ‘So, it is our old enemy Gabriel, who always brings commands from heaven against us! Then Allah, Exalted is He, revealed the following verse about the saying of one of the Jews, 'Abdullah Ibn Suriyyah, that Gabriel was the enemy of the Jews, saying:

**Angels and the revelation.**

’ Now angels, being the rarefied creatures that they are, do not hold grudges against ordinary mortals; they descend to earth only by divine command in order to carry out the tasks assigned to them by their Creator—in this case, the revelation of the Scriptures to the prophet whom God Himself had chosen. Some people say that 'il' means worshipper while whatever word that is added to it becomes Allah's Name, because 'il' is a constant in such conjunction. Why does a child resemble its father, and why does it resemble its maternal uncle?' Allah's Messenger said, "Jibril has just told me the answers." 'Abdullah said, 'He (i.e. Jibril), among all the angels, is the enemy of the Jews.' Allah's Messenger recited the Ayah,. This is why God says, "he it is who sent it down upon thy heart.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The perversity of the Jews was very fertile, and gave them ever-new excuses for denying the Holy Prophet . They also added that they could have accepted the Holy Qur'an, if the Archangel Mika'il (Michael) had brought it down, for he is connected with rain and with divine mercy. So, why should the Jews be so particular about the messenger, and not look at the Book itself? This being what the Divine Books are meant for, the Holy Qur'an is evidently enough a Divine Book, and must, as such be obeyed. To deny it on account of one's hostility to Jibra'il is sheer stupidity or outright perversity. Now, as for the attitude of the Jews towards Jibra'il the Holy Qur'an declares that to be hostile to the angels (including Jibra'il and Mika'il or to the prophets is tantamount to being hostile to Allah Himself. Verse 98 puts down the enemies of angels and prophets as infidels (Kafirin) in saying that Allah is the enemy of the infidels. In other words, those who deny or oppose the angels and the prophets will have their due punishment in the other world.

99.text:
"Indeed, We have sent down to you O Prophet clear revelations" opens the verse with a statement of the sending down, and the word indeed marks it as a plain fact before any reply to a charge. The revelations are called clear, which gives the sentence its weight, because the verse does not argue the clearness but states it. "but none will deny them except the rebellious" closes the verse by naming the only people who will refuse. The word but turns the sentence from the clearness to the exception, and the exception is the rebellious. The sentence does not describe the proofs as doubtful. It places the refusal in the character of the ones who refuse, and the reader is asked to see that rejection of clear signs is a sign of rebellion. The verse before named the enmity toward Gabriel, and this verse answers the objection by stating that the signs are clear enough for anyone who is not rebellious. The commentary that follows gives the reply to the Jews who claimed that no clear sign had been sent, and it points out that their denial was not based on a lack of recognition.

**Clear revelations.**

And We have revealed to you O Muhammad clear proofs lucid ones bayyinātin ‘clear proofs’ is a circumstantial qualifier; this was in response to Ibn Sūryā saying to the Prophet s ‘You have not brought us anything’; and none disbelieves in them except the wicked these have disbelieved in them. (Verily We have revealed unto thee) sent you Gabriel with (clear tokens) with manifest signs expounding commands and prohibitions, (and only miscreants) the unbelievers and the Jews (will disbelieve in them) will deny the signs. I have revealed to you, O Prophet, clear signs proving the truth of your prophethood and revelation. And We have revealed to you clear proofs; and none disbelieves inthem except the wicked.

**The denial of the Jews.**

In denying the Holy Prophet the Jews used to say that no clear evidence or sign of his prophethood had been revealed to him such as they could recognize and accept. In reply to this the Holy Qur'an says that Allah has revealed a number of very clear signs and evidences of his prophethood which even they know and understand very well. So, their denial is not based on a lack of recognition or knowledge, but on their habitual disobedience, for, as a general rule, no one denies such evidence except those who are willful and stubborn in their disobedience. You did not bring anything that we know, and no clear token has been revealed to you by means of which we follow you .

**Not for lack of knowledge.**

(And indeed We have sent down to you manifest Ayat) means, "We have sent to you, O Muhammad, clear signs that testify to your prophethood. (And indeed We have sent down to you manifest Ayat) means, "You recite and convey this Book to them day and night, although you are an Ummi (unlettered) who never read a book. All arguments point to the fact that the Arab Prophet received the same message as was sent down to Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and that the revelation received by the Arab Prophet tallied exactly with the predictions made in previous divine scriptures. This proves beyond all doubt that it was sent by God Himself.

**Rebellion and the signs.**

The only people who reject these signs, despite its clarity, are those who have abandoned Allah’s path. One disbelieves in His clear signs only when one's eyes are blocked from perceiving and one's fate from God has already been determined as unfor tunate. Due to their negativism, they begin to make such representations as are outwardly correct but which, in terms of the inner reality, are totally meaningless. (And they learn that which harms them and profits them not.) means, it harms their religion and does not have a benefit compared to its harm.

100.text:
"Why is it that every time they make a covenant, a group of them casts it aside, In fact, most of them do not believe" opens the verse with a question that charges the people with a habit, and the words every time make the habit repeated. The covenant is the bond the people make, and the group casts it aside, so the sentence shows a part of the people breaking what the whole had agreed. The run then turns the sentence from the act to the state behind it. The phrase in fact sets the truth against the question, and the verse states that most of them do not believe. The breaking of the covenant is therefore not an isolated lapse. It is the outward sign of a disbelief that is spread through most of the group. The verse before named the clear signs, and this verse shows the people who turned away from the covenant that accompanied them. The commentary states that some among them did fulfil the pledges, so the verse does not condemn every one of them, and the reader is asked to see the difference between the faithful few and the many who cast the covenant aside.

**Every time a covenant.**

Why whenever they make a covenant with God that they will believe in the Prophet s when he appears or that they will not give assistance to the idolaters against the Prophet s does a party of them reject it? cast it away repudiating it this is the response to the clause beginning with kullamā the interrogative of rebuke. Nay bal indicates a transition but most of them are disbelievers. Why whenever they make a covenant does a party of them reject itḍ Nay but most of them are disbelievers. Why whenever they made a covenant...: their predetermined fate sābiq al-taqdīr confounded them and their subsequent contrivances lāḥiq al-tadbīr broke their covenant.

**The Torah and the pledge.**

Allah had, as the Torah itself reports, made the Jews take the pledge that they would have faith in the Holy Prophet when he appeared. Commenting on this effrontery, the Holy Qur'an says that this is not the only instance of such a conduct on their part, for the Jews have, in fact, never fulfilled even those pledges which they acknowledge, and one group or another from among them has always been breaking the compacts they have entered into, especially with regard to religious matters. Due to their corrupt state, a group of the Jews would always break any commitment that they made, including the duty to have faith in what the Torah revealed about the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. (Is it ever so that when they make a covenant) i.e. the Jewish leaders with Muhammad (a party of them set it aside?) reject and break it.

**Most of them.**

(Nay! (the truth is:) most of them believe not) means, "There is not a promise that they make, but they break it and abandon it. Most of them do not really have faith in what Allah revealed, because faith leads to keeping to and honouring commitments and promises. It can even be said that most of those who have been guilty of such gross violations, did not at all believe in the compacts which they made with Allah.

**Those who kept the pledge.**

For there were some among them who did fulfil the pledges, so much so that many Jews finally accepted Sayyidna Muhammad as a true prophet, and joined the ranks of the Muslims. (As if they did not know!) means, "They knew the truth but abandoned it, hid it and denied the fact that they even had it." Due to their negativism, they begin to make such representations as are outwardly correct but which, in terms of the inner reality, are totally meaningless. People make many protestation of their faith, but all these mouthings being hollow and meaningless, they bear no relation to true faith and piety.

**What else the same passage holds.**

On being reminded of it, the Jews flatly denied even having taken such a pledge. Going against a pledge is only a sin and transgression, but having no faith in the pledge which one gives to Allah is outright infidelity.

101.text:
"Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them, confirming their own Scriptures" opens the verse with the arrival of a messenger, and the word now marks the moment the account turns to the act of the people. The messenger is from Allah, and the sentence describes him as confirming the Scriptures that the people already held. "some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know" then gives the response, and the picture is of a book thrown behind the back, so that it is no longer before the eye. The phrase as if they did not know is the sharpest part of the sentence, since the people did know, and their pretence of ignorance is the charge.
