The phrase you are facing towards Allah makes the act of turning a matter of the heart, since the Lord is not confined to a place. "Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing" closes the verse with the attributes that make this possible, the one who encompasses all things and the one who knows them. The word surely confirms the statement, and the two attributes cover the whole of creation and all its knowledge. The verse before named the places of worship, and this verse answers any sense that a single place contains the Lord. The sources explain that the verse came as a response to the questions about the direction of prayer after it was changed, and the reader is shown that the direction is a command and not a limit on the Lord. The wider point is that the believer is asked to turn his face where the Lord has directed, and to know that the Lord is present in every direction he may turn.

**East and west belong to Allah.**

(So wherever you turn (yourselves or your faces) there is the Face of Allah (and He is High above, over His Throne) means, "Allah's direction is wherever you face, east or west. The Qiblah for the People of Al-Madīnah is what is between the East and the West. (What is between the east and the west is the Qiblah for the people of Al-Madīnah, Ash-Sham and 'Iraq.) (What is between the east and the west is a Qiblah.)

**The changed direction.**

When Allah changed the Qiblah that is to say, commanded the Muslims to turn towards the Ka'bah in their Salah, and not towards the Baytul-Maqdis --, the Jews raised all kinds of objections to it, and tried to produce in the minds of the Muslims doubts and misgiving which, had they taken root, would have led to the denial of the Holy Prophet g and to the giving up of prescribed Salah, thus laying waste the mosque of the Holy Prophet . For some sixteen or seventeen months after that, the Muslims had to, under the commandment of Allah, turn towards the Baytul-Maqdis (at Bayt al-Maqdis) while offering Salah. When we returned from our journey we asked the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, about this but he did not give us an answer. Allah, exalted is He, then revealed this verse (Unto Allah belong the East and the West)' .

**Not confined to a place.**

The Holy Qur'an, however, speaks in general terms of the mosques of Allah" so as to lay down a regular and permanent law, for all the peoples, covering all the possible cases of desecrating mosques and of hindering the "remembrance" of Allah in any way and thus laying them waste -- it denounces those who are capable of such a misdeed as being "unjust" or "cruel", and threatens them with humiliation in this world and dire punishment in the other, for the dignity of a mosque requires that one should enter it in a spirit of lowliness and respect, and with the fear of Allah in one's heart. The verse points out that had Allah been limited to any one direction, a fixed and permanent orientation would have been necessary for worshipping Him, but that, being infinite and beyond all possible limitations and qualifications, He is the Lord of the East and the West and of all conceivable directions -- He is everywhere, and surrounds everything. A human being, for instance, cannot be in two places at the same time, and, in consequence, people think that God is also to be found only in some particular place. True, He has prescribed a direction for us to face when we worship, but this is a purely organizational requirement for prayer; it does not mean that God is to be found in only one direction and not in any other.

**Turning the face.**

Then Allah mentioned the direction of prayer to Him, saying (Unto Allah belong the East and the West) as a direction of prayer for him who does not know the correct direction of prayer, (and whithersoever ye turn) your faces in prayer after ascertaining the direction, (there is Allah's Countenance) that prayer is performed in Allah's pleasure. This verse was revealed about a group of Companions of the Prophet ﷺ who prayed whilst travelling in the wrong direction after doing their best to determine the correct direction. It is also said that saying (Unto Allah belong the East and the West) means: the people of the East and the people of the West have one direction of prayer which is the Sacred Precinct, and therefore (there is Allah's Countenance) means: that is the direction of prayer to Allah, (Lo! Allah is All-Embracing) regarding the direction of prayer, (All- Knowing) of their intentions. Whether He instructs you to face Bayt al-Maqdis or the Kaaba, or you make a mistake in the direction of prayer or are not sure of it, then it is not an issue, because to Allah belongs every direction.

**All-Encompassing and All-Knowing.**

Allah has authority over the entire world, and He instructs His servants as He wills. Allah is vast in His blessings; He covers His creation with His mercy and ease. He knows their intentions and everything that they do. When those who have attributes become effaced how can any attribute of theirs remainḍ He said whithersoever you turn there is the face of God.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The following was revealed either when the Jews criticised the change of the direction of prayer qibla or concerning the supererogatory prayers on animal-back during journeys which one may pray in any direction To God belong the East and the West that is the entire earth because these two directions represent both sides of it the earth; whithersoever you turn your faces in prayer by His command there is the Face of God the direction of prayer with which He is pleased. In order to understand these two verses, one should keep in mind three different incidents connected with the three groups hostile to Islam, all of which were, in one way or another, guilty of preventing people from worshipping Allah in mosques and of laying them waste. God is Embracing His bounty embracing all things Knowing how to manage His creation. The Romans had once invaded Bayt al-Maqdis, and the ignorant among them had polluted the Baytul-Maqdis, which naturally prevented people from performing Salah in this mosque. The Christians in a way looked upon the Romans as their ancestors; moreover, the humiliation of the Jews was in itself pleasing to them.

116.text:
"They say, Allah has offspring" opens with the claim that the verse answers, and the word say is used of the people who make it. The claim is that Allah has a child, and the sentence gives it in the people's own words before the reply. The run "Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth" turns the claim away by praising the Lord above such a thing, and then corrects the claim with the truth of ownership, since everything in the heavens and the earth is His and so cannot be His offspring. The word belongs is the centre of the sentence, because a child would be of the same nature as the parent, while creation belongs to the Lord as a possession. "all are subject to His Will" closes the verse by widening the ownership into obedience. Everything that exists is subject to the Lord's will, and so none of it can share in His nature. The verse before named the Lord's direction and presence, and this verse removes any idea that the Lord has a family or a partner in His being. The sources explain that the claim of offspring was made by the Jews and Christians and by others among the idolaters, and the verse answers all of them with one statement of the Lord's ownership and His glory, so that the reader is not left to choose between their accounts of the Lord.

**Allah has offspring.**

And they the Jews and the Christians and those that claim that the angels are God’s daughters say read wa-qālū or simply qālū ‘God has taken to Himself a son’; God says Glory be to Him! as a way of exalting Himself above this; Nay to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth as possessions creatures and servants and this sovereignty contradicts having a child and is expressed by the particle mā ‘all that’ in order to include all creation that is not rational; all obey His will submitting to that which is required from each one of them here the emphasis is on rational beings. Then Allah mentions the claims of the Jews and Christians that Ezra and Jesus are the sons of Allah, saying: (And they) the Jews and Christians (say: Allah hath taken unto Himself a Son) Ezra and the Messiah (Jesus). The Jews, the Christians and the idolaters, who worship others alongside Allah, said that Allah had taken a son.

**Glory be to Him.**

(Be He glorified!) He is far exalted to have a son or partner it is not as they say, (but whatsoever is in the heavens and the earth) of creation (is His) are His servants. He is far above and beyond such a thing, because He has no need of His creation, and no one has a son unless he is needy; and to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He is pure, without fault, incomparable, the one Lord-one in forbearance, one in loyalty, one in love. (The Badī' (Originator) of the heavens and the earth.) which means, He created them when nothing resembling them existed.

**Ownership of the heavens and earth.**

(Nay, to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and on earth,) meaning, the truth is not as the disbelievers claimed, rather, Allah's is the kingdom of the heavens and earth and whatever and whoever is in, on and between them. Allah is the Supreme Authority in the heavens and earth, and He is the Creator, Provider and Sustainer Who decides all the affairs of the creation as He wills. Rather, to Him belongs what is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoted to Him.

**Subject to His will.**

(All are subservient unto Him) linked to Him by the bond of servitude and the declaration of His Oneness. All created beings are His servants, in submission to Him, glory be to Him! They are His servants and He deals with them as He wills. Firstly, all that exists in heaven or earth belongs to Allah.

**Knowledge and the claim.**

The commentator al-Baydawi has remarked that, Allah being the First Cause of the things, the earlier Shari'ahs had allowed the use of the title "Father" for Him, but that the ignorant misunderstood and distorted the sense of "Fatherhood" so badly that to entertain such a belief or to apply this title to Allah has now been declared to be an act of infidelity (Kufr). That is to say, the phrase does not signify that Allah actually addressed an existent and commanded it "to be", but it is an allegorical illustration of His omnipotence, suggesting that there is no interval between an act of will on His part and its realization. For, Allah is omniscient, and Divine Knowledge comprehends everything that has been, or is, or will be, so that what does not yet exist according to our reckoning does already exist in Divine Knowledge. If the servant does harm, He does not cut off from him, for He is one in forbearance.

**What else the same passage holds.**

As the Holy Qur'an reports in some other verses, some of the Jews called the Prophet Uzayr (Ezra) the son of God, as did the Christians in the case of Sayyidna Isa (Jesus)~ and most of them still do, while the mushrikin of Makkah considered the angels to be the daughters of God. These two verses show the absurdity of such assertions. For, even on rational grounds, it is totally impossible that God should have offspring. Were it at all possible, the situation would necessarily involve either of the two alternative characteristics -- the offspring would belong either to the same genus as the father does, or to a different genus. If it belongs to a different genus, that obviously is a defect, while God should in order to be God, be free of all defects -- as reason itself requires, and as Verse 116 affirms. If the offspring belongs to the same genus, that too is a contradiction in terms, for God has no equal and no existent can belong to the same genus as He does. God alone is the Necessary Being (Al-Dhat al-Wajib), and hence necessarily carries within Himself the Attributes of Perfection which are peculiar to Him alone and which cannot exist in any one other than God. Now, if we deny a necessary attribute to a certain being, we automatically deny the existence of that being. So, no one other than God can be a necessary being. Insofar as "necessity" is in itself the essence of the Ultimate Reality, or an inalienable quality of the Ultimate Reality, anyone other than God cannot share the Reality with Him. Hence, it would be a plain and simple contradiction in terms of claim that anyone other than God can belong to the same genus. Having refuted the false claims of the Jews, the Christians and the mushrikin, the two verses proceed to demonstrate how and why the Attributes of Perfection are peculiar to Allah Himself and Him alone. Secondly, everything is also subservient to Him -- in the sense that no one can interfere with His omnipotence (for example, with His power to create a.nd to destroy), even if some men may be lax in obeying the injunctions of the Shari'ah.

117.text:
"He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth" opens the verse with a title that names the Lord as the one who brings all things into being from nothing. The word Originator is the key, since it means the one who creates without a model, and the heavens and the earth are the first things named as His work. "When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, Be!" then describes how the creating happens. The Lord decrees a matter, and the decree is a single word, so the act needs no effort and no process. The word simply shows how little is required, because the one who speaks is the one who creates. "And it is" closes the sentence with the result, which is that the thing comes into existence the moment the word is given. The verse before showed that the Lord has no offspring, and this verse explains why, since a child would need to be made in the way that creatures are made, while the Lord creates by a word. The sources explain that the decree in the verse concerns the creation of things, and that the claim of a son was an error about the nature of the Lord. The reader is left with the Originator who needs only to say the word for the thing to be.

**The Originator.**

Creator of the heavens and the earth making them exist without any exemplary precedent; and when He decrees wills a thing to exist He but says to it ‘Be’ and it is that is to say it becomes fa-yakūnu a variant reading has fa-yakūna on account of it being the response in the subjunctive mood to the jussive statement. (The Originator of the heavens and the earth!) He originated them when they were nothing before. Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and all that is in them; and there is nothing in creation that is like Him.

**The decree and the word.**

If He decrees and wills something, He only says to it ‘Be’ and it is as He willed it. (When He decreeth a thing) when He wants to create a child without a father, like Jesus, (He saith unto it only: Be!) be a child without a father, just like Adam was without a father or mother, (And it is). When He decides on an affair nothing preordained maqdūr can oppose it and nothing created mafṬūr can separate itself from His decree.

**Mystery and the Lord's nature.**

Let us begin by saying that it is a mystery -- and we are using the word "mystery", not in the debased and the modern sense, but in the original meaning of the term which implies that certain realities are altogether beyond the reach of human understanding, and that certain other realities cannot and must not, even when partially or wholly understood, be given out to those who have no aptitude for receiving them, and that with regard to them it is advisable "to keep one's lips closed. " In these matters, when and what one chooses to reveal is ultimately not the question of liberalism or democratism or egalitarianism, but that of "spiritual etiquette. God alone is the Necessary Being (Al-Dhat al-Wajib), and hence necessarily carries within Himself the Attributes of Perfection which are peculiar to Him alone and which cannot exist in any one other than God. Hence, it would be a plain and simple contradiction in terms of claim that anyone other than God can belong to the same genus.

**Necessary Being.**

The Originator al-badīʿ according to the scholars is the One who brings the entity ʿayn into existence without any model lā ʿalā mithāl. According to the people of allusion He is the One and there is nothing like Him laysa lahu shayun mithlihi since this term alludes to both the negation of any likeness mithl to His essence and the negation of any model mithāl for His acts. (The Badī' (Originator) of the heavens and the earth.) which means, He created them when nothing resembling them existed. True, He has prescribed a direction for us to face when we worship, but this is a purely organizational requirement for prayer; it does not mean that God is to be found in only one direction and not in any other.

**No likeness to creatures.**

Another error into which they fell was to liken God to man. A human being, for instance, cannot be in two places at the same time, and, in consequence, people think that God is also to be found only in some particular place. But only those who have needs beget sons, and God is above all such imperfections and limitations. (Nay, to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and on earth,) meaning, the truth is not as the disbelievers claimed, rather, Allah's is the kingdom of the heavens and earth and whatever and whoever is in, on and between them.

118.text:
"Those who have no knowledge say, If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us" opens the verse with a demand, and the demand is put in the mouths of people who lack knowledge. The sentence places the wish for a direct word from Allah, or for a visible sign, at the heart of their speech. The phrase If only is the form of the wish, and it shows that they think the proof is missing rather than their own readiness to accept it. The verse does not describe them as searching. It describes them as asking for a particular kind of evidence that would suit their own terms. "The same was said by those who came before" then widens the scene. The sources read these words as the same demand made by earlier communities of disbelievers to their own prophets, so that the Meccans and the People of the Book are placed in a long line of people who asked for signs on their own terms. The sentence is therefore not about one group at one time. It is about a habit of mind that repeats itself. The run "Their hearts are all alike. Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith" explains why the demand repeats, and its second half closes the verse with the answer. The sources read the likeness of the hearts as the shared stubbornness and unbelief of those who refuse, whatever their time and place. The word alike is not a judgement on the people as individuals. It is a judgement on the state in which they stand before the message. The second half of that run closes the verse with the answer. The signs are clear, and the clearness is not a matter of the demands that the people make. It is available to those who are certain when the truth appears to them, and the verse turns the reader from the asking of the stubborn to the certainty of those who already see.

**The demand for a sign.**

The jalalayn-style reading gives the words of the disbelievers in the form of a complaint, asking why God does not speak to them to say that the Prophet is His messenger, and why a sign does not come to them of the kind they have requested, in order to show his sincerity. The reading presents the demand as a condition set in advance of belief. The demand is a test that the people impose on the message, and it is made in the form of a request that the proof be shown to them first. The short commentary reads the same demand in the same way, saying that the people were so set against the message that they would not accept it unless God spoke to them directly, or unless a sign confirming the prophethood of Muhammad appeared before them. The sources agree that the demand is the expression of obstinacy, and that it hides a refusal rather than a real search for the truth.

**The likeness of the hearts.**

The short commentary explains the phrase their hearts are all alike as meaning that their words and hearts are the same. The jalalayn-style reading says that their hearts are much alike in unbelief and stubbornness, and it adds that this is meant as a consolation for the Prophet, so that he does not think that the refusal of his own people is unique. The Maʿārif commentary takes the verse as tracing the origin of the demand to a distortion of the heart, in which all the ignorant, past or present, are alike, and it explains that the parrot-like repetition of the same demand throughout the ages is the sign of this distortion. The sources therefore treat the phrase as both a comfort and a diagnosis. The comfort is that the Prophet is not alone, and the diagnosis is that the refusal lies in the heart and not in the lack of signs.

**The clear signs for the certain.**

The mukhtasar reading explains that Allah makes His signs clear to those who are certain of the truth when it appears to them, not doubting or resisting it. The tanwir reading makes the signs the commands, the prohibitions, and the traits described in the Torah, which are clear to the people who believe. The jalalayn-style reading contrasts the people who are certain with the people who demand signs, and says that to request other signs after the clear ones would be obduracy. The verse thus draws a line between two groups. One group asks for more evidence after the evidence has been given, and the other group already has enough in the signs before them. The sources do not say that the signs are missing. They say that the certain see them and that the stubborn do not.

**Asking for a sign after the sign.**

The Maʿārif commentary states that the demands of the disbelievers were two in number. The first was that Allah Himself should speak to them, either directly as He spoke to the angels or through the angels as He spoke to the prophets, so that no new prophet would be needed. The second was that, if this were refused, they would ask for a sign or proof in confirmation of the prophethood of Muhammad. The commentary notes that the first demand was foolish enough on its face, and that the second was a way of keeping the argument open forever. The verse answers the pattern by showing that the signs have already been made clear, and that the request for more is a continuation of the refusal and not a sincere step toward faith.

**The line of those who came before.**

The verse links the demand of the people with the demands made to the earlier prophets, and the sources read this link as a warning that the same pattern will repeat. The tazkirul reading of the wider passage speaks of the way the people of every age looked for signs that suited their own taste, and failed to see the invisible but meaningful signs that the prophets carried in their lives and words. The reader is shown a people who measure the message by the material form they expect, and who are unable to see the truth when it comes in a form that does not match that expectation. The verse before this one named the Lord who gives direction and who is not limited to a place, and this verse shows the same people demanding that the Lord speak to them in a way they have chosen. The reader is left with the clear signs, and with the question of whether he is certain enough to see them without demanding more.

**Certainty as the condition.**

The verse closes on the people of sure faith, and the sources make certainty the condition of seeing the signs. The Maʿārif commentary and the short commentary agree that the verse is addressed to the Prophet with a consolation, and that the Prophet is not made responsible for the stubbornness of those who will not see. The reader can take from this that the signs do not fail, and that the failure to see them is the failure of the one who has not made himself certain. The verse therefore keeps the clearness of the signs and the stubbornness of the demand side by side, and asks the reader to choose the first.

The Maʿārif commentary also makes the point that the demand is no more than a foolish custom, one that ignorant people have unthinkingly practised in the earlier ages as well. The verse traces the origin of the custom to a distortion of the heart, and in that respect all the ignorant are alike. The commentary explains that the first demand, that Allah should speak directly, was on its face silly enough, since the people wanted the Lord to address them as He addresses the angels and the prophets, and yet they did not show readiness to accept what was said. The second demand, for a sign confirming the prophethood, was a way of keeping the argument open, so that no answer could ever be final. The verse answers both by showing that the signs have already been made clear, and that a request for more is part of the same refusal. The mukhtasar reading adds that disbelieving communities said similar things to their prophets in the past, even when they came from different times and places, and that the likeness is in the disbelief and not in the particular words. The reader is therefore asked to see the demand as a repeated pattern that the verse names once, so that it is recognised whenever it appears again.

119.text:
"We have surely sent you with the truth O Prophet as a deliverer of good news and a warner" opens the verse with the mission of the Prophet, and the word surely places the sending beyond doubt. The sentence states that he was sent with the truth, which is the guidance that stands behind every part of his message. The two roles are named together, the one who brings good news and the one who warns. The good news belongs to those who respond, and the warning belongs to those who do not, so the mission is set out as a double office in one sentence. "And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire" then turns the sentence to the limit of his responsibility. The word accountable is the key, because the Prophet is not asked to answer for the fate of those who choose the fire. The verse before showed the stubbornness of the people who demanded signs, and this verse meets the grief that such stubbornness might cause the Prophet by stating plainly what is required of him, which is to deliver the message and no more. The jalalayn-style reading treats the twofold office as the same message received in two ways, so that the same guidance brings good tidings or warning according to the response. The sentence is short, and its brevity gives the reader the full scope of the mission without any argument. The Maʿārif commentary makes the point that the Prophet was sent as a mercy for all the worlds, and that his function is twofold, so the verse keeps the two roles together. The tanwir reading names the truth he carries as the Qurʾān together with the declaration of the Oneness of Allah. The verse is the consolation that the Prophet needs at this point.

**The mission of good news and warning.**

The mukhtasar reading explains that the Prophet was sent with the religion of truth, in which there is no doubt, to bring the good news of Paradise to those who have faith and to warn disbelievers about the fire. The tanwir reading names the truth as the Qurʾān together with the declaration of the Oneness of Allah, so that the message he carries is both the book and the belief that it teaches. The jalalayn-style reading gives the same double office, a bearer of good tidings of Paradise for those who respond to the guidance and a warner of the fire for those who do not respond. The sources therefore read the two roles as one mission, and the verse places the mission before the limit that follows it.

**No accountability for the people of the fire.**

The Maʿārif commentary sets the verse against the one before, which says that those who persisted in their denial did so out of sheer malice and ignorance and could not be expected to reform. Since the Prophet had been sent as a mercy for all the worlds, the thought that they would not change was likely to make him sad on their account. The verse therefore offers consolation, and it assures him that he will not be held responsible or taken to account for those who willingly pursue the way to hell. All that he is required to do is to keep performing his own function, and not to worry about who accepts the truth and who does not. The sources state this as the plain meaning of the verse, and they use it to show that the Prophet's duty is clear even where his hope is disappointed.

**The meaning of the negative.**

The tanwir reading takes the phrase you will not be asked about the owners of hellfire as meaning that it is not befitting for the Prophet to ask about the dwellers of hell, and it adds that some have read it as an instruction not to ask for the forgiveness of those in hell. The jalalayn-style reading records a variant reading in which the verb is in the form of an imperative, do not ask, and it notes that the sense is the same, since the Prophet is not to press for an answer about the fate of the disbelievers. The sources therefore agree that the verse concerns the Prophet's own task, and not the judgement of the people, which is in the hands of Allah.

**The limit of the duty.**

The short commentary and the Maʿārif commentary both draw the same lesson from the verse, which is that the Prophet should not be sad at the refusal of his people. The duty is to deliver the message clearly, and the outcome belongs to Allah. The tazkirul reading of the wider passage, which speaks of the Lord as not confined to a place and not begetting a son, places this verse within a discussion of right belief, and it uses the verse to show that the Lord is the one who guides and who judges, while the messenger is the one who delivers. The reader sees that the duty is limited, and that the limit is a mercy, since it removes from the Prophet the burden of answering for those who refuse.

**The shape of the mission.**

The verse is short, and the sources read its brevity as a sign of its weight. The sentence names the truth, the good news, the warning, and the limit of responsibility, and each of these is a complete thought. The reader does not need a long argument to see that the mission is clear and that its outcome is not in the Prophet's hands. The verse therefore leaves the one who reads it with the duty to deliver the message in the form it has been given, and with the knowledge that those who choose the fire are not the messenger's responsibility.

**The consolation of the Prophet.**

The Maʿārif commentary links the verse to the one before it, which says that those who persisted in their denial did so out of sheer malice and ignorance. The commentary observes that the Prophet had been sent as a mercy for all the worlds, and that the thought of their being incorrigible was likely to make him sad on their account. The verse is therefore a consolation, and it arrives at the point where the Prophet might feel the weight of the refusal most. The commentary states that he has been sent down to men, bearing the truth and the genuine faith, and that his function is twofold, to give glad tidings to those who accept and to warn those who deny. The verse does not leave him to carry the outcome alone. Allah assures him that he will not be held responsible for those who willingly pursue the way to hell, and that his task is to keep performing his own function. The consolation is given in a single clear sentence, and the sources read its clarity as a comfort in itself, since the Prophet knows exactly where his duty ends.

The jalalayn-style reading explains the mission with the phrase a bearer of good tidings and a warner, and it names the good tidings as Paradise for those who respond to the guidance and the warning as the fire for those who do not. The reading makes clear that the response is the hinge of the whole matter, since the same message brings good news to one group and warning to another, depending on how the message is received. The Prophet's role is therefore to set the message before the people in full, and the response is theirs. The tanwir reading adds that the truth he was sent with is the Qurʾān together with the declaration of the Oneness of Allah, and that the Paradise is for the believers while the fire is for those who disbelieve in Allah. The sources do not treat the twofold task as a burden that falls on the Prophet alone. They treat it as the form that a faithful delivery of the message must take.

The sentence about the owners of the fire is also read by the sources as a statement about the limit of the Prophet's concern. The tanwir reading notes that it is not befitting for the Prophet to ask about the dwellers of hell, and the jalalayn-style reading records the variant in which the verb takes the form of an imperative, so that the instruction is not to ask after the fate of those who have chosen the fire. Both readings place the question of the fate of the disbelievers in the hands of Allah, and both leave the Prophet free from the anxiety of having to know the outcome of each person. The verse thus turns the Prophet's attention from the question he cannot answer to the mission he has been given, which is clear and within his power to complete.

120.text:
"Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith" opens the verse with a plain statement that the two groups will not be satisfied with the Prophet. The word never is a firm denial, and the condition until you follow their faith names what would have to happen for their pleasure to come. The sentence does not describe a passing dislike. It describes a demand that can only be met by the Prophet giving up the message. The condition "until you follow their faith. Say, Allah’s guidance is the only true guidance" joins the demand to the answer that refuses it, and the second half of that run is the command to the Prophet to state the truth in his own words, and the word only excludes every other guidance from the claim. The sentence is short and firm, and it leaves no space for compromise. The verse does not leave the Prophet to weigh the two demands on his own, since the answer is given to him to say and the decision about the message is already settled. "And if you were to follow their desires after all the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah" closes the verse with the warning. The conditional sets the following of their desires against the knowledge that has come, and it shows that such a following would leave the Prophet without any protection or helper against Allah. The sentence treats the desire of the people as the thing to be refused, and it makes the refusal the test of the Prophet's faithfulness.

**Pleasure that cannot be bought.**

The mukhtasar reading explains that Allah addresses and warns His Prophet, telling him that the Jews and the Christians will never be happy with him unless he leaves Islam and follows what they do. The tanwir reading names the Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran, and it says that the demand was that the Prophet should follow their creed and their direction of prayer. The Maʿārif commentary explains that the denial of the two groups was not due to a lack of convincing arguments, but was motivated by pride and self-satisfaction. Each of the two groups believed its own religion to be the only genuine one, and neither would be pleased until the Prophet accepted its religion.

**Guidance is Allah's.**

The jalalayn-style reading gives the words of the command as saying that God's guidance, which is Islam, is the true guidance, besides which there is only error. The tanwir reading expands the phrase to mean that the religion of Allah is Islam and that the direction of prayer is the Kaʿba. The Maʿārif commentary explains that the religions of the Jews and the Christians had once been genuine and had been instituted by Allah, but that each had since distorted its religion. Islam, as the final law, had abrogated the earlier ones, and so in this last age it is the only guidance that is acceptable to Allah. The verse therefore names the guidance as the single source of truth, and the sources explain why the earlier faiths no longer serve in that role.

**Desires after knowledge.**

The Maʿārif commentary observes that the verse equates the earlier religions, in their present distorted state and after their abrogation, with desires, the plural of a word meaning personal wish or baseless conjecture. The jalalayn-style reading treats the conditional as hypothetical, so that the following of their desires would bring no friend and no helper against Allah. The mukhtasar reading says that the verse makes clear the seriousness of leaving the truth and of following people of falsehood. The sources therefore read the warning as a general principle, that knowledge once given must not be traded for the wishes of others, and that doing so cuts a person off from every protection except the protection of the Lord.

**The protection that is lost.**

The tazkirul reading of the wider passage speaks of the prophets who were confronted by people who asked why they were not blessed with worldly treasures, and who measured the messenger by the standards of this life. The reading shows that the pressure on the messengers was constant, and that the people always tried to bend the message toward their own tastes. The verse before named the clear signs and the demands of the stubborn, and this verse names the pressure to follow the desires of the two groups. The sources agree that the Prophet is not to yield, and that a yielding would leave him exposed, since the protection of Allah is only for those who keep to the knowledge they have.

**The firmness of the message.**

The verse is firm in its statement, and the sources read the firmness as the meaning of the whole passage. The Prophet is told to say what is true, and he is warned against the desires that would draw him away from it. The reader sees that the message does not change to please those who hold other faiths, and that its truth is not reduced by the displeasure of the people who reject it. The verse leaves the one who reads it with the guidance of Allah as the only guidance, and with the warning that to follow other desires after knowledge has come is to lose every helper.

**The pride of the two groups.**

The Maʿārif commentary explains that the Holy Prophet was anxious to save as many men as possible from misguidance, and that he took great pains to convince those who denied him, being especially lenient and gentle with the People of the Book. The verse informs him that their denial is not due to any lack of convincing arguments or proofs. It is motivated by pride and self-satisfaction, since each of the two groups believes its own religion to be the only genuine one. The commentary therefore reads the verse as a correction to the Prophet's hope. He might have expected that the arguments would bring them round, and the verse tells him that the root of their refusal lies in their own sense of themselves. The mukhtasar reading makes the same point in plain terms, saying that the Jews and the Christians will never be happy with him unless he leaves Islam and follows what they do, and that this demand cannot be met by any argument. The sources read the verse as a teaching that pride is not moved by proof, and that a messenger must not bend his message to satisfy it.

The tanwir reading names the two communities as the Jews of Medina and the Christians of Najran, and it explains that the demand was that the Prophet should follow their creed and their direction of prayer. The reading makes the demand concrete, since the direction of prayer was a matter on which the people had strong views, and the verse uses the question of direction to test the Prophet's firmness. The Maʿārif commentary explains that the religions of the two communities had once been genuine and had been instituted by Allah, but that each had since distorted its religion out of shape. The sources therefore do not say that the earlier faiths were without origin. They say that the origin was true, that distortion followed, and that the final law of Islam had abrogated the earlier ones, so that the guidance of Allah in this last age is the one that stands.

The tanwir reading explains the knowledge that has come to the Prophet as the knowledge that the religion of Allah is Islam and that His direction of prayer is the Kaʿba, so that the following of their creed and their direction would mean giving up exactly what had been revealed to him. The mukhtasar reading states the consequence in plain words, that without Allah there would be no friend and no helper, and that the one who follows desires after clear truth stands alone before the chastisement of his Lord. The sentence therefore ends where it began, with the fact that the Prophet is not to be moved from the guidance he has been given, since the protection of Allah is the only protection there is.

121.text:
"Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed" opens the verse with the people who have received the Book, and the phrase as it should be followed names the manner of their reading. The Book is the object of their following, and the verse says that they follow it in the right way and not carelessly. The sentence is a description of a group, and it is also a standard against which the other group is measured. "It is they who truly believe in it" then gives the result of such reading. The word truly marks the belief as real, and it is the reading that makes the belief sincere. The people who read the Book as it should be read are those who believe in it, and the verse ties the belief to the manner of the reading. "As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers" closes the verse with the contrast. The rejecters are described as losers, and the word losers is the consequence of their rejection. The sentence does not say that they are simply mistaken. It says that they have lost something, and the reader is left to see that the loss is the greatest loss a person can suffer. The verse is short, and its three clauses move from the reading, to the belief, to the loss, so that each step follows from the one before. The Maʿārif commentary states that these honest readers used their intellect and their will, and the verse joins the two.

**Reading as it should be read.**

The jalalayn-style reading explains that the phrase as it should be followed is a circumstantial qualifier, and it says that the people who recite the Book as it was revealed are those who follow it properly. The mukhtasar reading describes this group as the people of the Scripture who know the revealed texts they were given and who follow them properly. The tanwir reading takes the phrase to mean that these people describe the Book as it is, do not alter it, expound what is lawful and unlawful, and act according to what is clear while believing in what is ambiguous. The sources therefore agree that the right reading is one that keeps the text intact and acts on its meaning.

**Those who truly believe.**

The Maʿārif commentary explains that Allah has given a Book to the Christians as well as to the Jews, and that the men who read it as it should be read were not like most of their co-religionists. They had neither distorted the words nor the meanings, and they had not tried to conceal the prophecies about the coming of the Prophet. They used their intellect to understand the meanings and their will to accept the truth and to follow it. The commentary states that by acknowledging the Qurʾān they affirmed their own Books and acted upon them, since those Books foretold the coming of the last prophet and the last Book.

**The people who were honest and just.**

The jalalayn-style reading gives a particular occasion, saying that the verse was revealed concerning a group of Ethiopians who presented themselves to the Prophet and accepted Islam. The tanwir reading names the believers from among the People of the Book, including a certain companion who had been a Jew and others who had come to faith, and it presents them as the people who read the Torah rightly and therefore believed in Muhammad and the Qurʾān. The sources offer these men as examples of the honest and just people who recognised the truth when it came, and the verse is read as a witness to the possibility of such recognition within the same tradition that the rejecters claimed for themselves.

**Those who reject and lose.**

The jalalayn-style reading explains that the one who disbelieves in the Book, by distorting it, will be destined for the fire to remain in it forever. The tanwir reading says that the rejecters are duped in that they lose both this world and the world to come. The Maʿārif commentary adds that those who persist in denial are bound to suffer the greatest loss, since they have refused to believe in the last revelation and have shown little belief in their own Books. The verse before named the pressure of the two groups to follow their desires, and this verse shows the consequence of holding to those desires against the Book, which is that the holder loses both worlds.

**The tazkirul reading on the same passage.**

The tazkirul reading of the wider passage speaks of the messengers of God who were confronted with people who could think only in worldly terms, and who expected the messenger to match their materialistic standards. It describes how the people failed to comprehend the arguments of the preacher because of their negative mindset. The reader can see in this reading the same division that the verse makes, between those who receive the Book with a clear mind and those whose minds are closed by worldly expectation. The verse therefore asks the reader to read the Book as it should be read, and to believe in it with a sincere heart, so as not to be counted among those who lose.

**The turning of the verse.**

The Maʿārif commentary explains that the verse before this one dealt with the hopeless condition of the opponents of Islam among the People of the Book. The present verse turns, in the usual manner of the Qurʾān, to the other aspect, and it speaks of those Jews and Christians who were honest and just, and who, having recognised the truth, affirmed the Prophet and accepted Islam. The commentary observes that the Qurʾān gives both aspects of a community in one passage, so that the reader is not left with a single picture of those who received the Book. The turn is significant because it shows that the recognition of the truth was possible within the same tradition, and that the difference lay in how the Book was received and not in the community to which a person belonged.

The Maʿārif commentary explains how it was possible for these men to effect a radical change in themselves. They read the Book observing the rights of its recitation, which means that they neither distorted the words nor the meanings, and that they did not misinterpret or conceal the prophecies about the coming of the Prophet. The commentary states that they used their intellect in trying to understand the meanings, and their will in accepting the truth and following it. The verse thus joins two faculties, understanding and willingness, and the sources read it as the condition of true reading. A reader who has the understanding but not the will is in the position of the rejecters, and a reader who has the will but not the understanding cannot judge what the Book requires.

The mukhtasar reading describes the honest group as the people who find in their scriptures signs pointing to the truth of the Prophet Muhammad, and who for this reason have faith in him at once. The reading contrasts them with the group that sticks to its disbelief, and for whom there is loss. The jalalayn-style reading gives the particular occasion as a group of Ethiopians who presented themselves to the Prophet and accepted Islam, and it explains the phrase observing the right recitation as a circumstantial qualifier, so that the reading is joined to the manner in which the Book was recited. The sources therefore agree that the honest readers are identified by the signs they find in the text and by the readiness with which they accept them.

122.text:
"O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others" opens the verse with a direct address to the Children of Israel, and the call to remember is the first thing the sentence asks of them. The word remember is repeated across the passage and it marks the moment when the account turns back to the favours given to them. The favours are called My favours, which places the gift in the hands of the Lord who gave it. The second part of the sentence says that the Lord honoured them above the others, so that the favour is also a distinction. The verse is short, and its brevity is a reminder that the gifts are known and need no long argument. The verse opens the Israelites back to the favour they had been shown, so that the reader sees the gift before any warning. The reader is asked to hold the favours in mind as a basis for gratitude, and as a reason for the people to return to the path that the Lord had opened for them.

**The call to remember.**

The mukhtasar reading explains that the verse calls the Israelites to remember the blessings, sacred and worldly, which were given to them, and to remember that they were favoured over those of their time with prophethood and authority. The jalalayn-style reading gives the same sense, saying that the favour was the gift by which they were preferred over all the worlds, and it notes that a similar verse has already been mentioned earlier in the surah. The tanwir reading explains that the favour was that the forefathers of the people were delivered from Pharaoh and his people, and that the bounties and blessings were given to them, and it adds that the preference was for Islam among the people of their time.

**The favours and the honour.**

The Maʿārif commentary explains that the verse is part of a larger section of the surah that deals with the conduct of the Israelites through their history, and that the statement with which the account begins is repeated at its end. The purpose of the repetition is to make the two ideas sink deep into the mind. The verse encourages the Israelites to come back to the straight path by reminding them of the blessings that Allah has bestowed on them, and it prepares for the warning about the Day of Judgment that follows. The honour in the verse is therefore a basis for responsibility as well as a cause for pride.

**The calling of the Israelites.**

The tazkirul reading describes the Children of Israel as selected by God to perform a special task, which was to call other nations to turn to God and to impress on them that they were answerable to their Lord for their actions. The reading names the prophets who came from among them, among them Abraham, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David, Solomon, Zachariah, John the Baptist, and Jesus. The reading explains that over the centuries the community began to degenerate, and that it took its privileged position as an indication of ethnic superiority instead of a charge to be carried out. The verse is read in this light as a reminder of the task that the favour carried with it.

**The favour that was misread.**

The tazkirul reading goes on to say that the coming of the Arab prophet signified the replacement of the Children of Israel by the Children of Ishmael as the chosen people for the task of communicating God's word. It notes that those among the Israelites who were truly pious recognised that the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad came from the same source as the prophets before him, and that those who denied him acted from prejudice. The verse before named the book and the honest among the people of the Book, and this verse calls the whole people back to the favour they had been given, so that they can see whether they have kept it.

**Gratitude as the response.**

The sources agree that the response to the favour is gratitude, and that gratitude is shown by keeping to the path that the favour opened. The jalalayn-style reading and the mukhtasar reading both treat the call to remember as an invitation to return, and the tanwir reading sees the favour as the deliverance and the honour as the gift of Islam. The reader is left with the same favours that the verse names, and with the question of how far they have been remembered in the way the verse asks. The verse thus opens the next section of the account by calling the people back to what was given them, so that they may answer it with thanks.

123.text:
"And guard yourselves against the Day when no soul will be of any help to another" opens the verse with a command to guard oneself, and the day named is the one on which no soul can help another. The sentence sets the guarding against the day, so that the reader is asked to be ready for something that is coming. The phrase no soul will be of any help to another states the limit of every human bond, since a parent, a child, or a friend cannot carry the burden of another on that day. "No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted, and no help will be given" then names three ways in which a person might hope to be spared, and the sentence closes each of them. The ransom is the payment, the intercession is the request of another, and the help is any support from outside. The verse before dealt with the claim of the people of the Book to a special place with the Lord, and this verse answers that claim by saying that the day will remove every special place. The sentence keeps the list short and firm, so that no hope is left unnamed and no door is left open. The reader is asked to see that the guarding of the self is the only guard that can be kept on that day, and that it must be kept now, before the day comes.

**The day of guarding.**

And beware of fear a day when no soul shall for another on this Day be requited that is when no soul for another shall be of any avail and no compensation no ransom shall be accepted from it nor any intercession shall benefit it neither shall they be helped against God’s chastisement. (And guard against a day) fear the torment of a day, i.e. the Day of Judgement (when no soul will in anything avail another) no unbelieving soul will be able to drive away anything from another unbelieving soul; it is also said that this means: no righteous soul will be able to drive away anything from another righteous soul; and it is said that this means: no father will be able to drive away anything from his son and no son will be able to drive away Allah's punishment from his father, (nor will compensation be accepted from it) no ransom will be accepted, (nor will intercession be of use to it) no intercessor will intercede for it: not a close angel, a sent messenger or a righteous servant; (nor will they be helped) will be prevented from what they will face. Protect yourself from the torment of the Day of Return by following the instructions of Allah and keeping away from what He has prohibited, because on that day no soul will be able to help another soul in any way; no ransom will be accepted for it, no matter how great; and no one pleading on its behalf will benefit it, no matter how high their position. And beware of a day when no soul will be requited for another and no compensation will be accepted from it nor will any intercession benefit it neither will they be helped.

**No help from another.**

On that day, a soul will have no helper other than Allah. Everyone on that day will be saying My soul my soul but our Prophet will say My community my community. In this world one person is able to bear the burden of another; sometimes intercession is accepted; sometimes one can free oneself by giving compensation; sometimes a helper is at hand to see one through a difficult situation. In the next world, however, none of these mitigating factors will be allowed to come into play.

**No ransom and no intercession.**

As for the enemies nothing [that is no payment or compensation] will be accepted from them. The intercession of intercessors will not benefit the disbeliever for this is a determination made for each community with their prophet. The rule that applied to Abraham applies to every generation: only those who prove themselves worthy will be granted a share in God’s covenant; those who do not will meet the same fate as any other offenders in God’s sight, regardless of the nation to which they belong. The statement is of a general and principal kind, and the verses which come in between the beginning and the end are, so to say, a detailed demonstration of the statement.

**The lessons of the passage.**

On the one hand, it encourages the Israelites to come back to the Straight Path by reminding them of the blessings which Allah has bestowed on them; on the other hand, it warns them of the consequences of their lapses by depicting the Day of Judgment. For, what is aimed at in a discussion is the affirmation of certain basic and general principles -- being succinct, they are easily kept alive in the mind, and, being comprehensive and readily applicable to particular situations, they make it easy for one to remember the details too. In the art of writing and speaking, it is considered to be one of the most effective means of carrying conviction that, before starting on a long analytical discussion of a subject, one should define the basic ideas very briefly and clearly which are always helpful in comprehending the details and the particularities, and that, in concluding the argument, one should repeat these ideas by way of a summary. Remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the nations) And fear the Day (of Judgement) when no person shall avail another, nor shall compensation be accepted from him, nor shall intercession be of use to him, nor shall they be helped.

**Warnings and the people of the Book.**

We mentioned a similar Ayah at the beginning of this Surah, and it is mentioned here to emphisize the importance of following the Ummi Prophet and Messenger, who is described for the People of the Scriptures in their Books by his characteristics, name, the good news about him and the description of his Ummah. Allah warned them against concealing this information, which is among the favors that Allah granted them. They should not envy their cousins, the Arabs, for what Allah has given them, the Final Messenger of Allah being an Arab. They recognized that the word he preached emanated from the same source that had inspired the prophets before him.

124.text:
"Remember when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain commandments, which he fulfilled, Allah said" opens the verse with a call to remember and with the trial that the Lord set for Abraham. The word tested is the key, since it places him in a trial that came from the Lord, and the commandments are the measure by which the trial was measured. The verse states that he fulfilled them, and the word fulfilled marks the trial as one that Abraham completed. The sentence then turns on the verb said, which introduces the Lord's reply to the completed trial. "I will certainly make you into a role model for the people, Abraham asked" gives the reward first and then the question that Abraham put in return. The word certainly makes the promise firm, and the role model is a standing that Abraham receives from his obedience. The question that follows is not a demand but a hope, and it shows that Abraham looked to the future of his family as well as to his own state. "What about my offspring, Allah replied" sets the request and the answer side by side, so that the reader hears the hope and the reply in one movement. "My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers" closes the verse with the answer. The covenant of the Lord is given to the righteous and not to those who do wrong, and the reply sets a limit that the descendants must meet by their own conduct. The verse before named the day when no soul can help another, and this verse shows that the covenant of the Lord is not inherited by lineage alone. The reader is left with the test of Abraham, the promise to him, and the condition that governs the promise to his offspring. The sentence keeps the words plain, so that the trial and its answer stand out clearly to anyone who reads them. The verb tested is set against the trial that followed, so the sentence keeps the reader on the point of the test. The verb tested recurs in the account of the people who were tried before, and the reader is asked to keep the same standard in view when judging the claim of any descent to the favour of the Lord. The phrase certain commandments is left unnamed in the verse, and the sources fill it in with the many duties that Abraham took up, so the verse keeps the trial open rather than closing it with a list.

**The words of the trial.**

And mention when his Lord tested tried Abraham Ibrāhīm also read Ibrāhām with certain words with certain commands and prohibitions with which He charged him it is said that these included the rituals of the Pilgrimage the rinsing of the mouth snuffing up water into the nostrils to clean them cleaning of the teeth trimming facial hair combing of the hair trimming the fingernails shaving armpit and pubic hair circumcision and washing one’s private parts after elimination; and he fulfilled them he performed them thoroughly; He God exalted said to him ‘I make you a leader an exemplar in religion for the people. (with Kalimāt (words) which means, "Laws, commandments and prohibitions." 'Words' as mentioned here, sometimes refers to what Allah has willed, such as Allah's statement about Maryam,. What were the Words that Ibrahim was tested with? (And when his Lord tried Abraham with some words) He commanded him to fulfil ten traits: five in relation to his head and five to his body, (and he fulfilled them) he complied.

**A role model for the people.**

This is why Allah made Ibrahim a role model for the people, and an Imam whose conduct and path are imitated and followed. What God had demanded of Abraham was the most difficult sacrifice—his son’s life—and when God finally intervened before Abraham could actually sacrifice his own son, it was because Abraham had demonstrated his perfect willingness to make any sacrifice demanded of him by God, no matter how great or how terrible it might have been. The rule that applied to Abraham applies to every generation: only those who prove themselves worthy will be granted a share in God’s covenant; those who do not will meet the same fate as any other offenders in God’s sight, regardless of the nation to which they belong.

**The request for offspring.**

’ Said he ‘And of my seed?’ my progeny make leaders from among them; He said ‘My covenant of leadership shall not reach the evildoers’ the disbelievers from among them this indicates that the covenant will reach only those who are not evildoers. Abraham asked Allah to make also his descendants leaders who people would be guided by. Not only his people, but his own family also was sunk deep in idol-worshipping; in opposition to their creed and customs, he was given 'Al-Din al-Hanif ', "the Pure Religion", and was asked to go out to his people, and to bring them back to the Straight Path. This is because Allah accepted the supplication of His Khalil, Ibrahim, when he asked Allah to make the hearts of people eager to visit the House.

**The covenant and the wrongdoers.**

Allah (said: My covenant) with you and My promise to you and the honour and mercy I bestowed upon you (includeth not wrong-doers) from among your offspring; it is also said that this means: My covenant will not include the wrong-doers in the Hereafter but it will include them in this life. Allah told His prophet Abraham that He would make his manners and behaviour an example for people to follow. Allah replied by saying that His promise to him of sacred leadership would not extend to the wrongdoers among his descendants.

**The Friend of Allah.**

"The Friend of Allah" had so annihilated his own will and desire, and was so anxious to obey his Lord that he did not allow even a moment to lapse between the command and its execution, and started on his journey without informing his wife. "Men and women who perform what Islam enjoins upon them, men and women who are true believers, obedient men and obedient women, truthful men and truthful women, men and women who are patient, men and women who possess humility, men and women who give in charity, men who fast and women who fast, men and women who guard their private parts, men and women who remember Allah abundantly - for them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward. In short, all we wish to point out is that the nature of prophethood is a degree of reality which we can understand only partially and that too only with the help of Divine Books, and hence it is not a sphere in which human fantasy may be allowed to roam at its sweet will. In the next world, however, none of these mitigating factors will be allowed to come into play.

**What else the same passage holds.**

So far a whole section of this Surah has been dealing directly with the conduct of the Jews in the course of their history, and their present hostility to Islam, delineating the inner motives and mainsprings of this rabid opposition. As we have seen, they were proud of being the children of Jacob and of Abraham (Sayyidna Ya qub and Sayyidna Ibrahim), and believed that, being the chosen people of God, they had the exclusive privilege of being the leaders of humanity, and hence the station of prophethood could not be conferred on anyone who did not belong to their race. Now, the Holy Qur'an proceeds, in the present section of the Surah, to refute this line of thought in an indirect manner, by telling the story of Sayyidna Ibrahim and of his elder son Sayyidna Isma'il (Ishmael). This section is going to suggest some essential considerations in answer to the denial of the Holy Prophet on the part of the Jews:- He alone can be a guide to humanity who is not unjust and not a transgressor, and has successfully gone through the trial imposed on him by Allah -- and these qualifications the Jews do not fulfill.

125.text:
"And remember when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people saying, You may take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer" opens the verse with the making of the House, which is the subject of the remembrance. The word centre gives the House a place at the heart of the people's life, and the word sanctuary gives it a safety that sets it apart from the places around it. The sentence joins the two so that the House is both a meeting point and a refuge. The word entrusted is repeated in the account of the sanctuary, so the charge reads as a standing duty in every generation and at all times. The phrase saying introduces the instruction, and the instruction is that the people may take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer. The stone and the ground near the House become part of the worship, and the sentence makes the place of Abraham's standing a place where the people themselves may stand in prayer. "And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves in prayer" closes the verse with the duty given to the two prophets. The House is to be made pure for those who circle it, for those who stay in it in meditation, and for those who bow and prostrate themselves in prayer. The verse before named the day when no soul can help another, and this verse turns the reader to the House where the people come to remember the Lord. The sources show that the House was built as a place to turn to, and that its purity is the purity of the worship that takes place in it. The duty of the one who serves the House is therefore a duty to keep it clean for those who come to it, and the verse places that duty with the two prophets from whom the House descends in the account. The verse uses the word entrusted, so the duty is a charge laid on the servants of the House, and the reader sees it as a trust that must be kept in each generation.

**The House as a centre.**

Ibn Kathir reports from Mujahid etc. that Sayyidna Ibrahim was living in Syria when he received the revelation that Allah was going to indicate to him the site of the Ka'bah which he was required to build and keep clean for those who should assemble there for performing the Hajj and offering the Salah . And in those circumstances the intention of the command was not to start the reconstruction of the Ka'bah but only to place the wife and the son of Sayyidna Ibrahim in this locality so that a human settlement should begin to take shape. All the verses of the Holy Qur'an on the subject of the Ka'bah either say that the location had been indicated by Allah Himself, or report the divine command to keep the House clean, but never suggest that a new House was to be built in a new place. So, Verse 125 means that the whole of the Haram has been made a place of peace - that is to say, people have been forbidden from shedding blood or taking revenge within these precincts (ibn al- Arabi).

**The standing-place.**

(Ibrahim made Allah's House a Sacred Area and a safe refuge. I have made what is between the two sides of Al-Madīnah a Sacred Area. Therefore, its game should not be hunted, and its trees should not be cut.) An-Nasa'i and Muslim also recorded this Hadith. (as your place of worship the place where Abraham stood (to pray) a place whereby you turn in prayer. Allah tells people to make the stone which Abraham stood on while he was building the Kaaba into a place of prayer. It is said that the House was built of stone but it is a stone that attracts hearts just as a magnet attracts iron. [What kind of house is itḍ] A house...

**Purifying the House.**

(purify My House for those who are circumambulating it) means, "From the idols, sexual activity, false witness and sins of all kinds." Allah instructed Abraham and his son Ishmael to purify the sanctuary from filth and idols for those who wish to worship in it, go around the Kaaba, stay there for worship, praying and so on. (And We imposed a duty upon) commanded (Abraham and Ishmael: Purify My house) from idols (for those who go around and those who meditate therein) those who live there (and those who bow down and prostrate themselves) those who perform the five daily prayers, regardless of their country of origin. Mention O Muḥammad when We appointed the House meaning the Kaʿba to be a place of visitation for people to come to and a sanctuary for them to return to to make their way to it from every direction.

**Those who circle and pray.**

Every year, the faithful come from all over the world to visit the Ka‘bah in Makkah, where no one is allowed to harm even the lowliest living creature; for Makkah has been made into a sacred place of worship for all time. Since people come to this place to remember God in an atmosphere of peace and solitude, it has to be cleansed of all impurities, and all activities that are contrary to this basic purpose are banned. Here the faithful bow and prostrate themselves, their greatest mark of respect for their Creator being the circumambulation of the Ka‘bah. It has also been made a safe place for them where they will not be attacked.

**A safe place.**

(I would have made two doors for the House on ground level, one eastern and one western. Do you know why your people raised its door above ground level?) She said, 'No.' He said, (To allow only those whom they wanted to enter it. When a man whom they did not wish to enter the House climbed to the level of the door, they would push him down) Allah then commanded people to emulate him, saying: (And when We made the House a resort) a place to turn to (for mankind) whereby they can turn and long for (and a sanctuary) for whoever enters it: The Qur’ān relates that Allah made the Kaaba a place for people to return to, as a means of connecting their hearts to Him.

**What else the same passage holds.**

In the course of the story of Sayyidna Ibrahim we now come to the building of the "House of Allah" - the Ka'bah . An answer is thus being given to the Jews who used to deny the Holy Prophet on the ground of their assumption that prophethood could not be given to anyone outside their own clan, and who used to scoff at the Muslims for turning towards the Ka'bah in their prayers, and to believe that the Hajj was no more than a custom of the ignorant Arabs. The earlier verse had made it clear that prophethood could not be given to the unjust and the disobedient, even if they belonged to the progeny of Sayyidna Ibrahim - a rule which destroys the very basis of the presumptuousness and vanity of the Jews. The present verse reminds them that the Ka'bah was built under divine commandment by Sayyidna Ibrahim himself with the help of his son Sayyidna Ismail and thus suggests that the performance of the Hajj and the orientation towards the Ka'bah have both been instituted by divine decree, and that the Holy Prophet is a direct descendant of Sayyidna Ibrahim and Sayyidna Ismail and is reviving the Abrahamic Way, which the Jews too must follow. Verse 125 briefly outlines the history of the re-construction of the Ka'bah, the characteristic qualities of the "House of Allah" and the city of Makkah, and the injunctions with regard to the respect which has to be paid to this sacred place. The Holy Qur'an returns to the subject again and again in different chapters, providing more details. We shall cite Verses 26 and 27 from the Surah "Al-Hajj" which deals particularly with the annual pilgrimage: And when We appointed for Ibrahim the place of the House:

126.text:
*And remember when Abraham said, My Lord, make this city of Mecca secure and provide fruits to its people* opens the verse with a prayer that Abraham made for the city and its people. The word secure asks for safety, and the word provide asks for food, so that the prayer covers both the protection of the place and the sustenance of those who live in it. The prayer is addressed to the Lord directly, and it asks for the people of the city to be given what they need. "those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day, He answered" limits the favour to the believers, so that the prayer is not a blanket request for everyone, and the answer that comes back is given in the same breath. "As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while, then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire" gives the reply, which divides the people into those who believe and those who do not. The disbelievers are given a short enjoyment and then the torment, so the enjoyment of this life is not the same as the reward of faith. "What an evil destination" closes the verse with the judgment on the end of those who disbelieve. The verse before named the House that was made secure, and this verse brings in the prayer for the city around it. The reader sees a prayer that asks for peace and provision for the believers, and a reply that does not extend the same favour to those who refuse. The sources treat the prayer as an example of a request that is shaped by the worshipper's care for others, since Abraham asks first for the safety of the place and only then for the fruit that sustains it. The reader is also shown that the favour of the Lord is measured by faith, and that the short enjoyment of this life has a limit that the verse sets with the fire. The contrast between the prayer and the reply keeps the two halves of the verse in view, so that the reader does not take the provision of the city to be the same as the acceptance of its people.

**The city made secure.**

The same prayer occurs in Surah "Ibrahim" (14:35), but employs the construction Al-balad ("the city"), while the present verse employs Baladan ("a city"). Coming back to the verse under discussion, we see that Sayyidna Ibrahim also prayed for this city to be made "a place of peace" - that is to say, safe from slaughter and plunder as from calamities, and secure against the domination of the infidels. (Ibrahim made Allah's House a Sacred Area and a safe refuge. I have made what is between the two sides of Al-Madīnah a Sacred Area. Therefore, its game should not be hunted, and its trees should not be cut.) An-Nasa'i and Muslim also recorded this Hadith. Remember, O Prophet, when Abraham prayed to his Lord, asking Him to make Makkah a safe place, where no one would be faced with evil; and to provide the people who live there with all types of crops, and a special provision for those who have faith in Allah.

**Fruits for the believers.**

If it is the fruits of trees that are intended here, the word "Yujba ("drawn") is a sufficient indication that in granting the prayer Allah had not promised to produce them in Makkah itself, but to send them to the city from other places. The word should, then, cover not only the fruits of trees, but also the products of all kinds of crafts and industries in fact, all that is needed to sustain human life. Now listen to the call of your servant and make this town a place of peace, and make special provision for the material needs of its citizens; for the land that they inhabit is uncultivable. Abraham's request was not for his own concern ḥaẓẓ but rather for the right ḥaqq of his Lord may He be exalted and glorified.

**Enjoyment and the torment.**

Allah said that He would give some enjoyment to the disbelievers by giving them provision in this life; but in the next life they will be forced into the torment of the fire of Hell – a miserable place to which they return on the Day of Judgement. (And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you (O Muhammad). To Us is their return, and We shall inform them what they have done. Verily, Allah is the Knower of what is in the breasts (of men). We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We shall oblige them to (enter) a great torment.)(31:23-24) and,. (And when Abraham prayed: My Lord! Make this a region of security) free of perturbation (and bestow upon its people fruits) different kinds of fruit, (such of them as believe in Allah and the Last Day) in resurrection after death, Allah (answered: As for him who disbelieveth) as well, (I shall leave him in contentment for a while) I shall provide for him a little in this life, (then I shall compel him) force him (to the doom of fire, a hapless journey's end!) to which he shall come. When Abraham was mindful of the required etiquette in seeking provision for those who believed they were granted that-but so were those who did not believe. [On the other hand] when he spoke about leadership saying And of my seedḍ [2:125] without [divine] permission [the request] was denied and it was said to him My covenant shall not reach the evildoers [2:125].

**The prayer of Abraham.**

Four thousand years ago Abraham was commanded to take his family into an ‘uncultivable valley’, in that part of Arabia known as Hijaz, and settle them there.
