Abraham bowed to the will of God without slightest hesitation. ’ Abraham’s prayer was answered: the land of Hijaz has remained an abode of peace and plenty up to the present day. And when Abraham said My Lord make this land secure and pro vide its people with fruits; such of them as believe in God and the Last Day He said And whoever disbelieves to him I shall give enjoyment a little then I shall compel him to the chastisement of the fire-how evil a journey's end!

**The request as it was made.**

" Also, Ibn Jurayj said, "I said to 'Ata', 'What is Allah's 'Ahd?' He said, 'His command.'" Also, Sa'id bin Jubayr said that Ibn 'Abbas commented on the Ayah,. Hence, when 'Abdul-Malik realized that 'A'ishah had narrated the Hadith of the Messenger of Allah on this subject, he said, "I wish we had left it as Ibn Az-Zubayr had made it. The word should, then, cover not only the fruits of trees, but also the products of all kinds of crafts and industries in fact, all that is needed to sustain human life.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Sayyidna Ibrahim always carried out the commandments of Allah without losing a moment, and was ready to make all kinds of sacrifices in His way, whether they involved worldly goods, or wife and children, or his own likes and dislikes. All the same, having affection and love for one's family is not only a natural urge in man, but also a divine commandment. This is what manifests itself in the present verses, where we find him praying for the well-being of his family in this world as much as in the other. The prayer begins with the word Rabb , which lexically signifies One who gives nurture. " Thus, it teaches us the proper mode of praying to Allah, for this form of address in itself draws the mercy and grace of Allah on the man who is praying. The first thing Sayyidna Ibrahim prayed for was that Allah may turn the barren desert where he had left his family under divine commandment, into a city, so that his wife and son should not feel lonely, and that their daily needs should be easily satisfied. The difference probably arises from the fact that the prayer reported here was made when the place was still a desert and Sayyidna Ibrahim wished "a city" to grow in this barren land, while the prayer reported in Surah "Ibrahim" was made when "the city" had already risen and was quite well-known, for near the end of the same Surah we find him saying ‌ "Praise be to Allah who has given me, in my old age, Ismail and Ishaq " (14:39), which suggests that the second prayer was made after the birth of Sayyidna Ishaq (Isaac), an event that occurred thirteen years after the birth of Sayyidna Ismail (Ishmael).

127.text:
"And remember when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael, both praying, Our Lord! Accept this from us" opens with the building of the House by Abraham and Ishmael, and the phrase both praying shows that the work was joined to a prayer. The foundation is the base of the House, and the word raised names the act of building it up from the ground. The verb raised is the same used for the foundations, and the sentence keeps the labour and the prayer side by side from its first words. The two men are named together, and the verse presents them as partners in both the labour and the prayer. "Our Lord! Accept this from us" is the first request, and the word accept asks that the work be received by the Lord. The request is made with the plural our, so that the prayer belongs to both men and to the people who follow them. "You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing" closes the prayer with the attributes that make the request possible. The Lord hears the prayer and knows the intention behind it, and the two attributes give the reason for asking. The verse before showed the prayer for the city and the reply to it, and this verse turns to the building of the House itself. The reader is shown a work done with humility, a prayer offered with it, and an assurance in the names of the Lord who hears and knows.

**Building the foundation.**

And mention when Abraham raised up the foundations the supports or the walls of the House building it min al-bayt ‘of the House’ is semantically connected to yarfa‘u ‘raises up’ and Ishmael with him wa-Ismā‘īlu is a supplement to Ibrāhīmu both of them saying ‘Our Lord! 128.text:
"Our Lord! Make us both fully submit to You and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you" opens with a prayer in the first person plural, so that Abraham and Ishmael speak together as the builders of the House. From their descendants the prayer asks for a nation that will submit, so the submission is to be carried by the family and by the community that follows it. "Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace" makes the next request. The rituals are the acts of worship that the Lord is asked to show them, and the verb turn asks the Lord to turn toward them with mercy. The verse before named the House and the work of building it, and this verse turns that work into a prayer for guidance in how it is practised. "You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful" closes the prayer with the two names that make the request reasonable. The Lord accepts repentance and shows mercy, and the sentence gives those names as the ground for asking. The Maʿārif commentary treats the prayer as coming from the same sense of fear and humility, and it places the request for a nation of submitters on the descendants' side as well as the builders' side. The reader is asked to see one prayer for a faith that is kept by the family and by the people who come after them.

**The submission of the two.**

And make us submissive compliant to You and make of our seed our progeny a community a people submissive to You min in the phrase min dhurriyyatinā ‘of our seed’ here is partitive and is used here in accordance with God’s above-mentioned saying My covenant shall not reach the evildoers; and show us teach us our holy rites our ceremonies for worship or for the pilgrimage and relent to us. Verse 128 reports that he further prayed to Allah "to make" him and his son obedient to His commandments and to His Will. This prayer too proceeds from the same sense of fear and awe, and from the same knowledge. But you will have no exclusive right to the water here.' They said, 'We agree.'" It is prayer of this kind that is most pleasing to God, so He accepted their prayer and a permanent fountain of spiritual life for the whole world gushed forth from the barren desert of Arabia.

**What else the same passage holds.**

He has, all his life, been performing exemplary deeds of obedience, and yet he prays to "be made" obedient. It is so, because the more one grows in one's knowledge of Divine Majesty, the more one comes to realize that one is not being faithful and obedient as is due. It is significant. that Sayyidna Ibrahim included his descendants too in his prayer. This shows that the "men of Allah" who never hesitate in sacrificing themselves and their children in the way of Allah, yet love them deeply. All the same, they know what the proper requirements of parental love are, and how they should be fulfilled. This is something beyond the reach of average men, who suppose the well-being of their children to reside in physical health and comfort alone, and spend all their love and care on providing just this to their family. But those who have received the favour of Allah show a much greater solicitude for the spiritual well-being of their children than for the physical, being more anxious as to what happens to them in the other world than in this. The sentence keeps the reading before the teaching and the teaching before the purifying, so the reader sees a sequence in which the revelation is recited before it is understood. "and purify them, Indeed, You alone are the Almighty, All-Wise" closes the prayer with the two names that give the Lord the power and the judgement behind the request. The word alone limits that power to the Lord, so the messenger can come only by His doing. The verse before asked for the submission of the descendants, and this verse asks for the means by which that submission would be taught to them. The Tazkirul commentary reads the messenger's first task as the unveiling of the signs that the Lord has set in human nature, and the Tanwīr gives the answer to the prayer as the sending of Muhammad to them. The verse keeps the prayer in the first person plural, as the verse before did, so the two requests read as one. The reader is shown the prayer of Abraham as the start of a line that runs from the building of the House to the arrival of the one who would recite and teach in it.

**Raise among them a messenger.**

And send among them the people of this House a messenger one of them and God granted him this petition with the sending of Muhammad who shall recite to them Your signs the Qur’ān and teach them the Book the Qur’ān and Wisdom that is what the former contains of judgments and purify them cleanse them of idolatry; You are the Mighty the Victor the Wise in His creation. The Arabic word Yatlu (translated in English as "recite", or "read out") comes from the word Tilawah, which lexically signifies "to follow, to obey", but in the terminology of the Qur'an and the Hadith denotes the recitation or reading of the Holy Qur'an or of a Di-vine Book, for one who reads a Divine Book is also required to obey it fully. **The Book and wisdom.**

(I am the Messenger of Allah unto you, confirming what is before me in the Tawrah, and giving glad tidings of a Messenger to come after me, whose name shall be Ahmad)(61:6) But these signs have to be unveiled by God’s messenger: he shares his divine insight with them so that they may have a glimpse of God’s glory. And Allah answered his prayers and sent unto them Muhammad ﷺ; and these are the words with which Allah tried him, and he fulfilled them by asking Allah for them in his prayer.

(and purify them) means, "With the obedience of Allah." (There will always be a group of my Ummah who will be on the truth, undeterred by those who fail or oppose them, until the command of Allah comes while they are on this.) Now, to proceed with the commentary, let us consider why Sayyidna Ibrahim in praying for the well-being of his descendants in this world and in the other, requested Allah to send a prophet from among them.

**Almighty and All-Wise.**

(Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Mighty) Who is vengeful against whosoever does not answer Your Messenger whom You sent to them, (the Wise) in sending the Messenger. He is the Mighty in His essence, and the Wise in what He does and in His decrees. Now, to proceed with the commentary, let us consider why Sayyidna Ibrahim in praying for the well-being of his descendants in this world and in the other, requested Allah to send a prophet from among them.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The prayer of Ibrahim for the Holy Prophet Let us start by commenting on certain words which occur in this verse. The word also suggests that it is obligatory to read the Holy Qur'an exactly as it has been revealed by Allah, and not to add or sub-tract a word on one's own part, not even to change the pronunciation of a word which often may, in the Arabic language, change the very meaning of the word concerned. In his "Mufradat al-Qur'an ", Imam al-Raghib al-Isfahani says that the word Tilawah cannot, in current idiom, be applied to the reading of any book other than the Word of Allah. The word Kitab (Book) in this verse, of course, refers to the Holy Qur'an itself. As to the word Hikmah (usually translated in English as "wisdom"), it carries various meanings in Arabic - for example, arriving at the truth , justice, exact knowledge, etc. According to al-Raghib al-Isfahani when the word is used in speaking of Allah, it connotes the total and perfect knowledge of all existents, and flawless creation; but when applied to someone other than Allah, it connotes a proper knowledge of the existents, and good deeds. In connection with the present verse, Maulana Mahmud al-Hasan has interpreted the word as "profound truths, or subtle realities", while Maulana Ashraf Ali Thanavi has taken it to mean "the art of understanding properly". But the truth of the matter is that in spite of the apparent variety of expressions used, the substance of all these statements is the same - namely, the Way (Sunnah) of the Holy Prophet and the Hadith. This is the interpretation reported from Qatadah by Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarir. Firstly, the appearance of a prophet from among them would in itself be an honour and a blessing. Secondly, the prophet being a member of their own group, they would be thoroughly familiar with his past and present and with his ways, and thus find it easy to have trust in him, and to profit from his guidance. According to a hadith, in accepting this prayer Allah promised that this prophet would be sent in the last of all ages.

"And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool" opens with a question that is also a rebuke. Abraham (in the world) by taking him as a friend; as it is said this means:

**What else the same passage holds.**

The earlier verses have defined the basic principles of the religion of Sayyidna Ibrahim called upon men to follow it, and warned them against the dangers involved in turning away from it. And We gave him good in this world, and in the Hereafter he shall be of the righteous.)(16:120-122). (And Ibrahim's invoking (of Allah) for his father's forgiveness was only because of a promise he (Ibrahim) had made to him (his father). But when it became clear to him (Ibrahim) that he (his father) was an enemy of Allah, he dissociated himself from him. Verily, Ibrahim was Awwah (one who invokes Allah with humility, glorifies Him and remembers Him much) and was forbearing)(9:114), and,.

**One religion of the prophets.**

" Let us add that the word of command employed in this verse is Aslim which comes from the same root as the word Islam. The reply makes it clear that the basic principle of the religion of Sayyidna Ibrahim and its very essence is contained in one word, Islam, which signifies total obedience and willing submission of oneself to Allah. Consequently, each of these religions - whether one calls it Judaism or Christianity or something else - must in its essence be Islam, in the general sense of the word - namely, total submission to Allah. Their laws even if they differed in details were of one origin.

**Self-deception and the faith.**

Such men are, indeed, trying to be clever with Allah Himself who knows every particle of the universe and who can look into the deepest recesses of the human heart - the Almighty before whom nothing avails but complete surrender and total submission. It leads one to imagine that just as one has been attached to them in this life, one will remain attached to them in the next. The People of the Book were immersed in this form of wishful thinking to the extent that they had invented a dogma of ancestral salvation, pinning all their hopes on the holiness of their elders. But it is sheer self-deception to think that one person will receive the reward of another’s actions.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Verse 131 defines the basic principle of the religion of Sayyidna Ibrahim . Allah asked him to submit himself, and he willingly and gladly agreed to submit himself to "the Lord of the worlds. It is difficult to find an exact English equivalent, for the word signifies "to obey, to submit oneself, to surrender one's will. " Anyhow, we should notice that in reply to the divine command, he did not say, as one would have expected, : "I submit myself to you," but, more elaborately: : " This particular form of reply expresses the attitude of respect and awe proper to the occasion, and includes the praise of Allah which the moment of receiving the honour of divine address demanded. It also carries a recognition of the fact that in submitting himself to the Lord of the worlds he was only performing the essential duty of a servant towards the Master of All, and doing it for his own benefit.

133.text:
"Or did you witness when death came to Jacob?" opens with a question that places the listeners outside the scene. The verb witness asks whether they were present at the hour of his death, and the sentence assumes they were not. "He asked his children, Who will you worship after my passing, They replied, We will continue to worship your God, the God of your forefathers, Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac, the One God." The phrase after my passing places the question at the moment of death, so the father's concern is for what remains of the faith after him. The answer names three fathers and gives the one God they share, so the line of the faith runs through the family and not only through the sons. The reply closes with "And to Him we all submit," and the word submit gives the answer its whole content. The sons answer at once, and the short clauses of the reply follow one another with no break, so the answer reads as a single breath. The verse sets the father's question and the sons' pledge side by side so the reader can see both. The Wāḥidī commentary links the verse to the Jews of the time, whose claim was tied to the death of Jacob. The Tazkirul commentary describes the self-deception a people can fall into when it trusts its own place in the family. The Maʿārif commentary takes the family line as the vehicle of the faith, so that the children of the prophets are asked to keep the submission their fathers kept. The reader is asked to see the verse as a question put to people who claimed a place in that family, and a reply that names the One God as the only object of worship, which they make their own.

**The question of the witness.**

When the Jews said to the Prophet s ‘Do you not know that on the day of his death Jacob charged his sons with Judaism?’ the following was revealed Or were you witnesses present when death came to Jacob? (Or were ye witnesses) or were you, O assembly of Jews, present (when death came to Jacob) regarding what he enjoined his children, i.e. whether he enjoined them to follow Judaism or Islam, (when he said unto his sons: What will ye worship after me?) after I die? Were you present at the time of Jacob’s death, when he asked his sons what they would worship after he had died? Or were you witnesses when death came to Jacobḍ When he said to his sons What will you worship after meḍ They said We will worship your God All of them ḍ followed one way in declaring [God's] oneness tawḥīd and submission islām.

**Jacob's last question.**

When he said unto his sons, "What will you worship after me? " They said, "We shall worship your AIlah (God Allah) the Ilah of your fathers, Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael), Ishaq (Isaac), One Ilah, and to Him we submit (in Islam) That was a nation who has passed away. Do you not know that when Jacob was about to die he advised his sons to follow Judaism? It leads one to imagine that just as one has been attached to them in this life, one will remain attached to them in the next.

**The answer of the sons.**

(They said: We shall worship thy God) we worship, (the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac, one God) i.e. we worship one God, (and unto Him we have surrendered) we acknowledge to worship Him and declare that there is only one true God. They replied to him, saying that they would worship Allah, the Lord of his forefathers – Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac – namely, the One Allah without partners; and they said that they surrendered in devotion to Him alone and were bound to Him. They inherited that one after another from their forefathers and [they] were the people of the house of intimacy deserving of nearness and purified in truth by God. and the God of your fathers Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac One God to Him we submit. [Jacob's sons] did not say Our God out of respect for [Jacob's] special status inasmuch as they accepted his superiority and saw themselves as attached to his station maqām. [Rather] they said of themselves that they were followers of [Abraham Ishmael and Isaac] when they said and to Him we submit. This was revealed about the Jews when they said:

**Children and the faith of the fathers.**

So, even prophets love their children, the only difference being that while ordinary men consider the good things of this world alone to be worthwhile and wish to leave to their children as much of these as they can, in the eyes of the prophets and their genuine followers the only thing that counts is Iman (faith) and good deeds - in one word, Islam - and it is this eternal wealth which they wish and strive to transmit wholly to their descendants. This practice of the prophets provides a special guidance to parents: just as they are keen to secure the worldly comfort and happiness of their children, they should pay equal, if not greater, attention to the discipline of their external and internal behaviour according to the requirements of the Shari'ah. The main reason for the ignorance and the indifference towards Islam which is wide-spread among the Muslims today, is that even when the parents themselves are good Muslims in every way, they leave their children to themselves and let the social environment mould them in its own fashion. Their only worry is to see their children doing well in this world, and they never think of what will happen to them in the next.

**Self-deception about one's place.**

It makes one feel that their surplus of good deeds will make up for one’s own shortcomings. But it is sheer self-deception to think that one person will receive the reward of another’s actions. Yet one who is firm in the faith will not be put off by adversity; he will persevere, making sure that he leaves this world as a believer, so that he can look forward to God’s blessings in the next world.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The previous verses have defined the religion of Sayyidna Ibrahim and the essence of Islam. When idh ‘when’ substitutes for the preceding idh he said to his sons ‘What will you worship after me?’ after I die?; They said ‘We will worship your God and the God of your fathers Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac in recognition of the predominant mention of the father figures Ishmael is also counted as a father and also because the status of an uncle is akin to that of a father One God ilāhan wāhidan ‘One God’ substitutes for ilāhaka ‘your God’ to Him we submit’ the initial am of the phrase am kuntum ‘Or were you …’ is similar to the hamza of denial sc. a-kuntum the sense being ‘You were not present at his death so how do you ascribe to him what does not befit him?’. Now, these two verses bring before us another aspect of the question. Call it the religion of Sayyidna Ibrahim or Islam, it is in any case meant for the whole world. Then why have the descendants of Sayyidna Ibrahim and Sayyidna Ya qub been specifically mentioned here, and why should have these two great prophets been so particular in giving this counsel to their sons? We shall say that these specifications show that love for one's progeny and solicitude for their well-being is in no way incompatible with the station of prophethood or even with that of "the Friend of Allah". For, Sayyidna Ibrahim who was, on one occasion, not only willing but happy to be sacrificing his son in obedience to the commandment of Allah, did on a different occasion pray for the well-being of his progeny in this world and the other, and wished, while departing from this world, to offer them what was the greatest blessing in his eyes - namely, Islam.

134.text:
"That was a community that had already gone before." opens with the word community, meaning the generation that went before, and it puts that generation at a distance. The next sentence gives the principle of account: "For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned." Each side is given its own deeds, so the earlier generation's record does not pass to the later one. The verse ends with "And you will not be accountable for what they have done," which tells the listeners that they are not answerable for the acts of their forefathers. The sentence comes straight after the claim of descent in the verse before, so the reader sees the answer to that claim in plain terms. The Mukhtaṣar gives the sense as the statement that no one is held to account for the disobedience of another, and that the listeners should keep their attention on their own work. The Maʿārif commentary takes the verse as setting aside the claim that the good deeds of forefathers protect their children. The Tazkirul commentary describes the mind that thinks its surplus of good deeds will carry it as one that deceives itself. The verse therefore moves the matter from inherited standing to personal record. The first clause is short, and the rest of the verse carries the weight of the principle. The word earned ties the account to the action of each person rather than to the name of the group, so the verse makes the record personal. The contrast is drawn in two halves that mirror one another, and each half keeps its own portion of the account. The listeners are asked to read the verse as a settled rule rather than as a comfort for their ancestry.

**A community that went before.**

When he said unto his sons, "What will you worship after me? They shall receive the reward of what they earned and you of what you earn. That tilka is the subject of this sentence and denotes Abraham Jacob and his sons and is feminine because it agrees with the gender of its predicate is a community that has passed away has gone before; theirs is what they have earned the reward for their deeds lahā mā kasabat theirs is what they have earned’ constitutes the commencement of a new sentence and yours the Jews are being addressed here is what you have earned; you shall not be asked about what they did in the same way that they will not be asked about what you did this latter statement being an affirmation of the former. Verse 134 tells us that the good deeds of one's forefathers shall not suffice one, if one has not been performing good deeds oneself, and that, similarly, one shall not have to suffer for the misdeeds of one's forefathers, if one's own account is clean.

**No one answers for another.**

It follows upon this principle that children of mushrikin (associators) and Kafirin (infidels), if they die before having come of age, shall not be punished in the other world on account of the disbelief of their parents. No one is held to account for the disobedience of another, but everyone is rewarded according to their own actions. The verse also refutes the claim of the Jews that irrespective of what they had been doing they would go to Paradise on account of the good deeds of their forefathers.

**What was earned.**

They gained whatever they did in their lives, earning either good or evil; and you will gain what you have earned. ("What will you worship after me?" They said, "We shall worship your Ilah (God Allah) the Ilah of your fathers, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq,") (Theirs is that which they earned) of goodness (and yours is that which ye earn) of goodness.

**Self-deception and inherited merit.**

It leads one to imagine that just as one has been attached to them in this life, one will remain attached to them in the next. It makes one feel that their surplus of good deeds will make up for one’s own shortcomings. But it is sheer self-deception to think that one person will receive the reward of another’s actions. Yet one who is firm in the faith will not be put off by adversity; he will persevere, making sure that he leaves this world as a believer, so that he can look forward to God’s blessings in the next world.

**Heed your own account.**

You should not be distracted from paying attention to your own behaviour by looking at what those before you did. (And ye will not be asked) on the Day of Judgement (of what they used to do) or say. "Beware, 0 Banu Hashim, let it not be that on the Day of Judgment while others bring their good deeds with them, you on your part, having neglected good deeds, bring with you only the trust in being my relations, and so I have to tell you that on that day, I cannot save you from the wrath of Allah." It leads one to imagine that just as one has been attached to them in this life, one will remain attached to them in the next.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub (Jacob)? " They said, "We shall worship your AIlah (God Allah) the Ilah of your fathers, Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael), Ishaq (Isaac), One Ilah, and to Him we submit (in Islam) That was a nation who has passed away. And you will not be asked of what they used to do Let this be a warning to those Muslims who, being the descendants of the Holy Prophet or of a saint, delude themselves with the hope that their sins would go unpunished in consideration of this privileged position. Ya'qub's Will and Testament to His Children upon His Death In fact, the Holy Qur'an is very explicit and very insistent on this point. This Ayah contains Allah's criticism of the Arab pagans among the offspring of Isma'il as well as the disbelievers among the Children of Israel Jacob the son of Isaac, the son of Ibrahim. When death came to Jacob, he advised his children to worship Allah alone without partners. "Each man shall reap the fruits of his own deeds, and no one shall bear the burden of another" (6:164). Addressing his own clan, the Holy Prophet said: Mentioning Isma'il here is a figure of speech, because Isma'il is Jacob's uncle. An-Nahas said that the Arabs call the uncle a father, as Al-Qurtubi mentioned). Another hadith says: :"He who has been pulled back by his deeds cannot be pushed forward by his ancestry." This Ayah is used as evidence that the grandfather is called a father and inherits, rather than the brothers (i.e. when his son dies), as Abu Bakr asserted, according to Al-Bukhari who narrated Abu Bakr's statement from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Az-Zubayr.

135.text:
The Jews and Christians each say, "Follow our faith to be rightly guided." Say, O Prophet, "No! We follow the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not a polytheist." The opening names two communities, each offering its own religion as the path to guidance, and the word rightly marks the claim as one of guidance. The reply rejects the offer at once, and it names the faith the Prophet follows as the faith of Abraham. The word upright gives the character of that faith, and the closing phrase makes Abraham's faith the opposite of association with others. The Wāḥidī commentary links the verse to the leaders of Medina, who argued with the Muslims over the faith. The Tazkirul commentary states that the religion taught by the Prophet was the same faith as that of Abraham, and that the Jews turned from him for their own motives. Each claim is answered in turn, first the claim of being Jews or Christians and then the claim of guidance, so the reply moves from the question to the faith it sets up. The sentence also names the upright in a single word, so the faith of Abraham reads as a straight path rather than a mixture of creeds. The reader is asked to see the verse as the claim of two communities met by a single reply that rests the believers on the faith of the patriarch. The phrase "who was not a polytheist" is placed last, so the description of Abraham ends the reply on the point that separates him from every other claim. The reply therefore answers the claim of the two communities without naming either of them as the source of guidance.

**Be Jews or Christians.**

And they say ‘Be Jews or Christians the particle aw is for detail; the first of these is the saying of the Medinan Jews while the second is that of the Christians of Najrān and you shall be guided’. And they say, "Be Jews or Christians, then you will be guided. Both the Jews and Christians said to the believers:

**The answer that follows Abraham.**

Say to them ‘Nay we follow rather the creed of Abraham a hanīf hanīfan is a circumstantial qualifier referring to Ibrāhīma that is to say one that inclines away from all other religions to the upright religion; and he was not of the idolaters’. (Say (to them O Muhammad), "Nay, (we follow) only the religion of Ibrahim, Hanif) means, "We do not need the Judaism or Christianity that you call us to, rather,. Tell them, O Prophet, in answer, that you follow the religion of Abraham, who turned away from other false ways of life to the way of truth. Say Nay rather the creed of Abraham a ḥanīf; and he was not of the idolaters. [That is] When the groups contended with you [Muḥammad] they demanded that you agree muwāfaqa with them.

**Upright and not a polytheist.**

(Nay, but the religion of Abraham, the upright) the Muslim; rather follow the religion of Abraham, the upright, the Muslim, the sincere-only then you will be guided, (and he was not of the idolaters) i.e. he did not follow the religion of the Jews or Christians. He did not worship others next to Allah, as some do. Follow the way of the Friend al-khalīl in withdrawing from the group whether it be one's own father or anyone else who is not in accord lā yuwāfiqu with his Protector. The religion that the Prophet Muhammad taught was the religion of the Prophet Abraham, the very religion to which the Jews and the Christians claimed allegiance.

**The dispute with the leaders.**

This was revealed about the Jewish leaders of Medina: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn al-Sayf, Wahb ibn Yahudha, Yasir ibn Akhtab, and also about the Christians of Najran. This is because when they argued with the Muslims regarding religion, each one claimed to have a better right to the religion of Allah, exalted is He, than anyone else. Allah mentioned after this the dispute of the Jews and Christians with the believers, saying:

**Stand firm.**

Stand firm in opposing that to which they call you and turn your attention increasingly to Us. Therefore, follow us, O Muhammad, and you will be rightly guided. (Be Jews) you shall be guided from error (or Christians) and the Christians also say the same, (then ye will be rightly guided. Say) to them, O Muhammad: it is not as you claim: (And they say, "Be Jews or Christians, then you will be guided.") Allah's statement,.

**What else the same passage holds.**

" Say (to them O Muhammad), "Nay, (we follow) only the religion of Ibrahim, Hanif (Islamic Monotheism), and he was not of Al-Mushrikin (those who worshipped others along with Allah Why was it, then, that they turned away from the Prophet Muhammad? The reason for this was that the religion brought by the Prophet, taught people to take on the hue of God; to devote themselves to Him entirely. With the People of the Book, religion had a different meaning. For them religion was reduced to a symbol of national pride. The message brought by the Prophet hurt their pride, so they turned against him. Those who consider their own race superior to others cannot accept the truth when it manifests itself in some nation other than their own. They would believe in prophets who came from amongst their own people, but not in those who appeared among other people outside their own community. The only personalities that they acknowledged were those who belonged to their own race. Those who look at religion as worship of God, on the other hand, recognize the truth of every piece of wisdom that God sends down, no matter who teaches it. For the theologians to realize that the Prophet was God’s final messenger was not a matter of insuperable difficulty. There was nothing to prevent them from seeing the truth of his religion. They should have proclaimed what, deep down in their hearts, they knew to be true. But they did not accept him as the final prophet, as was enjoined by God, for the simple reason that they were more concerned about their own position and prestige. In the second of these verses the progeny of Sayyidna Ya qub (Jacob) has been described as Asbat or "tribes. Muhammad bin Ishaq reported that Ibn 'Abbas said that 'Abdullah bin Suriya Al-A'war said to the Messenger of Allah, "The guidance is only what we (Jews) follow. " The reason is that he had twelve sons, and the offspring of each son came to form a tribe. Allah so blessed his seed that in Egypt, Sayyidna Yusuf (Joseph) and his brothers made up a group of twelve men, but their lineage flourished, and when the Israelites left Egypt along with Sayyidna Musa (Moses), their number ran into thousands. " Also, the Christians said similarly, so Allah revealed, Another form of this blessing was that the progeny of Sayyidna Ya qub included a large number of prophets. ((we follow) only the religion of Ibrahim, Hanif) meaning, on the straight path, as Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi and 'Isa bin Jariyah stated. Also, Abu Qilabah said, "The Hanif is what the Messengers, from beginning to end, believed in.")

136.text:
Say, O believers, "We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us" opens with the faith of the believers in the revelation given to them. The verse then widens the circle: "and what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants; and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord." The list runs from the patriarchs to the prophets of the Book, and each name is placed under the same Lord. The phrase "We make no distinction between any of them" states the central rule: the believers accept all of them alike. The verse ends with "And to Allah we all submit," which returns the whole statement to submission. The Mukhtaṣar gives the faith in the Torah given to Moses as part of this answer. The Qushayrī commentary states that the Prophet believed in everything that was revealed, and that his community did the same. The Tanwīr reads the opening as a teaching in the path of divine oneness. The word all in the closing phrase covers the whole list, from the first patriarch to the last prophet, and so the submission is the same for each. Each name in the list is kept separate by the word and, so that no one is left out of the faith the verse describes. The reader is shown a creed that moves from the revelation given to the believers, through the patriarchs and the prophets of the Book, to a single rule that refuses to separate them and a single submission at the end. The verse therefore names the revelation given to the believers first and the patriarchs second, so the believers' own faith is the starting point of the list.

**We believe in what was revealed.**

Say this address is to the believers ‘We believe in God and in that which has been revealed to us the Qur’ān and revealed to Abraham the ten scrolls Ishmael Isaac Jacob and the Tribes his sons and that which was given to Moses the Torah and Jesus the Gospel and the prophets from their Lord of Books and signs we make no division between any of them believing in some and disbelieving in others in the manner of Jews and Christians and to Him we submit’. "We believe in Allah and that which has been sent down to us and that which has been sent down to Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael), Ishaq (Isaac), Ya'qub (Jacob), and to Al-Asbat (the offspring of the twelve sons of Ya'qub), and that which has been given to Musa (Moses) and 'Isa (Jesus), and that which has been given to the Prophets from their Lord. (Say (O Muslims): We believe in Allah and that which is revealed unto us) i.e. in Muhammad and the Qur'an (and that which was revealed unto Abraham) i.e. we believe in Abraham and his Scripture, (and Ishmael) and we believe in Ishmael and his Scripture, (and Isaac) and in Isaac and his Scripture, (and Jacob) and in Jacob and his Scripture, (and the tribes) and in the sons of Jacob and their Scriptures, (and that which Moses and Jesus received) i.e. we believe in Moses and the Torah and in Jesus and the Gospel, (and that which the Prophets received) we also believe in all the prophets and their Scriptures (from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them) that Allah sent them as prophets to teach divine Oneness, (and unto Him we have surrendered) we acknowledge that we worship Him and declare that there is only one true God. We believe in God and in that which has been revealed to us and revealed to Abraham Ishmael Isaac Jacob and the tribes and that which was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord we make no division between any of them and to Him we submit.

**The prophets named.**

Say that you have faith in the Torah which Allah gave to Moses, and the Gospel which He gave to Jesus, and in all the scriptures that He gave to every one of the prophets, with no distinction between them, having faith in all of them, not only having faith in some and rejecting others. They would believe in prophets who came from amongst their own people, but not in those who appeared among other people outside their own community. In the second of these verses the progeny of Sayyidna Ya qub (Jacob) has been described as Asbat or "tribes.

**No distinction.**

(And wish to make distinction between Allah and His Messengers (by believing in Allah and disbelieving in His Messengers) saying, "We believe in some but reject others," and wish to adopt a way in between. They are in truth disbelievers)(4:150-151). Because our Prophet believed in everything that was revealed before him he was honored with everything that [God] had conferred in honor to [the prophets] before him. Tell them that you humbly surrender to Him alone. Then He taught the believers the path of divine Oneness so that the Jews and Christians had an indication of what this divine Oneness means, saying:

**Submission to Allah alone.**

When his community believed in everything that God revealed to His messengers and made no division between any of them they drew the highest share in honor and took precedence over all communities. When [God] proclaimed the harmony muwāfaqa of all [the messages of the prophets] He entrusted everything in existence [to fall] under [Muḥammad's] banner. Just as the people of old received their just deserts as individuals, so will latter-day generations receive what they merit on their own account, for truth is an individual, not an ancestral matter. " This means that the Asbat are the various tribes of the Children of Israel, among whom Allah sent several Prophets.

**Faith and the people of old.**

Why was it, then, that they turned away from the Prophet Muhammad? Those who consider their own race superior to others cannot accept the truth when it manifests itself in some nation other than their own. Another form of this blessing was that the progeny of Sayyidna Ya qub included a large number of prophets. Tell the Jews and Christians who make these baseless claims that you have faith in Allah and the Qur’ān which He revealed to you, and in what He revealed to Abraham and his sons Ishmael and Isaac, and to Jacob, and in what He revealed to the prophets from the descendants of Jacob.

**What else the same passage holds.**

We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we have submitted (in Islam). The Muslim believes in all that Allah revealed and all the Prophets " The reason is that he had twelve sons, and the offspring of each son came to form a tribe. Allah so blessed his seed that in Egypt, Sayyidna Yusuf (Joseph) and his brothers made up a group of twelve men, but their lineage flourished, and when the Israelites left Egypt along with Sayyidna Musa (Moses), their number ran into thousands. 137.text:
"So if they believe in what you believe, then they will indeed be rightly guided." opens with a condition that the Prophet and the believers would be glad to see fulfilled. The word indeed confirms that the guidance follows from the belief. "But if they turn away, they are simply opposed to the truth." The turning away is set against the belief, and the phrase simply opposed names the act for what it is. The verse then turns to the Prophet: "But Allah will spare you their evil." The promise is one of protection, and it removes the burden of their opposition from the Prophet. The verse closes with "For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing," which gives the reason the protection can be trusted: the Lord hears what they say and knows what they do. The Tanwīr reads the turning away as a refusal to believe in all that was sent. The Mukhtaṣar brings in the instruction not to be sad, since Allah will protect the Prophet. The Tazkirul commentary describes a faith that had become a rarity among a people who revered their own traditions, and the verse gives the believers a sure ground in the face of that. The word rightly marks the guidance as the result of belief, so the sentence makes the same measure for both sides. The phrase "they are simply opposed" uses the same measure in the other direction, and the verse keeps the two outcomes in clear view. The promise of protection comes after the warning, so the Prophet is comforted before he is told what the opposition will bring. The Maʿārif commentary takes the belief in the like of what the Prophet believes as the point on which the whole verse turns.

**If they believe as you believe.**

(And if they) i.e. the people of the Book (believe in the like of that which you believe) in all the prophets and their Scriptures (then are they right guided) from error by following the religion of Muhammad and Abraham. If they have faith in the like of that in which you have faith, they will have found guid ance; but if they turn away, they will have split from you.

**If they turn away.**

(but if they turn away) from truth to falsehood after proof had been presented to them,. (But if they turn away) refuse to believe in all the prophets and their Scriptures, (then are they in schism) in conflict with the true religion, (and Allah will suffice thee (for defence) against them) Allah will lift their burden from you, by killing and expelling them. Yet if they turn away from faith because they reject all the prophets or some of them, then they are in disagreement and are against you. When truth stands on its own, unsupported by history or tradition, as it was in the time of the Prophet, those who accept it do so for the pure and simple reason that it is the truth.

**Allah will spare you.**

Do not be sad, O Prophet, because Allah will protect you from their harm and evil, and give you victory over them. God will suffice you against them; He is the hearing, the knowing. We will suffice you against their business and We will remove their torment from you. Allah said, if they, the disbelievers among the People of the Book and other disbelievers, believe in all of Allah's Books and Messengers and do not differentiate between any of them,.

**Hearing and knowing.**

(And He is the Hearer) of what they say, (the Knower) of their punishment. Allah hears all that they say, and knows all their intentions and actions. Similarly, there are people whose minds and hearts are so befogged in modern materialism and the so-called "rationalism" that they find it difficult to accept the idea of the other world and the things that pertain to it, and then try to subject them to crooked interpretations, which they suppose to be an effort to make Islam more acceptable to the modern mind, and hence a great service to Islam. As for that, even the idolators of Arabia used to proclaim the authenticity of their 'Iman as do the Jews and the Christians even today, and as do even the heretics in every age, but since their faith in Allah, in the prophets and the angels, and in the Day of Judgment etc. did not conform to the 'Iman of the Holy Prophet it was not acceptable to Allah and was summarily rejected.

**A faith that had become rare.**

What was so special about that faith was that it amounted to acceptance of the truth on an abstract level; it was belief in truth for the sake of truth. This had become a rarity in a society which, revering the words of the ancient prophets, regarded as truth whatever had been sanctified by centuries-old tradition. Continued belief in such ‘truth’, embellished as it was by myth and legend, became a matter of national pride; to regard it in any other light would have been to deny a great legacy from the past. Thus, in doctrinal matters above all, their 'Iman has been placed before us as a model, and the verse is essentially a divine commandment, laying down the fundamental principle that the only 'Iman acceptable to Allah is the one which was adopted by the Holy Prophet and his blessed Companions, and that any doctrines or beliefs that deviate from it in the least are neither valid nor acceptable to Allah.

**What else the same passage holds.**

And if they the Jews and the Christians believe in the like mithl ‘the like’ is extra of what you believe in then they are truly guided; but if they turn away from belief in it then they are clearly in schism in opposition to you; God will suffice you O Muhammad against them and their schisms; He is the Hearer of their sayings the Knower of their circumstances God sufficed him with regard to them by killing Qurayza expelling Nadīr and exacting the jizya from them. From the beginning of the Surah Ai-Baqarah upto this place, different verses have been explaining the nature and essence 'Iman (faith), sometimes succinctly and sometimes in detail. Verse 137 defines 'Iman in a simple and short phrase which is at the same time so comprehensive that all possible details and explanations are inherent in it. The earlier verses having established that the only religion which is valid at present is Islam, this verse assures the Muslims that the Jews and the Christians can find the guidance only "if they believe just as you believe", or, in other words, "if they believe in what you believe in. " The immediate addressees of the phrase "you believe" are the Holy Prophet and his blessed Companions. That is to say, one should believe in Allah and His attributes, in the angels, in the Books of Allah, in the messengers and prophets of Allah and in their teachings exactly in the same manner as the Holy Prophet and the blessed Companions did, without adding or subtracting anything on one's own part and without advancing one's own interpretations or distorting the authentic meanings of the doctrines. Nor is one allowed to assign to the angels or the prophets a station higher or lower than the one assigned to them by the word or deed of the Holy Prophet . Moreover, one is also required to be sincere and pure in one's faith, for the contrary would amount to hypocrisy (Nifaq). This explanation helps us to see in its true proportions the situation of the heterodox sects among the Muslims - of those who make tall claims as to the genuineness of their 'Iman but do not possess 'Iman in the full sense of the term. To give a few examples, some of the associators of Arabia used to deny the very existence of angels, while others considered them to be the daughters of God.

138.text:
"This is the natural Way of Allah." opens with a claim about the Way, which the English gives as a path that belongs to Allah. The statement sets the Way in the faith that the verse has been building through the previous verses. The question "And who is better than Allah in ordaining a way?" follows, and it asks the listeners to name any better guide. The question has only one answer, and the verse keeps the answer unspoken. The verse ends with "And we worship none but Him," which turns the claim of the Way into a statement of worship. The Maʿārif commentary states that the verse presents Islam under the image of the colouring of Allah, and it treats the colouring as a commandment that the believers keep in their lives. The Qushayrī commentary opens its own reading with the question of who is more beautiful in colour than God. The Mukhtaṣar gives the sense that no one should worship others beside Allah, and that the believers must say they worship Allah alone. The reader is shown a verse whose claim is short, but whose answer is the whole of the believer's worship. The claim of the Way is kept short, so the next clause can answer it. The word better is used as a comparison, and the question leaves no other Way on the table. The believer is therefore asked to hold the Way of Allah as the measure of every other path, and to hold no other measure beside it. The verse gives the answer a practical shape, so that worship and the Way are spoken of in one breath.

**The Way of Allah.**

(Allah's Fitrah (i.e. Allah's Islamic Monotheism)(30:30) directs Muslims to, "Hold to it." Hold tightly to the religion of Allah which is the natural way of life for you, on the inside and outside. Verse 138 delineates Islam as the "colouring of Allah", and explains this "colouring" as the unalloyed worship of Allah and total submission to Him. ((We take our) colour from Allah) i.e. follow the Religion of Allah, (and who is better than Allah at colouring) better than the Religion of Allah.

**Better than Allah.**

There is no better way of life than the path of Allah, which agrees with our nature, benefiting us in every way and protecting us from evil and corruption. God's color-and who is more beautiful in color than God? " He who has painted a thousand worlds with color why would He buy my color and yours, O bankrupt man! If faith is to be of the kind which pleases God, it must be identical with that of the Companions of the Prophet.

**Worship none but Him.**

Say that you worship Allah alone and do not worship anything apart from Him. (And We are His worshippers) say: we are monotheists and acknowledge that we worship Him and declare that there is only one true God. This is the kind of belief that God recognizes and accepts. (then they are only in opposition. So Allah will suffice you against them) meaning, Allah will aid the believers against them,.

**The colouring as a commandment.**

The verse suggests that this colour is wasted away with the water, without leaving a trace outside or inside, nor does this kind of baptism serve the purpose of circumcision and cleanse a man of physical impurity. Then, the word Sibghah or "colouring" has a deeper meaning too. In this sense, the verse is a commandment, asking Muslims "to dye" themselves in the "colouring of Allah", outwardly and inwardly by offering unalloyed worship to Him alone, by submitting themselves totally to His commandments, and by gladly accepting His will. On this topic many stories are told about the shaykhs.

**True faith.**

This is true faith; only faith of such strength and purity is acceptable to God. This had become a rarity in a society which, revering the words of the ancient prophets, regarded as truth whatever had been sanctified by centuries-old tradition. Allah said, if they, the disbelievers among the People of the Book and other disbelievers, believe in all of Allah's Books and Messengers and do not differentiate between any of them,. One is that I bear witness that there is no god but God, and I bear witness that MuḤammad is God's messenger,' and he took off the sash. 'The other is that I say, "O God, if there is any danger here, then I will begin with this."' So he began.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The mark of God sibghata’Llāhi a verbal noun reaffirming the earlier āmannā and it is in the accusative because of the verbal construction implied that is to say sabaghanā’Llāhu ‘God has marked us’ this denotes His religion the one towards which He made human beings naturally inclined as it leaves its mark on a person in the same way that a dye leaves its mark on a garment; and who has that is none has a better mark sibghatan ‘marking’ is for specification than God? So if they believe in the like of that which you believe then they are rightly guided; but if they turn away, then they are only in opposition. And Him we worship the Jews said to the Muslims ‘We are the people of the first Book and our direction of prayer qibla is more ancient and prophets were never sent from among the Arabs; if Muhammad were a prophet he would have been one of us’. Verse 135 has identified Islam with "the religion of Ibrahim. " If we put Verse 135 and 138 together, it becomes clear that essentially Islam - or any authentic religion, for that matter – is the religion of Allah, and that the association of a religion with the name of a prophet can only be symbolised. Verse 138 presents religion as "colouring" (Sibghah). The expression carries within itself several levels of meaning. But the immediate allusion is to a certain ceremony of the Christians. On the seventh day of its birth, they used to bathe an infant in coloured (probably yellow) water, which was supposed to be a substitute for circumcision, and a sufficient guarantee for the external and internal purification of the infant - the fast and indelible "colouring" of Christian faith, so to say. And the verse declares that the only colouring worth the name is the colouring of a genuine and unabrogated religion - that is, Islam the only colouring which can guarantee physical and spiritual purification, and the only one which shall remain. Just as a certain colour is openly and clearly visible to the beholder, the signs of genuine and pure 'Iman should shine through the face, the movements, the habits and the behaviour of a Muslim.

139.text:
"Say, Would you dispute with us about Allah, while He is our Lord and your Lord?" opens with a question to the People of the Book, and the question asks why they would argue with the believers about Allah. The sentence gives the common ground, since He is the Lord of both parties. The verse then divides the account: "We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours." Each side answers for its own actions, and the believers are not bound by the choices of the other side. The verse closes with "And we are devoted to Him alone," which gives the believers' sincerity as the one thing they bring to the dispute. The Maʿārif commentary takes the word ikhlāṣ, sincerity, as the core of the verse's final phrase. The Tanwīr reads the sentence as a statement that the believers acknowledge sincerely the one Lord. The Mukhtaṣar tells the Prophet to say that his actions and theirs are separate, and that he is sincere to Allah in his worship. The Tazkirul commentary links the verse to a faith that pleases God, which must be held without the ornament of pride.

**The dispute about Allah.**

, O Muhammad, ((unto the People of the Scripture) dispute ye with us) do you argue with us (concerning Allah) concerning the Religion of Allah (when He is our Lord and your Lord?) when Allah is our Lord and yours? If the People of the Scripture argue with you, saying they have more right to Allah and His religion than you do because their way of life is older and their scriptures came before yours, then it will not benefit them.

**Our deeds and yours.**

(Ours are our works) we have our religion (and yours your work) your religion. Tell them, O Prophet, that you have your actions which they will not be asked about; and they have their actions which you will not be asked about. How can dispute with strangers be appropriate when they are covered by absence and shaded by concealment while the friends are lit by unveiling and the bright noon of witnessingḍ When is the state of one who is bankrupt by his absence equal to one whose selection and sincere devotion [and] immersion in acts of drawing near to Him has [already been] decreedḍ It is preposterous-there is no equality!

**Sincere and devoted.**

" According to Said ibn Jubayr, Ikhlas consists in worshipping no one but Allah, associating no one with Allah, and doing good deeds only for the sake of obeying Allah, and not for the purpose of winning the admiration of the people. (And we are sincere (in our faith) in Him) we acknowledge that we worship Him and declare that there is only one true God. Tell them that you are sincere to Allah in your worship and in doing as He instructs you, and that you do not worship anything apart from Him. (while He is our Lord and your Lord?) meaning, He has full control over us and you, and deserves the worship alone without partners.

**Your Lord and our Lord.**

Allah knows what they have been doing, and will judge them according to their own deeds, and not according to the deeds of their ancestors. Should the Jews and the Christians still continue, in their stubbornness, to deny, Allah asks the Holy Prophet and the Muslims to declare in plain and simple words that Allah, being the Lord of All, cannot show any special favour to any particular group of His creatures, and that on the Day of Judgment He will assess the Jews and the Christians as well as the Muslims according to what each has believed in and how each has been behaving - a principle which was accepted by the People of the Book too. If faith is to be of the kind which pleases God, it must be identical with that of the Companions of the Prophet.

**Faith that pleases God.**

What was so special about that faith was that it amounted to acceptance of the truth on an abstract level; it was belief in truth for the sake of truth. This had become a rarity in a society which, revering the words of the ancient prophets, regarded as truth whatever had been sanctified by centuries-old tradition. Continued belief in such ‘truth’, embellished as it was by myth and legend, became a matter of national pride; to regard it in any other light would have been to deny a great legacy from the past. It so happens with some pious people that once they start seeking this kind of "sincerity" in offering their enjoined prayers, they find that they cannot keep up an unbroken concentration of mind, and are so frightened by this lapse that they sometimes give up offering their prayers, believing such worship to be "insincere" and hence invalid.

140.text:
"Do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants were all Jews or Christians? Say, Who is more knowledgeable: you or Allah?" opens with a question that tests the claim. The list of the patriarchs and their descendants is set against the labels of Jew and Christian, and the question asks whether those labels can cover them. The contrast is between the knowledge of the listeners and the knowledge of Allah, and the answer is plainly the second. The next sentence reaches the matter of the testimony: "Who does more wrong than those who hide the testimony they received from Allah?" The concealment of testimony is named as the greatest wrong, and the phrase they received from Allah shows that the testimony was given to them. The verse closes with "And Allah is never unaware of what you do," which sets the account before the Lord. The Tanwīr gives the sense that Allah has already informed the believers that Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian. The Mukhtaṣar takes the verse as showing that the claim is a lie against Allah. The Maʿārif commentary, and the Tazkirul commentary after it, treat the knowledge of Allah as the measure that no claim of descent can escape. The question of who is more knowledgeable is put to the listeners directly, so they must answer it for themselves. The answer that Allah is more knowledgeable is left for the listeners to draw from the question itself, as the verse does not spell it out. The reader is asked to see the verse as a test of the listeners' honesty about the faith of the prophets, which they were given to make known and not to hide. The verse therefore leaves the listeners with a question they cannot answer in their own favour, and the rest of the passage keeps that question open.

**Do you claim?.**

Or nay do you say taqūlūna also read yaqūlūna ‘do they say?

**Who is more knowledgeable.**

’ Say to them ‘Have you then greater knowledge or has God? that is God has greater knowledge; He dissociated Abraham from both groups when He said Abraham was not a Jew nor a Christian Q. 367; and those mentioned with him Abraham are his followers in not belonging to either group. (Do ye know best, or doth Allah?) do you know best about their religion or does Allah? Ask, O Prophet, in reply to them, whether they are more knowledgeable or is Allah. Have you then greater knowl edge or has Godḍ And who does greater injustice than he who conceals a testimony received from Godḍ And God is not heedless of what you do.

**Hiding the testimony.**

And who does greater injustice than he who conceals hides from people a testimony he has received from God? that is there is none more unjust than him these are the Jews for they concealed God’s testimony about Abraham’s pure faith in the Torah; And God is not heedless of what you do’ this is a threat for them. Are those who have been drawn away from their own testimony like those who are veiled by itḍ Is the one who is snatched away from all of it equal to the one who is thrown back to what is like himḍ That is the conjecture of those who disbelieve-what misery is theirs! (And who is more unjust) in his disbelief and more insolent and daring vis-�-vis Allah (than he who hideth a testimony which he hath received from Allah) in the Torah concerning the prophethood of this Prophet ﷺ?

**Abraham was neither.**

Allah has already informed us that Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian. This shows that what they say is a lie against Allah and His Prophet, and that they hid the truth of what was revealed to them. Or say you that Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and Al-Asbat, were Jews or Christians? If they claim that they were Jews or Christians, then what they say is false, because they were sent and died before the Torah and the Gospel were revealed.

**Truth stands on its own.**

When truth stands on its own, unsupported by history or tradition, as it was in the time of the Prophet, those who accept it do so for the pure and simple reason that it is the truth. What was so special about that faith was that it amounted to acceptance of the truth on an abstract level; it was belief in truth for the sake of truth. This had become a rarity in a society which, revering the words of the ancient prophets, regarded as truth whatever had been sanctified by centuries-old tradition. When they by virtue of being outsiders [to the Real] judged the prophets [ ] according to their own state the Real threw their conjecture back upon them and left them with their own opinion.

**What else the same passage holds.**

These three verses bring to an end the section of the Surah in which certain claims of the Jews and the Christians have been refuted -- for example, their assertion that Sayyidna Ibrahim (Abraham), Sayyidna Ismail (Ishmael), Sayyidna Ishaq (Isaac), Sayyidna Ya qub (Jacob) and the prophets in his lineage were either Jews or Christians, and the claim that they were the chosen people and would have the exclusive privilege of being sent straight to Paradise which would be denied to Muslims. ’ ‘Abraham Ishmael Isaac and Jacob and the Tribes — they were Jews or they were Christians? The earlier verses have established that the religion of all these prophets was Islam, in the general sense of the term, but that the earlier Shari ahs have now been abrogated, and the title of "Islam" been specially given to the religion of Sayyidna Muhammad . Should the Jews and the Christians still continue, in their stubbornness, to deny, Allah asks the Holy Prophet and the Muslims to declare in plain and simple words that Allah, being the Lord of All, cannot show any special favour to any particular group of His creatures, and that on the Day of Judgment He will assess the Jews and the Christians as well as the Muslims according to what each has believed in and how each has been behaving - a principle which was accepted by the People of the Book too. The Muslims have also been asked to announce that they on their part recognize no other god but Allah, and have purified their religion of all traces of association (Shirk) - as against the Jews and the Christians who consider Sayyidna Uzayr (Ezra) and Sayyidna Isa (Jesus) respectively to be "the Son of God", and whose religions have, moreover, been abrogated. In this respect at least, Muslims have a superiority over them. If the People of the Book should, on account of their affiliation with the earlier prophets, still keep insisting on their own rectitude, the Muslims may ask them a basic question - who knows the truth better, Allah or the People of the Book? Allah has definitely and finally announced the truth in the Last Revelation, and the People of the Book themselves know that the religion of the earlier prophets was Islam. Yet they are trying to conceal the truth, and being unjust, in the gravest sense of the term. Allah knows what they have been doing, and will judge them according to their own deeds, and not according to the deeds of their ancestors. Thus, at the end of this section, Verse 141, which is a repetition of Verse 134, warns them against the consequences of their vanity and pretentiousness, and advises them to take care of themselves rather than relying on ancestral glory. Verse 139 brings out the essential and peculiar characteristic of the Islamic Ummah it has purified itself of all possible admixture of Shirk (association), and devoted itself, externally and internally, to Allah. The Arabic word in the text is Mukhlisun the plural of Mukhlis which signifies "one who has purified himself', and which is allied to the word Ikhlas "the act of purifying oneself.

141.text:
"That was a community that had already gone before." opens the verse with the same words as 2:134, and the text repeats the earlier verse word for word. The repetition is part of the text, and the commentary treats the verse as a restatement of the same principle of account. "For them is what they earned and for you is what you have earned." The earned deeds of each side keep their own account, and the later generation is not answerable for the earlier one. "And you will not be accountable for what they have done" is the closing sentence that the verse repeats, and it is the point the repetition makes clear. The Maʿārif commentary treats the first verses of the passage as having established that the religion of the prophets is one, so the restatement here sets the same measure against the new dispute. The Mukhtaṣar brings the sentence back to the sense that each person receives the reward of his own deeds. The reader is asked to hold the two verses together, so that the claim of descent and the claim of the forefathers' merit are both answered in the same terms.

**A community gone before.**

They shall receive the reward of what they earned, and you of what you earn. That is a community that has passed away; theirs is what they have earned and yours is what you have earned; you shall not be asked about what they did a similar verse has already been mentioned above.

(And if they belie you, say: "For me are my deeds and for you are your deeds! You are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do!")(10:41), and,. (So if they dispute with you (Muhammad) say: "I have submitted myself to Allah (in Islam), and (so have) those who follow me")(3:20).
