He commands you to commit what is even worse, that is, saying about Allah without knowledge.' So this includes every innovator and disbeliever. Verily, he is to you an open enemy He (Satan) commands you only what is evil and Fahsha' (sinful), and that you should say about Allah what you know not. Some commentators have said that su' here signifies sin as such, and fahsha' signifies major sins. Because of his audacity toward God he induces you to speak falsely about God.

**The Satanic suggestion.**

The expression ‌ (innama ya'murukum: he only orders you') means instigating a suggestion in the heart. Verily, he is to you an open enemy He (Satan) commands you only what is evil and Fahsha' (sinful), and that you should say about Allah what you know not. What actually happens is that the real God is replaced by a false god. It is akin to diluting man’s natural feelings of reverence and devotions meant only for God, and which should be exclusively reserved for God alone.

**Feelings of reverence diluted.**

It is the worship of something other than God in order to satisfy one’s feelings of devotion and veneration. That is why the Islamic law holds unlawful all those things which, in any degree, lead to deviation, i.e. diverting man’s natural desire for God in some other direction. the devil (enjoineth upon you only the evil) evil works (and the foul) transgressions, (and that ye should tell) lies (concerning Allah that which ye know not). The verse means: 'Your enemy, Satan, commands you to commit evil acts and what is worse than that, such as adultery and so forth.

170.text:
"When it is said to them, Follow what Allah has revealed, they reply, No! We only follow what we found our forefathers practicing." opens with the call to follow the revelation and the reply that refuses it. The people reply with a firm no, and the verse names the thing they choose to follow instead, which is what they found their forefathers doing. The sentence sets the revelation and the forefathers side by side, and the reply chooses the forefathers. "Would they still do so, even if their forefathers had absolutely no understanding or guidance?" The question turns the reply against itself. The verse asks whether the following would stand if the forefathers had no understanding or guidance. The question has its answer in the form of the question, and the verse leaves the listeners to face it. The Mukhtaṣar states that if these disbelievers are told to follow the guidance, they ask whether they should follow their fathers even though those fathers understood nothing. The Jalālayn gives the reply as a question, and it treats the question as one the disbelievers are asked. The Maʿārif commentary states that the following of forefathers, in the blind form that the verse censures, is shown to be without any basis. The Tazkirul commentary states that the real God is replaced by a false one, and it describes the polytheists who set animals free in His name. The reader is asked to see the verse as a question put against the habit of blind following.

**Follow what Allah has revealed.**

And when it is said to them the disbelievers ‘Follow what God has revealed’ pertaining to affirmation of God’s Oneness and the good things that He has made lawful they say ‘No; but we follow what we found our fathers doing’ in the way of idol-worship deeming unlawful the camel let loose and practising the slitting of the camel’s ear sc. bahīra. (And when it is said unto them) to the Arab idolaters: If these disbelievers are told to follow the guidance and light which Allah revealed, they say, resisting stubbornly, that they will follow the beliefs and customs that their fathers followed.

**We found our forefathers practicing.**

(Follow that which Allah hath revealed) follow the lawfulness exposited by Allah concerning what is cultivated and the cattle raised, (they say: We follow that wherein we found our fathers) regarding their unlawfulness. Do they follow their fathers even though they understood nothing of guidance or the light, and were not guided to the truth that Allah accepts? No doubt, this verse does censure the blind following of forefathers, but at the same time, it provides a rule and its attending conditions proving that following has its permissible aspect which has been indicated in (even though their forefathers used to understand nothing) and (nor had they been on the right path). This is good enough to prove that following forefathers in what is false is forbidden while it is permissible, rather desirable, in what is true.

**Even if their forefathers had no understanding.**

Whatḍ Even if their fathers do not understand anything and they were not guidedḍ There is no raising their eyes beyond that which is like them in form class kind and ancestry for they are set on their way. It is also said that this means: if their fathers did not understand about things in this world and did not follow the practice of any prophet, then how could you follow them? Had they known that their ancestors had no intelligence to restrain them nor guidance to unite them they would have withdrawn from them [understanding them to be] hostile and resisted them [understanding them to be] oppositional [to God's com mand]. Now we can see that following the model of those identified in the text cannot be permitted because they do not have a revealed set of laws from Allah, nor do they have the ability to deduce injunctions from the Word of Allah.

**Deaf, dumb and blind.**

(They are deaf, dumb, and blind.) means, they are deaf, as they do not hear the truth; mute, as they do not utter it; and blind, as they do not see or recognize its path and way. (So they do not understand.) means, they do not comprehend or understand anything. (And the example of those who disbelieve...) meaning, in their injustice, misguidance and ignorance, they are just like wandering animals, not understanding what they are told; if the shepherd heralds them or calls them to what benefits them, they would not understand what is actually being said to them, for they only hear unintelligible sounds. The disbelievers, in that state, do hear but not what is intended to correct them, so they are called 'deaf; and they are tight-lipped when it comes to accepting the truth, therefore, they are 'dumb'; and since they do not see their benefit or loss, they are 'blind'.

**Blind following.**

What actually happens is that the real God is replaced by a false god. That is why the Islamic law holds unlawful all those things which, in any degree, lead to deviation, i.e. diverting man’s natural desire for God in some other direction. The polytheists set certain animals free in the name of their deities. But the lights of insight were snatched from them and they were deprived of the proofs of certainty.

**What else the same passage holds.**

When these mushrik people were asked to follow the injunctions revealed by Allah through His Messenger, they refused to do so and insisted that they would rather follow the customary practice they had inherited from their fathers because, as they assumed, their models were divinely appointed to follow the way they adopted. God says What? the hamza of a-wa-law is for repudiation do they follow them Even if their fathers do not understand anything concerning religion and they were not guided? to the truth. Allah Almighty refutes this position of theirs by asking how could they go on following the ways of their fathers, under all conditions, to the exclusion of all other ways, even if their fathers did not understand much about the true faith, nor were they blessed with guidance given by their Lord? In their lack of understanding, the verse says that the disbelievers resemble the scenario of a person shouting his call to an animal who hears nothing meaningful or significant except a bland cry. Consequently, with their vital senses so dulled, they seem to understand nothing. It is from here that we find out that following the forefathers mentioned in the text of the Qur'an was censured because they lacked reason and guidance. 'Guidance' or the right path signifies injunctions revealed by Allah Almighty, openly and clearly, while aql or reason stands for imperative guidance deduced by the great armed vision of Ijtihad from the recognized sources of Islamic Shari'ah.

171.text:
"The example of the disbelievers not responding to the Messenger's warning is like a flock not comprehending the calls and cries of the shepherd." opens with a comparison drawn from the life of animals. The disbelievers are likened to a flock that hears a shepherd and does not understand him, so the sound reaches them without meaning. The comparison makes the failure one of comprehension and not of hearing alone. "They are wilfully deaf, dumb and blind so they have no understanding" completes the picture. The verse names their deafness, dumbness, and blindness as a wilful state, and it ends with the result, which is no understanding. The verse follows the question about blind following and the reply that refuses the Lord's call, so the flock is the image of those who follow without thought. The Mukhtaṣar states that they are deaf to hearing the truth, so that it will not benefit them. The Jalālayn gives the likeness as the attribute of those who disbelieve and the one who calls them. The Maʿārif commentary states that the disbelievers do hear but not what is meant. The Qushayrī commentary states that without the ears of comprehension and acceptance, their hearing is of no use. The Tazkirul commentary describes a stage at which people are totally unable to hear, and who act as if they have neither eyes nor ears. The reader is asked to see the verse as a picture of hearing without understanding.

**A flock and the shepherd.**

The likeness the attribute of those who disbelieve and the one who calls them to guidance is as the likeness of one who shouts to that which hears nothing save a call and a cry only a sound not understanding its meaning when they listen to an admonition they are like cattle that hear the cry of their shepherd but do not understand what he is saying; they are deaf dumb blind — they do not comprehend any admonition. (The likeness of those who disbelieve) vis-�-vis Muhammad ﷺ (is as the likeness of one who calleth unto that which heareth nothing) just like camels and sheep with their shepherd: his speech is unintelligible to them when he says to them, for example, eat or drink (except a shout and a cry. Deaf) concerning the Truth, (dumb) regarding the Truth, (blind) to guidance; i.e. they pretend to be deaf, dumb and blind when it comes to the Truth and guidance, (therefore they have no sense) they do not understand Allah's command and the call of the Prophet ﷺ just as camels and cattle do not comprehend the words of their shepherd. The likeness of those who disbelieve is as the likeness of one who shouts to that which hears nothing save a call and a cry; deaf dumb blind-they do not comprehend. And the example of those who disbelieve is as that of him who shouts to those (flock of sheep) that hear nothing but calls and cries.

**Wilfully deaf, dumb and blind.**

(They are deaf, dumb, and blind.) means, they are deaf, as they do not hear the truth; mute, as they do not utter it; and blind, as they do not see or recognize its path and way. They are deaf to hearing the truth so that it will benefit them, dumb as they are unable to speak about the truth, and blind to seeing it, and because of this they do not understand the guidance which you call them to. (And the example of those who disbelieve...) meaning, in their injustice, misguidance and ignorance, they are just like wandering animals, not understanding what they are told; if the shepherd heralds them or calls them to what benefits them, they would not understand what is actually being said to them, for they only hear unintelligible sounds. The disbelievers, in that state, do hear but not what is intended to correct them, so they are called 'deaf; and they are tight-lipped when it comes to accepting the truth, therefore, they are 'dumb'; and since they do not see their benefit or loss, they are 'blind'.

**No understanding.**

The example of those who disbelieve and stubbornly follow the path of their fathers is like the example of the shepherd who shouts, calling to his animals that hear his voice, but do not understand what he says. Without the ears of comprehension and acceptance their bodily hearing did not benefit them. Ibn Ishaq reported that Ibn 'Abbas said that this was revealed about a group of Jews whom Allah's Messenger called to Islam, but they refused, saying, "Rather, we shall follow what we found our forefathers following. But, this has nothing to do with following what is true which is, in fact, a basic religious principle, and a great means of protecting the religion of Muslims in as much as one who does not have the ability to do Ijtihad must rely on 'following' in matters of religion.

**Like the animals.**

They descended to the status of animals incapable of actualization taḥṣīl. Whoever is content to be like an animal man raḌiya an yakūn ka-l-bahīma does not have much worth lam yaqaʿu ʿalayhi kathīr al-qīma. Allah then gave a similitude regarding the unbelievers vis-�-vis Muhammad ﷺ saying: No doubt, this verse does censure the blind following of forefathers, but at the same time, it provides a rule and its attending conditions proving that following has its permissible aspect which has been indicated in (even though their forefathers used to understand nothing) and (nor had they been on the right path).

**Eyes and ears without use.**

Once an object, which is not God, is accepted as God as a result of man’s superstitious attitude, many other accompanying evils ensue. That animal is then held to be a means of achieving proximity to God and is expected to be a source of blessings. People reach a level where they are totally unable to hear or understand any argument put forward to them. They act as if they have neither eyes nor ears to see and hear, nor brains to give thought to any argument presented to them.

**What else the same passage holds.**

When these mushrik people were asked to follow the injunctions revealed by Allah through His Messenger, they refused to do so and insisted that they would rather follow the customary practice they had inherited from their fathers because, as they assumed, their models were divinely appointed to follow the way they adopted.

172.text:
"O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you." opens with the address to the believers, which turns from the call to all people to the call to those who have faith. The command is to eat the good things the Lord has provided, and the phrase We have provided names the provision as a gift from the Lord. "And give thanks to Allah if you truly worship Him alone." The thanks is tied to the worship, and the word alone closes the verse with the oneness that the verses before defended. The verse is placed after the warnings about forefathers and Satan, so the command to eat good things is given as the answer to both. The Mukhtaṣar states that being thankful to Him means acting with complete obedience, and it addresses those who have faith in Allah and follow His Messenger. The Tanwīr reads the lawfulness of eating the good things as the subject of the verse. The Maʿārif commentary states that eating and using what is halal plays a role in the believer's life. The Qushayrī commentary gives the lawful food as that for which there is no bad element. The Tazkirul commentary states that forbidden food should be avoided, and that the believer's attention is not to be diverted. The reader is asked to see the verse as the close of the food passage, in which the good things are a gift that calls for thanks.

**O believers.**

O you who have faith in Allah and follow His Messenger, consume the good things that Allah has provided and allowed for you; and be thankful to Allah, outwardly and inwardly, for the overwhelming blessings He has given you. (O ye who believe! Eat of the good things wherewith We have provided you) of the lawful things We have given you, (and render thanks to Allah) for it (if it is (indeed) He whom ye worship) it is also said that this means: if you really intend to worship Allah by declaring these to be unlawful, then do not declare them unlawful, for to worship Allah entails that you declare them to be lawful.

**Eat from the good things We have provided.**

Eat of the lawful things that We have provided you with, and be grateful to Allah, if it is indeed He Whom you worship He has forbidden you only the Maitah (dead animals), and blood, and the flesh of swine, and that which is slaughtered as a sacrifice for other than Allah. Then Allah mentions the lawfulness of eating what is cultivated on the land and the meat of cattle, saying: The permitted ḥalāl is that for which there is no [bad] consequence. Allah commands His believing servants to eat from the pure things that He has created for them and to thank Him for it, if they are truly His servants.

**Give thanks to Allah.**

Part of being thankful to Him is acting with complete devotion to Him and not going against Him, if you truly worship Him alone, and do not worship anything besides Him. The true meaning of thankfulness to Him is that you do not take a breath in anything other than the pleasure of the Real so long as the energy given to you by that [permitted and good] food remains. (...then there is no sin on him. Truly, Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.) "For what is eaten out of necessity. When the servant finds something that combines these two qualities it is permitted and good.

**Halal and the believer.**

Therefore, Allah Almighty has told all his prophets to eat from what is good and do what is righteous: 0 Messengers, eat of the good things and do the righteous. This shows that eating and using what is halal plays a vital role in doing what is good and virtuous. The Holy Prophet has said that there are many people, tired and distressed, who stretch their hands in prayer before Allah fervently calling '0 Lord, 0 Lord, yet haram is what they eat, haram is what they drink and haram is what they wear, how then, under these conditions, could they hope to have their prayers answered?' (The Sahih, Muslim, and Tirmidhi as quoted by Ibn Kathir)

**Forbidden food and attention.**

They should express themselves thus, ‘In accordance with God’s commandment, we are eating and drinking what God has provided us with. But this psychological make-up changes in the case of self-styled beliefs. In that case man’s attention is diverted to the supposed properties of the things he consumes. However, it is essential that such forbidden food should not be taken simply for the pleasure of the palate.

**What else the same passage holds.**

O you who believe eat of the good things that are lawful wherewith We have provided you and give thanks to God for what He has made lawful for you if it be Him that you worship. Earlier, the aim was to correct the error made by the mushrikin when they made unlawful what was good and permissible. Now, in the present Verse , the believers are being warned against falling into the same error. As a corollary, they are reminded of Allah's blessings and are taught to be grateful to Him. Later, in Verse 173 it is said that the prohibited must remain prohibited and should never be treated as lawful, something the mushrikin used to do when they ate carrion or animals slaughtered in a name other than that of Allah. Also implied is the warning that it is an error to declare any animal, other than those specified, as unlawful. Verse 172 forbids eating that which is Karam and along with it, allows eating that which is halal in all gratefulness to Allah. The reason is that the act of eating haram promotes evil instincts, kills the taste of ibadah and makes the prayers ineffective. In contrast, eating halal generates inner light, creates a distaste for evil deeds, leads towards high morals, and creates a state in which the heart welcomes ibadah and finds the very thought of sin sickening and of course, prayers are answered.

173.text:
"He has only forbidden you to eat carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah." opens with the word only, which limits the prohibition to the four things named. The list is short: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and the animal offered to a name other than Allah. The last item is the one that ties the food to worship, since the sacrifice is made in the name of another. "But if someone is compelled by necessity, neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need, they will not be sinful." The exception is set with two conditions, and both must hold. The person must be compelled by necessity, and must neither seek the food from desire nor go beyond what the need calls for. The verse ends with the pardon that follows from these conditions, so the rule is strict and the relief is given within it. The Mukhtaṣar states that Allah has only forbidden the eating of what died, and that the one who is forced to eat such things is forgiven. The Tanwīr reads the necessity as the one that drives a person to eat, and it places the forgiving of Allah beside the limits that the person must keep. The Qushayrī commentary treats the forbidden things as forbidden in outward circumstances, and it treats the inner companionship with them as forbidden to the heart. The Tazkirul commentary states that in cases of extreme necessity, where a man's life may be at stake, the rule gives way. The reader is asked to see the verse as a short statute with a narrow exception, in which mercy is shown without loosening the limit. "Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" closes the verse with the forgiveness that the necessity calls for.

**Only the four things.**

He has only forbidden you carrion that is the consumption of it since this is the subject of the general address here and similarly the consumption of what follows all of which is what has not been slaughtered in accordance with prescriptions of the Law; to this the Sunna adds as also constituting carrion what has been severed from a living creature. (He hath forbidden you only carrion) which He has commanded to immolate, (and blood) and shed blood, (and swineflesh, and that which hath been immolated to any other than Allah) that which is offered as sacrifice purposefully in any other thing than the Name of Allah, i.e. to idols. Allah has only forbidden you from consuming that which died without being sacrificed according to the sacred law and having its blood flow, the meat of pigs and what has had other than Allah’s name mentioned over it when it was sacrificed.

**Compelled by necessity.**

Yet whoever is constrained forced by dire need to eat of the above-mentioned not desiring to rebel against Muslims nor transgressing committing aggression against them by waylaying them no sin shall be on him for eating it. (But he who is driven by necessity) compelled to eat carrion (neither craving) neither rebelling nor declaring it lawful (nor transgressing) nor committing highway robbery nor purposefully eating it without being driven by necessity, (it is no sin for him) then such a person, who is compelled to eat it without having his fill and without taking anything with him, has not transgressed. Yet if someone is forced to eat something of these forbidden types, and does not sin by eating it when they are not in need, nor do they go beyond the limit of what is necessary, then they have done no wrong and will receive no punishment. Yet whoever is constrained that is anyone who has not found a means to annihilation in the realities of the Real should only travel by way of the law.

**Neither driven by desire nor exceeding need.**

(Lo! Allah is Forgiving) that he ate more than he needs to preserve himself, (Merciful) when He gave him legal dispensation to eat carrion. " This indicates that eating dead animals for those who are in need of it for survival is not only permissible but required. which means that the injunction has been relaxed for a person who is extremely compelled by hunger, and is not looking towards enjoying his food, nor is likely to go beyond the level of his need, then he, in that situation, will not incur any sin if he eats what is unlawful.

**Forgiving and merciful.**

Allah is Forgiving and Compassionate to whomever repents to Him; and it is from His mercy that He overlooks the eating of forbidden things when it is necessary. God is Forgiving to His friends Merciful to those who are obedient to Him for He has granted them wide berth in this matter. Eat of the lawful things that We have provided you with, and be grateful to Allah, if it is indeed He Whom you worship He has forbidden you only the Maitah (dead animals), and blood, and the flesh of swine, and that which is slaughtered as a sacrifice for other than Allah.

**Life at stake.**

In cases of extreme necessity where a man’s life may be at stake, he may eat food otherwise forbidden, for instance when suffering extreme hunger and when no other food is available, or in illness, or other such circumstances as may compel him to do so. However, it is essential that such forbidden food should not be taken simply for the pleasure of the palate. If something is held unlawful by God, it is not owing to the sacredness of that thing but rather because it is something impure or the divine law has testified to its uncleanness, e.g. carrion, blood, swine or an animal sacrificed in the name of some idol instead of in the name of God. Here, the eating of things forbidden even under a situation of compulsion (idtirar ‌) has not been made lawful as such by the noble Qur'an, instead, the expression used is (there is no sin on him) which means that these things continue to be haram as they are, but the sin of using what is haram has been forgiven because the eater has done so under the compulsion of necessity.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The word ‌ (innama harrama) is a restrictive particle, therefore, the sense of the verse is that Allah Almighty has forbidden only those things which have been mentioned later, other than which, nothing else is forbidden. A special status is however accorded fish and locusts; blood poured forth as in sūrat al-An‘ām see Q. 6145 the flesh of swine the meat is singled out for mention because that part is what people mostly seek every other part being implied thereby; what has been hallowed to other than God that is to say what has been slaughtered in other than His Name al-ihlāl is the raising of one’s voice which they used to do when sacrificing for their gods. So, in this verse, it is the word, innama which points out to the given sense, while in another verse (6:145): ‌ the same thing has been stated more clearly. Here, the Holy Prophet has been asked to proclaim that, in what has been revealed to him, there is nothing haram except the few things mentioned later on. The aggressor and the transgressor are excluded from this dispensation and to these two categories one should also add every person that sets out on a journey in disobedience such as the fugitive or the excise collector for whom it would be unlawful to eat any of the mentioned unless they repent of their disobedience; this is the opinion of al-Shāfi‘ī. At this stage, we have a problem on our hands. The fact is that the unlawfulness of many things stands proved on the authority of other verses from the Qur'an, and also from ahadith. If so, what would be the meaning of this 'restriction' and how are we to explain the negation of 'there is nothing haram except the few things mentioned later on'?

174.text:
"Indeed, those who hide Allah's revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain consume nothing but fire into their bellies." opens with the group who conceal the revelations of Allah, and the offence is set in the trade of the revelations for a fleeting gain. The word fleeting marks the gain as small and passing, so the bargain is a poor one. The sentence then gives the consequence, which is that they consume nothing but fire into their bellies. The fire is what they take in, and the verse uses the image of eating to show what the gain has become. "Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment, nor will He purify them." The two negatives close off the speech and the purifying, which are the two things the Lord gives to the faithful on that day. "And they will suffer a painful punishment" closes the verse with the sentence of pain. The Mukhtaṣar states that those who hide what Allah has revealed in the scriptures, and who exchange it for worldly goods, will not be spoken to on the Day of Judgement. The Tanwīr reads the painful doom as a torment that will not end. The Maʿārif commentary takes the verse as a warning to the scholars who would go to the limit of distorting the verses for the sake of wealth. The Tazkirul commentary describes the people who hide the truth for worldly considerations, and it places their propensity to divide ahead of their loss. The reader is asked to see the verse as the price of trading the truth for a little gain.

**Hiding the revelations.**

Those who conceal what God has revealed of the Scripture comprising all the descriptions of Muhammad meaning the Jews and sell it for a little price in this world taking this little price in its place from the debased ones among them for fear of losing out if they were to manifest it sc. the truth of Muhammad — they shall consume nothing in their bellies but the Fire because that is their journey’s end; God shall not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection out of anger with them neither purify them from the filth of sin; and theirs is a painful chastisement that is the Fire. Those who hide what Allah revealed in the scriptures and the signs of the truth and prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ – as the Jews and Christians did, getting something small in return for what they hide, such as leadership, status or money – they only fill their stomachs with that which will cause them to suffer in the fire of Hell. Those who conceal what God has revealed of the scripture and sell it for a little price-they shall consume nothing in their bellies but the fire; God shall not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection neither purify them; and theirs is a painful chastisement. (Lo! Those who hide anything of the Scripture which Allah hath revealed) what Allah has exposited in the Torah regarding the description and traits of Muhammad, (and purchase) by concealing this (a small gain therewith) a small profit, this was revealed about Ka'b Ibn al-Ashraf, Huyayy Ibn Akhtab and Judayy Ibn Akhtab (they eat into their bellies) they put into their bellies (nothing else than fire) except the unlawful; and it is also said that this means: they eat nothing except that which will turn into fire in their bellies on the Day of Judgement.

**Consume nothing but fire.**

This is because Allah is furious with them for concealing the truth. Some perceptive Ulama' have said that unlawful wealth is, in reality, the very fire of Hell, even though we do not sense it as such during our lifetime in the mortal world, but once one dies, his or her deeds will appear in the form of fire. Hence, they opposed the guidance, that is, not announcing the Prophet's description they find in their Books, the news about his prophecy and the good news of his coming which the previous Prophets proclaimed, as well as following and believing in him. They may revel in such compromises as bring them wealth and honour, but in the eyes of God, they are the worst offenders.

**Not spoken to and not purified.**

Then on the Day of Judgement, Allah will not speak to them with words that make them joyful; but they will only hear that which makes them sad: they will not be praised, and they will have a painful punishment. (And Allah will not speak to them) nicely (on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He make them pure) He will not absolve them of their transgressions; it is also said that this means: (That is because Allah has sent down the Book (the Qur'an) in truth.) means, they deserve this painful torment because Allah has revealed Books to His Messenger Muhammad , and the Prophets before him, and these revelations bring about truth and expose falsehood. When comes the Qiyamah (Doomsday), Allah Almighty will not speak to them affectionately, nor will He purify them by forgiving their sins.

**Painful doom.**

(Theirs will be a painful doom) a painful torment that will extend to their hearts. They would go to the limit of distorting the verses of the Torah to suit the desire of their client. In this, there is a veiled warning given to the ulama', the religious scholars of the community of the Last of the prophets, that they should keep away from such practices and never fall short in disclosing the true injunctions of Allah for any material reason or vested interest of their own. They, thus, mocked the Ayat that Allah revealed to His Messengers, and this is why they deserved the torment and the punishment.

**Worldly considerations.**

When superstitious beliefs about prohibitions have been accepted by the masses as religious beliefs and held sacred, the religious scholars of the community fail to muster enough courage to declare openly that those beliefs have nothing to do with true religion, for they are afraid that if they did so, they would be severing themselves from the general public to whom they owe their popularity. Hiding the truth for worldly considerations is not one of those offences that God will ignore in the Hereafter. They develop a propensity to divisiveness and ultimately they stray so far from the truth that there remains no chance of their returning. If [the scholars] conceal the proofs of the different types of knowledge they will be bridled with a bridle of fire nār.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Mentioned in the earlier verses were unlawful things which are tangible. Now, the verses that follow take up the intangible deeds that have been made unlawful. For instance, religious scholars among the Jews were addicted to giving out false verdicts in favour of people who bribed them. There is no doubt that people who conceal the contents of the Book of Allah and in return for this breach of trust, collect insignificant worldly gains are simply eating fire. Their punishment will be terrible for they are the kind of people who, during their mortal life, chose to abandon guidance and adopt error, and in the Hereafter, they missed forgiveness and became deserving of punishment. They must be very courageous in that they are all set to go into Hell. All these punishments to them are because they elected to stray away from the Book of Allah, something so clear and true. It is evident that they must be victims of serious intransigence and are far out in schism, as a result of which they can expect to deserve a matching punishment.

175.text:
"They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment." opens with the people who make the trade, and the sentence repeats the trade in its two halves. Guidance is given up for misguidance, and forgiveness is given up for punishment. The two exchanges mirror one another, so that the reader sees the same bargain made twice. "How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire" closes the verse with an exclamation that marks their persistence. The word persistent names the steadiness with which they go toward the Fire, and the question form makes the reader wonder at how firm they are in their course. The Jalālayn gives the statement as one intended to provoke amazement, and it reads the phrase bought error at the price of guidance as the sense of the trade. The Mukhtaṣar states that those who hide knowledge exchange guidance for misguidance, and it reads their determination as the way that will lead them to the Fire. The Tanwīr reads the strife as their eagerness for the Fire. The Maʿārif commentary states that their punishment will be terrible, and it takes the kind of people described as victims of serious error. The Tazkirul commentary describes a people who prefer the compromises that bring wealth. The reader is asked to see the verse as the close of the account of the concealers, in which the trade is named and its end is shown.

**Trade guidance for misguidance.**

Those are they that have bought error at the price of guidance taking the former in place of the latter in this world and chastisement at the price of pardon the pardon that would have been prepared for them in the Hereafter had they not concealed this matter; what makes them so patient for the Fire? that is how great is the extent of their patience? Those who hide knowledge exchange guidance for misguidance, as they hid the truth, and exchange the forgiveness of Allah for His punishment. They are those who have bought error at the price of guidance and chastisement at the price of pardon; what makes them so patient for the fireḍ That is because God has revealed the Book with the truth; and those that are at variance regarding the Book are in schism far removed. (Those are they who purchase error at the price of guidance) they purchased disbelief for the price of faith, (and torment at the price of pardon) Judaism for the price of Islam; it is also said that this means: they chose that which leads to the Fire instead of that which leads to Paradise.

**Forgiveness for punishment.**

Verily, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book, and purchase a small gain therewith (of worldly things), they eat into their bellies nothing but fire. Their punishment will be terrible for they are the kind of people who, during their mortal life, chose to abandon guidance and adopt error, and in the Hereafter, they missed forgiveness and became deserving of punishment. It is evident that they must be victims of serious intransigence and are far out in schism, as a result of which they can expect to deserve a matching punishment. It is also said that this means: what made them so bold as to enter the Fire?

**How persistent in pursuit of the Fire.**

This statement is intended to provoke amazement in the believers at the way in which they the disbelievers commit sins that necessitate their punishment in the Fire with complete indifference. How determined they are to do things that will lead them into the fire of Hell, as if they do not realize what suffering it contains! (How constant are they in their strife to reach the Fire) how bold are they to delve into the Fire? And it is also said: how they indulging indeed in the works of the people of the Fire.

**Amazement and the cause for it.**

In reality they would have no patience whatever to endure the Fire. Truly those that prefer the other ghayr over the unseen ghayb the cre ation khalq over the Real ḥaqq the lower self nafs over intimacy uns [with God] how hard are their hearts ma aqsā qulūbahum how shameless what they love and seek wa-mā awqaḥa maḥbūbahum wa-maṬlūbahum how cheap their worth and how disgraceful for those who have eyes to see! (...they eat into their bellies nothing but fire,) meaning, whatever they eat in return for hiding the truth, will turn into a raging fire in their stomachs on the Day of Resurrection. Some perceptive Ulama' have said that unlawful wealth is, in reality, the very fire of Hell, even though we do not sense it as such during our lifetime in the mortal world, but once one dies, his or her deeds will appear in the form of fire.

**Compromises for wealth.**

When superstitious beliefs about prohibitions have been accepted by the masses as religious beliefs and held sacred, the religious scholars of the community fail to muster enough courage to declare openly that those beliefs have nothing to do with true religion, for they are afraid that if they did so, they would be severing themselves from the general public to whom they owe their popularity. They may revel in such compromises as bring them wealth and honour, but in the eyes of God, they are the worst offenders. They develop a propensity to divisiveness and ultimately they stray so far from the truth that there remains no chance of their returning. Hence, they opposed the guidance, that is, not announcing the Prophet's description they find in their Books, the news about his prophecy and the good news of his coming which the previous Prophets proclaimed, as well as following and believing in him.

176.text:
"That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth." opens with the reason for the punishment of the verse before, and the reason is that the Book was revealed in truth. The word truth is the ground on which the punishment rests, since the concealment is set against a Book that is true. The sentence is short, and it places the cause of the trade in the nature of the revelation. "And surely those who differ regarding it are totally engrossed in opposition." The verse turns to those who disagree about the Book, and it describes them as wholly taken up with opposition. The word totally marks the extent of their engrossment, and the opposition is named as the thing that fills them. The Mukhtaṣar states that the punishment is what they receive for hiding knowledge and for disagreeing with the sacred scripture. The Tanwīr reads the torment as the punishment for the Book that was revealed in truth. The Maʿārif commentary states that the people who conceal the contents of the Book are punished in this way because they chose to do so. The Qushayrī commentary connects the Book revealed in truth to the Book in its own right. The Tazkirul commentary states that worse still are those who, instead of accepting the truth, set themselves against it. The reader is asked to see the verse as the second half of the account, in which the cause of the punishment is the truth itself.

**The Book revealed in truth.**

(That is) the torment (because Allah hath revealed the Scripture) He sent down Gabriel with the Qur'an and the Torah (with the Truth) with an exposition of the Truth and falsehood, but they disbelieved. (That is because Allah has sent down the Book (the Qur'an) in truth.) means, they deserve this painful torment because Allah has revealed Books to His Messenger Muhammad , and the Prophets before him, and these revelations bring about truth and expose falsehood. That is because God has revealed the Book in truth and made its decree and rule come to pass in sincerity and brought them to that for which He prepared them and established them on the way He has fashioned for them. Now, the verses that follow take up the intangible deeds that have been made unlawful.

**Totally engrossed in opposition.**

(Lo! Those who find disagreement in the Scripture) those who contravene that which is in the Book regarding the description and traits of Muhammad ﷺ and further conceal the latter (are in open schism) are too much in disagreement with guidance. Also, those who disagree with the sacred scripture, believing some of it and hiding some of it, have taken a position that is far from the truth. Truly those that prefer the other ghayr over the unseen ghayb the cre ation khalq over the Real ḥaqq the lower self nafs over intimacy uns [with God] how hard are their hearts ma aqsā qulūbahum how shameless what they love and seek wa-mā awqaḥa maḥbūbahum wa-maṬlūbahum how cheap their worth and how disgraceful for those who have eyes to see! They, thus, mocked the Ayat that Allah revealed to His Messengers, and this is why they deserved the torment and the punishment.

**The punishment they receive.**

That punishment is what they get for hiding knowledge and guidance, because Allah revealed the sacred scriptures in truth, which must be made clear and not hidden. This is because Allah is furious with them for concealing the truth. All these punishments to them are because they elected to stray away from the Book of Allah, something so clear and true. There is no doubt that people who conceal the contents of the Book of Allah and in return for this breach of trust, collect insignificant worldly gains are simply eating fire.

**Hiding and disagreeing.**

Verily, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book, and purchase a small gain therewith (of worldly things), they eat into their bellies nothing but fire. Verse 175 tells us that a person who changes the injunction of Shari'ah in his greed for worldly gains, he should know that these worldly gains he consumes are like embers of fire he is storing in his stomach because that is the ultimate end of his deeds. Worse still are those, who, instead of accepting the truth when it is presented to them start engaging in meaningless discussions. Hiding the truth for worldly considerations is not one of those offences that God will ignore in the Hereafter.

**The propensity to divide.**

When superstitious beliefs about prohibitions have been accepted by the masses as religious beliefs and held sacred, the religious scholars of the community fail to muster enough courage to declare openly that those beliefs have nothing to do with true religion, for they are afraid that if they did so, they would be severing themselves from the general public to whom they owe their popularity. They develop a propensity to divisiveness and ultimately they stray so far from the truth that there remains no chance of their returning. They are those who have bought error at the price of guidance and chastisement at the price of pardon; what makes them so patient for the fireḍ That is because God has revealed the Book with the truth; and those that are at variance regarding the Book are in schism far removed. There is no doubt that people who conceal the contents of the Book of Allah and in return for this breach of trust, collect insignificant worldly gains are simply eating fire.

177.text:
"Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west, Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets; who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, needy travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives; who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make; and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in the heat of battle." opens with the statement that the true meaning of righteousness is not found in the direction of prayer. The verse turns from the question of the qiblah to the substance of the faith, and it gives the answer in the form of a negation. The east and the west are named as the directions that people quarrel over, and the sentence sets them aside. "Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets." The word rather turns the sentence to the positive account, and the list of beliefs names the core of the faith in order. The verse keeps the direction and the belief together, so that the direction is in service of the faith and not the faith in service of the direction. The Mukhtaṣar states that doing good that pleases Allah does not just mean turning the face, and that it is having faith in Allah as the only God. The Jalālayn gives the sense that it is not piety to turn the faces in prayer to the east or the west, and it gives the occasion as the claim made by the Jews. The Tanwīr reads the verse as the whole of righteousness, and it names those who keep their treaty and those who are sincere. The Maʿārif commentary takes the verse as the subject that continues to the end of the surah, and it treats the sabirīn as among the righteous. The Tazkirul commentary states that the pleasure of the Almighty can be earned only by the faith that pervades the whole person. The reader is asked to see the verse as a definition of righteousness that begins with the faith and moves through the deeds that the faith produces. The verse closes with "It is they who are true in faith, and it is they who are mindful of Allah," so the righteous are named by their faith and by their fear of the Lord.

**Not the east or the west.**

This was revealed in response to the claim made by the Jews and the Christians to this effect. Doing good that pleases Allah does not just mean turning towards the east or the west or disputing about that.

**Rather, the righteous.**

Rather, piety is he who has faith in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets; who gives wealth despite lov ing it to kinsfolk, orphans, the indigent, the son of the road, beggars, and slaves; and who per forms the prayer and gives the alms tax; those who are loyal to their covenant when they make a covenant; those who are patient in misfortune, hardship, and moments of peril. Rather, it is having faith in Allah as the only God, the Day of Judgement, all of the angels, all of the revealed scriptures and all of the prophets, without distinguishing between them; charitable spending, despite loving and valuing wealth, to relatives, orphans, the poor, the stranger who is cut off from his family and homeland because of a journey, and whoever has a need that makes it necessary for them to ask people for help; giving money to free slaves from captivity; establishing the prayer as Allah instructed; giving Zakat; being true to promises; and patience in poverty, hardship, illness and in times of conflict without fleeing. This subject which continues through the end of the Sarah has been unfolded by presenting and explaining the cardinal concept of birr ‌, an umbrella word in Arabic used for what is good in the absolute sense and which combines in itself all acts of righteousness and obedience, inward or outward.

**Faith in Allah and the Last Day.**

In short, the Almighty’s pleasure can be earned only by displaying true faithfulness and not just by turning our faces in one or the other direction. Believing in God is to trust in God in the full sense of the word. Believing in the angels means believing in God’s emissaries who are running this world at the divine command. The faith in all these matters must so deeply pervade the believer’s psyche that he helps the needy and others in distress by spending his wealth, says his prayers by surrendering himself totally to God, and pays the poor due—his only motivation being to earn God’s pleasure.

**Charity and the keeping of the prayer.**

(The Miskin is not the person who roams around, and whose need is met by one or two dates or one or two bites. Rather, the Miskin is he who does not have what is sufficient, and to whom the people do not pay attention and, thus, do not give him from the charity.) (performs As-Salah (Iqamat-As-Salah) means those who pray on time and give the prayer its due right; the bowing, prostration, and the necessary attention and humbleness required by Allah. For instance, spending on your kin, when they have a valid excuse of not being able to earn their own living, is necessary; or there may be some needy person dying in poverty while you have already paid your Zakah , then, it becomes obligatory for you to save his life by spending your wealth on the spot. This is because they have achieved faith in the heart and realized it in deed and upon the tongue.

**Those who keep their treaty.**

(And those who keep their treaty) those who fulfil the pledges that are between them and their Lord or between them and other people (when they make one, and the patient in tribulation) i.e. fear, affliction and hardship (and adversity) illness, pain and hunger (and time of stress) upon engagement in fighting. (Such are they who are sincere) who have fulfilled their pledges. (It is not righteousness) it is not all of righteousness; it is also said that (It is not righteousness) means: it is not faith (that ye merely turn your faces) in prayer (to the East) towards Makkah (and the West) towards Bayt al-Maqdis; (but righteous is) but faith amounts to agreeing with (he who believeth in Allah) and it is also said: the faithful is he who believes in Allah (and the Last Day) in resurrection after death (and the angels) all the angels (and the Scripture) all the revealed Books (and the prophets) and all the prophets; Allah then mentions the obligated duties after mentioning faith, saying:

**What else the same passage holds.**

It is not piety that you turn your faces in prayer to the East and to the West. From the beginning to this point, the Sarah al-Baqarah is reaching its half-way mark. Until now, the message was addressed mostly to its deniers since the truth of the Holy Qur'an was the first thing to be established. In that context, mention was made of those who accepted it and those who rejected it, which was followed by providing proof of Allah's Oneness and the Prophethood. Then, recounted were Allah's blessings and favours on the progeny of Ibrahim right through the verse ‌ ‌ (2:124). Thenceforth started the issue of the Qiblah which continued until it was resolved when the status of Safa and Marwah was identified as a sign from Allah (Verse 158). Then, the affirmation of Allah's Oneness was rightfully followed by a refutation of the principles and subsidiaries of Shirk the act of associating others with Allah. The approach this far is full of warning mostly given to the deniers of the message of the Qur'an; any reference to Muslims was only as a corollary. The verses that follow contain nearly the other half of Sarah al-Baqarah where the primary purpose is to educate Muslims in the principles and the subsidiaries of their religion and any address to non-Muslims is by implication only. So, when the verse begins, basic principles such as belief in the Book, spending of wealth in charity, fulfillment of promises and patience in distress have been stressed upon which, incidentally, include the basic principles behind all injunctions of the Holy Qur'an. The fact is that the articles of belief, the deeds in accordance with them and the morals are the essence of all religious injunctions while all details fall under these basics.

178.text:
"O believers! The law of retaliation is set for you in cases of murder." opens with the address to the believers, and it gives the first rule of the passage, which concerns the killing of a person. The retaliation is set as a law, so the rule is fixed and it is given to the community. "A free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female." The rule names the equal parts of the case, free for free, slave for slave, and female for female, so the penalty follows the status of the victim. "But if the offender is pardoned by the victim's guardian, then blood money" begins the turn to pardon. "Then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously." The verse gives the option that the victim's family may take the blood money, and it sets the pardon beside the law. The verse is one of the first statements of the law in the passage, and it is placed beside the account of concealment. The Mukhtaṣar states that if the person killed had forgiven before his death, or his heirs had done so, the blood money may be paid. The Tanwīr reads the verse as revealed about two Arab clans, and it treats the pardon as an alleviation and an appeasement. The Maʿārif commentary takes the mention of the free and the slave and the female as the matter of the first injunction, and it describes the situation in which the aggrieved party relents on its own. The Tazkirul commentary describes retribution as the forfeiture of the killer's own life, and it names the blood money as a settlement that has special advantages. The reader is asked to see the verse as a law that gives the victim's family both justice and the choice of mercy. The lead keeps the phrase "then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously" in view, and it treats the payment as something to be made with courtesy and not with grudging. "This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord" follows, so the settlement is a gift of mercy from the Lord. "But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment" closes the rule, so that the one who breaks the settlement after it is made faces the painful punishment.

**The law of retaliation.**

O you who believe prescribed made obligatory for you is retaliation on equal terms regarding the slain both in the attributes of the one slain and in the action involved; a free man is killed for a free man and not for a slave; and a slave for a slave and a female for a female. (O ye who believe! Retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the murdered ones; the freeman for the freeman) a freeman who premeditatedly kills another freeman, (and the slave for the slave) a slave who premeditatedly kills another, (and the female for the female) a female who premeditatedly kills another. O you who have faith in Allah and follow His Messenger, it is decreed for you that in cases where someone deliberately attacks and kills someone, the punishment for the murderer should be the same as their crime: the freeman killed for the freeman; the slave for the slave; and the female for the female. If you want to step into the street of friendship, first detach your heart from life and toss away everything you know about states and deeds, for in the shariah of friendship your life will be taken as retaliation, and everything you know will be the wergild, though more is needed.

**Free for free, slave for slave.**

The mention of 'free man for a free man' and 'female for a female' in this verse refers to a specific event in the background of which it was revealed. Hence, (they made it a law that) when a person from Nadir kills a person from Quraizah, he is not killed in retaliation, but only pays a hundred Wasq of dates. This verse was revealed regarding two Arab clans but is abrogated by the verse: Under the first injunction in this connection, the verse prescribes the law of Qisas (even retaliation), that is, the killer will be killed, irrespective of the status of the parties involved.

**Pardoned by the guardian.**

(But if the killer is forgiven by the brother (or the relatives) of the killed (against blood money) means the killer is pardoned by his brother (i.e., the relative of the victim) and accepting the Diyah after capital punishment becomes due (against the killer), this is the 'Afw (pardon mentioned in the Ayah). (And for him who is forgiven somewhat by his brother) whoever forgives the killing and takes instead blood money, (prosecution according to usage) Allah commands the person who asks for blood money to claim this money according to practised usage: three years if it is a full blood money, two years if it is half of the blood money, or one year if it is a third (and payment unto him) the person who is required to pay blood money is commanded to give the custodians of the murdered person what is due to them (in kindness) without the need to go to court or making it difficult for them. If the person killed had forgiven before his death, or his guardian has forgiven in return for the payment of blood money (a sum of money paid by the murderer in return for being pardoned), then the person who forgives should ask for the sum of money fairly, and not follow that up with insult or injury, and the murderer should pay the sum of money in a good way, without hesitation or delay. If the aggrieved party somewhat relents on its own and forgives the Qisas but does not forgive the offence totally, it will become necessary for the killer to pay diyah or blood-money as fixed, in a fair manner, and promptly.

**The alleviation of pardon.**

(This) this pardon (is an alleviation) appeasement (and a mercy from your Lord) towards the killer such that he is not killed. Hence, 'pardoning' or 'forgiving' means accepting blood money in intentional murder cases. In allowing this forgiveness and the payment of the blood money your Lord makes things easier for you, and this is a mercy for the Muslim nation.

**Retribution and blood money.**

Retribution for a killer means the forfeiture of his own life. In this way, on the one hand, a capital crime like the taking of life is effectively discouraged, for the fear of losing one’s own life deters one from taking another’s life and, as a result, the life of all the members of a society become protected. The heirs of the deceased person may, of course, opt for the execution of the killer, but they may also, if they so wish, accept blood-money instead, or even forgive him. Then the principle of blood-money has the special advantage of giving the bereaved family monetary compensation for the death of one of its members.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The Sunna makes it clear that a male may be killed in retaliation for a female and that religious affiliation should be taken into account also so that a Muslim cannot be killed in return for an disbeliever even if the former be a slave and the latter a free man. But if anything of the blood is pardoned any one of those who have slain in relation to his brother the one slain so that the retaliation is waived the use of the indefinite shay’un ‘anything’ here implies the waiving of retaliation through a partial pardon by the inheritors of the slain; the mention of akhīh ‘his brother’ is intended as a conciliatory entreaty to pardon and a declaration that killing should not sever the bonds of religious brotherhood; the particle man ‘any one’ is the subject of a conditional or a relative clause of which the predicate is the following fa’ittibā‘un let the pursuing that is the action of the one who has pardoned in pursuing the killer be honourable demanding the blood money without force. The fact that the ‘pursuing’ results from the ‘pardoning’ implies that one of the two actions is a duty which is one of al-Shāfi‘ī’s two opinions here.

179.text:
"There is security of life for you in the law of retaliation, O people of reason." opens with the statement that the law gives security, and the word life is the one that the verse places at the center. The retaliation is named as the source of life for the community, which turns the harsh law into a guarantee against further killing. The address to the people of reason shows that the verse is directed to those who can see the purpose of the law. "So that you may become mindful of Allah" completes the sentence with the goal. The purpose of the law is not only the protection of life but the piety that follows from it, so the law is tied to the fear of Allah. The verse closes the passage of retaliation, and it moves from the legal rule to the reason for it. The Jalālayn gives the sense that in retaliation there is a great life for the community. The Mukhtaṣar states that those with sense understand the law of equivalent punishment, which is decreed by Allah, and it reads the phrase as the mark of those who are mindful of Allah. The Tanwīr reads the life as a continuation, and it places it within the law that Allah has set. The Qushayrī commentary reads the life as the continued existence of the one who kills and the one who is killed, and it treats the allusive sense as a deeper life. The Tazkirul commentary states that Islam has laid down the principle of retaliation in like for like, and that qisas opens the way to a settlement. The reader is asked to see the verse as the reason that the law of retaliation is a mercy to the community.

**Security of life.**

In retaliation there is life for you that is great longevity O people of pith possessors of intellect because if the would-be killer knew that he would be killed in retaliation he would refrain from such action and would have thereby given life to himself and to the one whom he had intended to kill; and so it retaliation was stipulated by the Law so that you might fear killing fearing retaliation. (And there is a life for you in retaliation) a continuation of existence and a lesson, (O men of understanding) those who possess sound minds among people, (that ye may ward off (evil) that you may ward off killing one another for fear of retaliation. In the law of equivalent punishment decreed by Allah there is life for you, because it spares your blood, stopping further attacks between you.

**O people of reason.**

Those with sense understand this: who are mindful of Allah, keeping to His sacred law and doing as He instructs. In carrying out the retaliation there is life because when one knows that if he kills he will himself be killed he refrains from killing. In the end, the verse points out that wise people should have no difficulty in seeing that the law of even retaliation does not take life, instead, it gives life, for such a deterrent law will make people fear the punishment of killing somebody and thus lives will be saved. (So after this whoever transgresses the limits, he shall have a painful torment.) means, those who kill in retaliation after taking the Diyah or accepting it, they will suffer a painful and severe torment from Allah.

**So that you may be mindful.**

In this there is life for the one who kills and the one who is killed. (And there is a life for you in retaliation) a continuation of existence and a lesson, (O men of understanding) those who possess sound minds among people, (that ye may ward off (evil) that you may ward off killing one another for fear of retaliation. Under the first injunction in this connection, the verse prescribes the law of Qisas (even retaliation), that is, the killer will be killed, irrespective of the status of the parties involved. The reason behind this statement is that (the Jewish tribe of) Banu An-Nadir invaded Qurayzah (another Jewish tribe) during the time of Jahiliyyah (before Islam) and defeated them.

**Retaliation and the settlement.**

Islam has laid down the principle of retaliation in like measure (qisas). However, qisas in Islam permits a settlement to be arrived at between the killer and the killed. Retribution for a killer means the forfeiture of his own life. In this way, on the one hand, a capital crime like the taking of life is effectively discouraged, for the fear of losing one’s own life deters one from taking another’s life and, as a result, the life of all the members of a society become protected.

**The reason behind the law.**

Hence, (they made it a law that) when a person from Nadir kills a person from Quraizah, he is not killed in retaliation, but only pays a hundred Wasq of dates. Hence, how many a man who thought about killing, but this Law prevented him from killing for fear that he will be killed in turn. In case the pardon is not that full, for instance, as illustrated above, one of the two surviving sons does pardon the killer while the other does not, the result will be that the killer will stand released right there from the retaliatory punishment, but the one who has not pardoned the killer will be entitled to half of the blood-money (diyah). But according to the allusive explanation there is greater life in aban doning retaliation because when one has been annihilated in Him He is the successor for him and his life from Him is more perfect for him than his remaining with himself.

180.text:
"It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you, if they leave something of value, a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness." opens with the statement that a will is prescribed when death approaches. The obligation is placed on the one who is near death, and it names the wealth he leaves as the reason for the will. The will is to be made in favour of parents and the immediate family, and it is to be made with fairness. "This is an obligation on those who are mindful of Allah." The obligation is given to those who fear the Lord, so the duty is tied to piety. The verse keeps the will in the hand of the one who is dying, and it places the decision in the context of the fairness owed to the family. The Mukhtaṣar states that it has been decreed that the one about to die should make a will, and it treats the making of the will as a firm duty on those who are mindful of Allah. The Tanwīr reads the will as a duty for all who ward off evil. The Maʿārif commentary takes the hadith that Allah has given each of the heirs his share as the principle that limits the will, and it treats the will as a matter of the wealth and its fair division. The Tazkirul commentary states that one who fears God should follow this injunction regarding the family. The Qushayrī commentary, reading the recognizers, treats the presence of death as an occasion for awe. The reader is asked to see the verse as the first rule of the will, which sets fairness to the family as the duty of the one who is dying.

**It is prescribed when death approaches.**

(It is prescribed for you, when death approacheth one of you, if he leave wealth, that he bequeath unto parents and near relatives) kinsfolk (in kindness) more so and even better to the parents. It has been decreed for you that if one of you is about to die, and they are leaving a large amount of wealth behind, then they should make a will for their parents and close relatives, according to the sacred laws, not exceeding one third of the wealth (the rest of the wealth being distributed according to the laws of inheritance). It is written for you, when death is present for one of you and he is leaving behind some good, to make a will for parents and kinsfolk honorably, as something rightfully due from the godwary. After someone’s death the problem arises as to how to deal with his or her wealth.

**Parents and immediate family with fairness.**

This Ayah contains the command to include parents and relatives in the will, which was obligatory, according to the most correct view, before the Ayah about inheritance was revealed. Where there is a member of a family, like an orphaned grandson, or any other needy member of the family who does not inherit under the Islamic inheritance scheme, the testator may provide for him, as he has been given the power to dispose of up to one third of his property by making a will in his favour. When the verses about inheritance were revealed it was made clear who should inherit from the person who has died and how much they should inherit. It should, however, be borne in mind that according to the consensus of the Muslim Ummah it is not obligatory on the dying person to necessarily make a will in favour of relatives who have no fixed shares in the inheritance.

**An obligation on the mindful.**

(A duty for all those who ward off (evil) those who ascribe no partners to Allah; but this verse is abrogated by that on inheritance. One who fears God should follow this injunction regarding the disposal of intestate property in the spirit of justice. When the recognizers are afraid, this is called "awe," and when the disobedient are afraid, it is called "fear.

**The will and the law of inheritance.**

This ruling was revealed before the verses about inheritance. The essence of the hadith is that Allah Almighty has Himself fixed the shares of the inheritors, therefore, the executor need not make a will anymore, in fact, he does not even have the permission to make a will in favour of an heir; however, should other inheritors allow the enforcement of such a will, it will then be permissible. Imam Al-Jassas says that this hadith has been reported from a group of the blessed Companions and the jurists of the Muslim community have accepted it unanimously, therefore, this is an uninterruptedly ensured hadith which makes the abrogation of the verse of the Qur'an permissible. Although the hadith which invalidates a will in favour of an heir is a solitary report, (Al-Khabar al-Wahid), however, the fact that this hadith comes from the sermon of the last Hajj of the Holy Prophet g when he openly proclaimed this before the largest ever gathering of the blessed Companions, and then their consensus and the consensus of the Muslim community make it clear that this hadith is, according to them, absolutely proven, otherwise in the presence of the slightest doubt, they would have never abandoned the verse of the Qur'an and agreed to this abrogating command through the hadith.

**Death present and the turning to the Lord.**

When he put his head on the pil low of death, they said to him, "O Shaykh, you were the kiblah of those burned, emulated by the yearners, the sun of the world. Now that you have turned your face to the Exalted Presence, give some advice to these burnt ones, say some words that will be their reminder. This act would not constitute an alteration in the will and this is why Allah mentioned it specifically, so that it is excluded from the prohibition (that prohibits altering the will and testament) mentioned in the previous Ayah. But unless this is the objective, the changing of the provisions of a will is unlawful.

**What else the same passage holds.**

Literally, al-wasiyyah means an order to do something, either in the lifetime of the maker of wasiyyah or after his death. But, in commonly accepted usage, it refers to what must be done after death. Out of the many meanings the word khayr has in Arabic, 'wealth' happens to be one of them, for instance, in the verse ‌ (Surely he is passionate in his love for good things) where, according to the unanimous agreement of commentators, 'khayr' means 'wealth'. In early Islam, when shares in inheritance: were not fixed by the Shari'ah, the rule was that a dying person could make a will within the one third of inheritance, leaving behind in the name of his parents and relatives in whatever proportion he chose. This much was their right; the rest went to children.

181.text:
"But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those who made the change, Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing." opens with the warning against changing a will once it has been heard. The word changes names the act, and the phrase after hearing it places the sin on those who knew the terms and altered them. The blame is placed on the changers, so the innocent are not made answerable for the change. The verse closes with the Lord who hears what is spoken and knows what is done. The sentence gives the reason the change will be known and weighed, since the Lord hears the will as it was spoken and knows the alteration. The Mukhtaṣar states that whoever changes the will, adding to it or taking away from it, is to be blamed, and that Allah hears all that His creation say. The Tanwīr reads the changing as the act of altering the will of the deceased after hearing it. The Maʿārif commentary takes the hadith that invalidates a will in favour of an heir as one of the matters discussed in the context of this verse. The Qushayrī commentary reads the distorting of an utterance as the evil and harm of that act, and it reads the punishment as denial of the scent of the garden. The Tazkirul commentary states that this will create a brotherly atmosphere in society, and that the changing of the will defeats the purpose of the law. The reader is asked to see the verse as the warning that closes the rule on the will.

**Whoever changes the will.**

Then if anyone whether a witness or a trustee changes it that is the testament after hearing it and knowing it the sin resulting from the changed testament shall rest upon those who change it here the explicit subject stands in place of the implicit one; surely God is Hearing of the testator’s words Knowing of the deeds of the trustee requiting each accordingly. (And whoso changeth) the will of the deceased person (after he hath heard it-the sin thereof) the onus thereof (is only upon those who change it) and the deceased bears no responsibility. Whoever then changes the will, adding to it or taking away from it or stopping something when they know what the will contains, the sin of it will be upon those who changed it, and the person who wrote the will is not held responsible for what they did. Then if anyone changes it after hearing it the sin shall rest upon those who change it; surely God is Hearing Knowing.

**After hearing it.**

(Then whoever changes it after hearing it, the sin shall be on those who make the change. Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower.) means, whoever changed the will and testament or altered it by addition or deletion, including hiding the will as is obvious, then. Whoever distorts an utterance the evil and harm of that becomes his. Thus, out of fear of sin, people used to execute the will of a deceased person as it was even when the latter transgressed in that will,. This act would not constitute an alteration in the will and this is why Allah mentioned it specifically, so that it is excluded from the prohibition (that prohibits altering the will and testament) mentioned in the previous Ayah.

**The blame on the changers.**

His punishment is that he is denied the smell of the fragrance of sincerity. Whoever aids the religion dīn God aids him and whoever provides aid against the religion God forsakes him. (For Allah is Hearer) of the will and words of the deceased, (Knower) if he transgresses or changes it; it is also said that this means: Allah hears all that His creation say, and knows all that they do; and He knows every detail of the situations they are in.

**Allah hears and knows.**

(Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower.) means, Allah knows what the dead person has bequeathed and what the beneficiaries (or others) have changed in the will. This Ayah contains the command to include parents and relatives in the will, which was obligatory, according to the most correct view, before the Ayah about inheritance was revealed. Imam Al-Qurtubi has said that the scholars of the Muslim community unanimously agree that an injunction which comes to us through the Holy Prophet and we know about it with full certitude, as is the case with mutawatir and mashhur reports, it will be at par with the injunction of the Holy Qur'an and will have to be taken as the command of Allah Almighty. Although the hadith which invalidates a will in favour of an heir is a solitary report, (Al-Khabar al-Wahid), however, the fact that this hadith comes from the sermon of the last Hajj of the Holy Prophet g when he openly proclaimed this before the largest ever gathering of the blessed Companions, and then their consensus and the consensus of the Muslim community make it clear that this hadith is, according to them, absolutely proven, otherwise in the presence of the slightest doubt, they would have never abandoned the verse of the Qur'an and agreed to this abrogating command through the hadith.

**A brotherly atmosphere.**

After someone’s death the problem arises as to how to deal with his or her wealth. This will create a brotherly atmosphere in society, preventing litigation and quarrels over property. Where there is a member of a family, like an orphaned grandson, or any other needy member of the family who does not inherit under the Islamic inheritance scheme, the testator may provide for him, as he has been given the power to dispose of up to one third of his property by making a will in his favour. But unless this is the objective, the changing of the provisions of a will is unlawful.

"Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will and brings about a fair settlement among the parties will not be sinful." opens with the exception to the warning of the verse before. The one who suspects an error or an injustice in the will is not blamed, if he brings about a fair settlement among the parties. The condition is the settlement, which is to be fair, and the person who makes it is acting to end the wrong. "Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful." The verse closes with the forgiveness and mercy of the Lord, which covers the one who acts to put right the will. The sentence is an exception within the warning, and it shows that the aim of the rule is justice. The verse is placed after the warning that the changers will bear the blame, so the reader sees the way in which the mercy of the Lord keeps the honest settlement open. The Mukhtaṣar states that whoever knows there is an error in the will from the testator, and brings about a settlement, is not blamed. The Tanwīr reads the one who fears injustice as one who knows that the testator may have erred, and it states that Allah forgives the deceased if he erred. The Maʿārif commentary takes the word khayr in the verse in several of its senses, and it states that the hadith on the will is relevant here. The Qushayrī commentary reads the one who recognizes a weakness as the person who gives counsel. The Tazkirul commentary states that a brotherly atmosphere is the aim of such settlements. The reader is asked to see the verse as the close of the passage on the will, in which fairness is served by a settlement and not by a change of terms.
